These only matter if you used to have [Mirage](/docs/beta/about-the-project/mirage), Floe's predecessor, installed.

Windows

macOS

Linux

-   Preferences: `C:\ProgramData\FrozenPlain\Mirage\Settings\mirage.json`
-   Preferences (alternative): `%APPDATA%\FrozenPlain\Mirage\mirage.json`
-   VST2: `C:\Program Files\VSTPlugins\mirage64.dll`
-   VST2 (alternative): `C:\Program Files\Steinberg\VSTPlugins\mirage64.dll`
-   VST2 (alternative): `C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST2\mirage64.dll`
-   VST2 (alternative): `C:\Program Files\Common Files\Steinberg\VST2\mirage64.dll`

---

# Folders

> Managing sample library and preset folders in Floe

Floe keeps your sample libraries and presets as ordinary files in ordinary folders. You choose which folders it looks in, so you can keep large libraries on an external drive, keep your own presets somewhere you back up, and organise everything with your usual file manager.

There are two separate kinds of folder: sample library folders and preset folders. Floe scans each one, including all its subfolders, and shows what it finds in the browsers. It also watches them, so anything you add, remove or change appears in Floe straight away, without a restart. Floe keeps no separate record of what's installed: whatever is in your folders is what Floe has.

You manage the folders on the _Folders_ tab of Preferences.

![The Folders tab of Floe's preferences](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/folders.9b45bf20f066bfe9.png)

Each kind of folder has its own list. The first folder in each list is Floe's default one, which is always scanned. Under each folder, Floe shows how many presets or sample libraries it contains.

-   **Add folder** — choose a folder for Floe to scan. Pick a top-level folder, such as "Floe Libraries", rather than each library inside it, since the subfolders are scanned too. You can select several folders at once.
-   **Open folder** — show the folder in your file manager.
-   **Stop scanning this folder** — remove a folder you've added from the list. Nothing is deleted from your computer; Floe simply stops looking there. The default folders can't be removed.

## Installing to your own folders

When you install a package, Floe puts its sample libraries and presets in the install folders chosen on the _Packages_ tab. They start as Floe's default folders on your main drive. To install somewhere else, such as an external drive, choose a different folder from the _Sample library install folder_ and _Preset install folder_ menus. Each menu lists the folders Floe already scans, plus _Add folder_ to add a new one and select it in a single step. See [Installing to a different drive](/docs/beta/installation/install-packages#installing-to-a-different-drive).

## Moving your libraries or presets

For now, moving is done using your file manager (Finder, File Explorer, etc.). Floe doesn't have a 'move' button.

1.  **Create the new folder** in your file manager. For example, "Floe Libraries" on your external drive.
2.  **Add it to Floe** with _Add folder_ on the _Folders_ tab. Be sure to use the right list: sample libraries and presets are separate.
3.  **Open the old folder** with its button.
4.  **Move everything across** in your file manager, usually by selecting it all and dragging it, or by cutting and pasting.

Floe notices the change and updates its browsers instantly. If anything is missing, restart your DAW. To have future packages install into the new folder too, choose it as the install folder on the _Packages_ tab.

## Telling libraries and presets apart

If you lose track of which files are which:

-   **Sample libraries** are folders, usually named like `Developer Name - Library Name`. They usually contain a `floe.lua` file and a `Samples` folder.
-   **Preset banks** are folders, usually named like `Library Name Factory Presets`. They usually contain category subfolders full of small `.floe-preset` files.

We recommend keeping libraries and presets in separate folders, but Floe copes if they're mixed: add the same folder to both lists.

## Why libraries and presets are separate

Most sample libraries come with a preset bank, so it's fair to wonder why they live apart. There are a few good reasons:

-   **They're edited differently.** Libraries are built by developers with programming tools and you rarely change them. Presets are made and changed by musicians all the time. Keeping them apart means you can save and reorganise presets freely without touching a library.
-   **They're different sizes.** A sample library can be large, with hundreds of audio files, so it often belongs on a big external drive. Presets are tiny, easy to back up and easy to share.

-   **A preset bank can use several libraries.** Its presets aren't tied to a single library, so they don't belong inside one.

See [How Presets Are Stored](/docs/beta/presets/preset-storage) for more about preset files, and [File Locations](/docs/beta/installation/file-locations) for where the default folders are.

---

# Install Packages

> How to install Floe packages containing sample libraries and presets

Sample libraries and presets come to you in _packages_. Download your package file, then present it to Floe via its _Install package_ button.

1.  **Download your package(s)** — files ending `.floe-pkg` or `.floe-pkg-enc`.
2.  **Open Floe** in your DAW. If you haven't installed it yet, see [Install Floe](/docs/beta/installation/download-and-install-floe).
3.  **Open Preferences** from the top panel, and choose the _Packages_ tab.
4.  **Click _Install package_** and select your package file. You can select several at once.

![The Packages tab of Floe's preferences](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/install-packages.732780b46497022b.png)

## Entering your license key

Some packages, often paid ones, are locked and need a license key. They install in the same way, but Floe first asks for the key to unlock them. These packages end in `.floe-pkg-enc` and need Floe version 2 or later. Everything happens offline, without an account or an internet connection.

There are two ways to give Floe your key:

-   **Load a license file** — if your purchase came with a `.floe-license` file, choose _Load license file_ and select it. One file can hold keys for several packages, so it unlocks everything you've selected in one go.
-   **Enter a key manually** — paste your key into the box, using _Paste_, then click _Activate_.

A license key is personal to you and contains your details. The summary at the end of the installation shows who the package is licensed to.

## When the installation finishes

The new libraries and presets are ready to use straight away, without restarting Floe or your DAW.

Floe shows a summary of what it installed, with a couple of optional extras:

-   **Send to Trash** — delete the package file. Floe doesn't need it once it's installed, though you might like to keep a copy as a backup.
-   **Load Preset** — load the preset bank's default preset. If Floe was blank when you installed, this preset is loaded for you instead.

Click _Done_ to close the summary.

## What is a package?

A package is simply how content is delivered to Floe. It usually holds one sample library plus a bank of factory presets for it, but it can hold any mix: just presets, several libraries, or both.

Floe doesn't keep track of packages; they're just the means of getting sample libraries and presets installed into your [folders](/docs/beta/installation/folders). To remove things, see [Uninstalling](/docs/beta/installation/uninstalling).

## Installing to a different drive

Floe installs into its default folders on your main drive unless you tell it otherwise. To install somewhere else, such as an external drive with more space:

1.  On the _Packages_ tab, open the _Sample library install folder_ menu.
2.  Choose _Add folder_ and pick or create the folder you want, such as "Floe Libraries" on your external drive. Floe adds it to the folders it scans and selects it for installing.
3.  Do the same with the _Preset install folder_ menu, if you want your presets somewhere else too.

Future packages install into the folders you've chosen. Libraries and presets you've already installed stay where they are, but Floe updates them in place when you install a newer version. To move them, see [Folders](/docs/beta/installation/folders).

## Updates and conflicts

Whenever a new version comes out, install it in the same way. Floe handles upgrades for you:

-   If you have an older version, Floe updates it where it is.
-   If you already have the same or a newer version, Floe skips it.
-   If you've changed the installed files yourself, Floe asks before touching them. You can skip that part to keep your changes, or overwrite it. For presets, you can also keep both.

Whenever Floe replaces something, the old version goes to your Trash or Recycle Bin, with a name ending in something like `(old-3KJ9)`. If you change your mind, restore it from there and remove that ending from its name.

## ZIP packages

Older packages (from Floe v1) are ZIP files (`.zip`). Floe still installs them. Don't extract the ZIP first: select the ZIP file itself with _Install package_.

On macOS, Safari extracts ZIP files after downloading them. To stop it, untick _Open "safe" files after downloading_ in the _General_ tab of Safari's settings.

## Installing by hand

You don't usually need to, but you can install a package without the _Install package_ button. This works for `.floe-pkg` and `.zip` packages, not ones that need a license key.

A `.floe-pkg` file is really a ZIP file with a different ending. Rename it to end in `.zip` instead (on macOS: right-click › _Get Info_ › _Name & Extension_; on Windows, first turn on _File name extensions_ in File Explorer's _View_ menu, then rename it), and extract it with your usual tools.

Then copy the contents of its `Libraries` folder into one of Floe's sample library folders, and the contents of its `Presets` folder into one of its preset folders. You'll find them on the _Folders_ tab of Preferences, and the button opens them. Floe picks up the new files straight away.

## Mirage libraries

If a package contains a library made for [Mirage](/docs/beta/about-the-project/mirage), Floe's predecessor, you may see an error saying _Mirage Compatibility - FrozenPlain_ isn't installed. To fix it, download the [Mirage Compatibility package](https://github.com/FrozenPlain/floe-mirage-compatibility/releases/download/v1.2/FrozenPlain.-.Mirage.Compatibility.Package.floe-pkg) and install it like any other package.

---

# Uninstalling

> Instructions for uninstalling Floe and removing libraries and presets

You can remove sample libraries, preset banks and Floe itself separately. To remove everything, work through the sections below in order. Libraries and presets are easiest to remove from inside Floe.

When Floe removes a library or preset bank, it sends it to your Trash or Recycle Bin rather than deleting it outright, so if you remove one by mistake, you can restore it from there.

You might be wondering why there's no mention of _packages_ on this page. Packages are just the means of installing content into Floe. Sample libraries and presets are what actually get installed, so they're what you uninstall.

## Uninstalling sample libraries

1.  Open the menu in the top panel and choose _Info_.
2.  On the _Libraries_ tab, click _Uninstall_ on the library you want to remove, and confirm.

![A library's card in Floe's Info panel, with the Uninstall button](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/uninstall-library.18c5ba53660143ab.png)

You can also right-click a library's name in the Instrument or IR browser and choose _Uninstall_.

## Uninstalling presets

1.  Open the preset browser by clicking the preset's name in the top panel.
2.  Right-click the preset bank in the right-hand panel and choose _Uninstall_, then confirm.

![The right-click menu of a preset bank in the preset browser](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/uninstall-preset-bank.15ae5974b3fe9596.png)

The same works for a single folder of presets. Repeat for each preset bank you want to remove.

## Uninstalling Floe

### Windows

Close your DAW, then uninstall Floe like any other program, from _Installed apps_ (or _Add or Remove Programs_) in Windows' settings, where it's listed as _Floe Audio Plugin_. See [Microsoft's guide](https://support.microsoft.com/en-gb/windows/uninstall-or-remove-apps-and-programs-in-windows-4b55f974-2cc6-2d2b-d092-5905080eaf98) if you need help.

This removes the Floe plugins, but not your libraries or presets. The uninstaller can also remove Mirage, Floe's predecessor.

### macOS and Linux

There's no uninstaller: delete Floe's files yourself. The plugin files are the important ones, but you can delete the rest of Floe's files too, if you want to be thorough. See [File Locations](/docs/beta/installation/file-locations) for where they all are.

---

# About Floe

> What Floe is and its key features

## Welcome to Floe!

Floe is an audio plugin for your digital audio workstation (DAW). It's a platform for performing, finding, and transforming sounds from compatible sample libraries. It hosts sample-based instruments (sampled pianos, synths, textures, and so on) and exposes an extensive set of parameters for venturing into sample-based synthesis. A comprehensive presets system with powerful browsers, macros, a random variation generator, and other features makes it a formidable engine for sample libraries.

![Floe's Perform page](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/floe-whole-gui-4.a40ff59a2509fcb3.png)

It focuses on ease of use and performance, designed to offer a curated experience for producing music rather than overwhelming complexity.

Floe is not designed for ad-hoc sampling — you can't currently import your own samples. Instead, it's an open platform for professional, curated, sample-library products. For those with programming experience, the means to make custom libraries is fully open.

Floe itself is free and open source. It works offline, with no accounts or logins.

## Key features

-   3 independent layers to blend and mix, even with Instruments from different libraries
-   12 effects in a reorderable rack
-   Powerful [granular synthesis](/docs/beta/usage/playback-tab#granular-synthesis)
-   Per-layer [arpeggiator](/docs/beta/usage/arp-tab)
-   Comprehensive [browsers](/docs/beta/usage/browsers) for finding the right sound or preset
-   [Random variations](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation) for spontaneous inspiration
-   [Macros](/docs/beta/usage/macros) that shape a preset with a single knob
-   Sound-design friendly: undo/redo, and a switch to compare your edits with the original preset
-   All the fundamentals: envelopes, filters, EQ, MIDI CC and sustain pedal support
-   Efficient: multiple instances of Floe share the sample libraries they've loaded, keeping memory use low
-   Resizable window
-   Totally free and open source: offline, no logins, no catches
-   [Free sample libraries](/packages) to get you started

---

# Loading Presets

> How to find, load and audition Floe presets

Presets are the quickest way into Floe's sounds. Each one is a complete, production-ready setup. Load one and it's ready to play in your track straight away.

The factory presets give you a whole palette of sounds to start from. Their names hint at the sound or how you might use it, and they're sorted into folders so you can narrow down to the kind of sound you need.

Presets are also how you keep sounds of your own. Save it as a preset and you can load it into any instance of Floe in the future. See [Saving Presets](/docs/beta/presets/saving-presets).

Loading a preset replaces all your settings, except for your [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls). You can always use the _Undo_ button in the top panel to undo a preset load.

## The preset box

The preset box in the top panel shows what's loaded and gives you quick ways to move between presets.

![Floe's top panel, with the preset box outlined](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/top-panel.6c17c53c76feceb5.png)

On the left is the name of the current preset, with a short description underneath. If the preset has changed since it was loaded, Floe shows _(modified)_ after the name. Click the name to open the preset browser.

The buttons on the right are:

-   **Previous/Next** — step to the previous or next preset.
-   **Random** — jump to a random preset.
-   **Save** — open the Save Preset panel. See [Saving Presets](/docs/beta/presets/saving-presets).
-   **Load from file** — load a preset file from anywhere on your computer, such as one someone has sent you. It doesn't need to be in one of Floe's preset folders.

Right-click the name for two more options. _Load Blank Preset_ resets every setting to its default and clears all the Instruments and IRs, ready to build a sound from scratch. _Open Containing Folder_ shows the current preset's file in your file manager.

## Finding presets

![The preset browser, open beneath the preset box](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/preset-browser.661d250ce632b3cd.png)

The preset browser is the place for browsing deliberately. Choose a folder or some tags in the dark panel on the right, then click presets on the left to hear them. The browser stays open, so you can play a few notes, click the next preset, and play again. Once you've loaded a preset, if you move your cursor outside of the browser it will close.

See [Browsers](/docs/beta/usage/browsers) for everything it can do: filtering, search, keyboard navigation and more.

For a quick audition without the browser, use the previous and next arrows, and . The large arrows on the _Perform_ page do the same. Both follow the filters you've set in the preset browser, so if you've chosen a particular folder or tag there, the arrows only step between presets that match. When you reach the end of the list, they wrap round to the start. Random follows the same filters, which makes it a handy way to dip into a chosen corner of your presets. For Floe's other ways to bring in an element of chance, see [Randomisation](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation).

## Default preset

The default preset is the one a new instance of Floe opens with, instead of a blank state.

There are two ways to set the default preset:

-   Right-click any preset in the [browser](/docs/beta/usage/browsers) and choose _Set as Default Preset_. The preset is then marked with a icon in the browser.
-   Or alternatively, load the preset, then open Preferences and, in the _Default Preset_ row on the _General_ tab, click _Use Current Preset_. Click the button to remove the default, so Floe opens blank again.

The default preset doesn't apply if you open a saved DAW project — Floe uses the sound saved in the project as usual.

After installing a preset bank a default preset will be set for you. You can always overwrite this using the options above. Once you set a custom default, installing further packages will not interfere with your choice.

---

# How Presets Are Stored

> Preset files, preset folders and preset banks

Each preset is a single small file ending in `.floe-preset`, kept in a folder on your computer. Because they're ordinary files, you can organise them with your usual file manager (Finder, File Explorer, etc.): rename them, move them into folders, or delete them. Floe watches its [preset folders](/docs/beta/installation/folders) and updates the preset browser as soon as anything changes.

The file name is the preset's name, so renaming the file renames the preset. The author, description and tags are stored inside the file: to change them, save over the preset in Floe. See [Saving Presets](/docs/beta/presets/saving-presets).

Presets are tiny, typically just a few kilobytes, so even large collections take up very little space.

## Sharing presets

You can simply share `.floe-preset` files. As long as the recipient has the same libraries installed, it works just the same. They can put it in one of their [preset folders](/docs/beta/installation/folders) so it appears in the preset browser, or do a one-off load with the load-from-file button.

## Preset banks

A preset bank is a folder of presets, including all its subfolders, that belongs together, such as a set of factory presets. Preset banks are the top level of organisation in the preset browser.

Presets in folders that aren't part of any bank might be grouped together as _Miscellaneous_.

Floe also recognises some older factory preset banks that don't have an info file.

---

# Saving Presets

> How to save your own Floe presets with a description and tags

You can save your own Floe presets ready to load into another project or another instance of Floe. It's worth doing whenever you've found something you'd hate to lose.

Click the save button in the [preset box](/docs/beta/presets/loading-presets#the-preset-box) to open the Save Preset panel. All of its fields are optional: you can click _Save_ straight away and just choose a name. Filling them in helps you find the sound again later, especially once you've saved lots of presets.

![Floe's Save Preset panel with the tags outlined](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/save-preset.feb3ad1cf1db22ab.png)

-   **Author** — who made the preset. The buttons beside it store your name, so you don't have to type it out every time: stores the current name, and fills in the stored name.
-   **Description** — a few words about the sound.
-   **Tags** — the outlined section, describing the sound so you can find it again with the preset browser's filters.

## Naming and saving

You name a preset by naming its file. When you click _Save_ or _Save As New_, your system's file dialog opens, and the file name you choose there becomes the preset's name. To rename a preset later, rename its file in your file manager (Finder, File Explorer, etc.). The files are portable. Copy/move them as you like.

The buttons at the bottom of the panel depend on where the current sound came from. _Cancel_ closes the panel without saving, and the others are:

-   **Save** — choose a file name and folder for a new preset. This is the only option after _Load Blank Preset_.
-   **Overwrite** — save over the preset file you loaded, keeping its name. It doesn't ask for confirmation, and _Undo_ won't bring back the old file, so only use it when you're sure.
-   **Save As New** — save a new preset, leaving the one you loaded untouched.

The first time you save, the file dialog opens in a `User` folder inside Floe's preset folder; after that it remembers where you last saved. Save inside one of Floe's [preset folders](/docs/beta/installation/folders) and the preset appears in the preset browser straight away.

The button at the top of the panel keeps it open, so you can step through presets and edit each one's author, description and tags as you go.

## Writing a description

When you load a preset, its description appears in two places on Floe's UI. As much as fits goes beneath the preset name in the top panel, and the rest continues on the _Perform_ page. To choose where it splits add a newline when you write the description: everything before the first line break goes in the top panel. If that line is too long to fit, Floe splits it where it runs out of room instead.

You can leave the description blank. When Floe loads a preset with no description, it generates one on the fly from what's in the preset and displays that instead, so even quick saves get something helpful.

## Choosing tags

Tags are grouped into categories such as sound source, sound type, mood and timbre. Choose the ones that describe the sound: they're what the preset browser's tag filters use.

Some tags turn grey once you've chosen a related one. That's a hint that the combination is unusual, such as a real instrument category on a synthesized sound, but you can still click them if they fit.

---

# Attribution

> Information about attribution requirements for sample libraries in Floe

Some sample libraries ask you to credit their creator when you share music made with them. If a library you're using requires attribution:

-   Floe shows you the exact attribution text.
-   Copy and paste the text wherever you share your music.
-   Your music is still yours: you can sell it, relicense it and so on. You just need to credit the creator of the sounds.

These points assume the license is the "Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International" license — a very common attribution-required license.

Disclaimer: whilst this page is based on research and understanding of the topic, it is not legal advice. You should check the license details yourself.

## About attribution-required licenses

A license tells you what you can and can't do with a sample library. Most developers choose a license that allows you to use the sounds in your music without having to credit them.

However, some developers choose an attribution-required license such as the widely-used [Creative Commons Attribution](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) license (also known as "CC BY").

This license allows you to use the sounds for free, even in commercial projects, as long as you credit the creator by including a bit of attribution text along with your music. For example, you might include the text in a caption on your website, in the album notes or in a credits roll (or any ["reasonable manner"](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode.en#s3a2)). The music that you create with sounds under this license is yours: you can sell it, stream it, relicense it or give it away; you are just required to credit the sound's creator.

For some people, giving attribution is a deal-breaker. But there are good reasons it might not be so bad:

-   Attributions support the creators of sounds, giving them recognition, traffic and potential customers.
-   Attributions can look professional and show a high level of care in your work.
-   Sharing where your sounds come from helps other musicians find great sounds too, raising the quality of music everywhere.

## How Floe helps

Floe makes attribution easy. When you load a sound from a library that requires it, a small red icon appears at the top of the window. Click it to see the exact text to copy and paste wherever you need it. Floe gathers the requirements from every instance of Floe you have open, so you only need to do this once.

![Attribution GUI](https://assets.floe.audio/website/attributions-gui.9ac958f1481aaf52.png)

---

# Glossary

> {/*

A few words have a specific meaning throughout this manual:

-   **[Package](/docs/beta/installation/install-packages#what-is-a-package)** — the file you download to install Floe content (`.floe-pkg` or `.floe-pkg-enc`). Packages may contain sample libraries, presets, or both.
-   **[Sample Library](/docs/beta/reference/sample-libraries)** — a collection of mapped, playable sounds along with images, tags, and other metadata. Sample libraries provide the Instruments and impulse responses that Floe loads.
-   **[Layer](/docs/beta/usage/layers)** — one of the three identical channels, which all play together. Each layer holds an Instrument and has its own playback, envelope, LFO and EQ controls.
-   **[Instrument](/docs/beta/reference/instruments)** — a playable sound source from a sample library, loaded into one of the layers. It might be a single recording or many samples mapped across the keyboard.
-   **[Impulse Response](/docs/beta/usage/effects#convolution-reverb)** — a recording from a sample library that gives the Convolution Reverb effect its character.
-   **[Preset](/docs/beta/presets/loading-presets)** — a saved sound: a snapshot of every parameter and option, along with a name, description and tags.

---

# Instruments

> Instruments are Floe's core building block

An Instrument is a playable sound source. It might be a single sample that loops, or many samples mapped across the keyboard, with velocity layers and round robins.

You load an Instrument into any of the three [layers](/docs/beta/usage/layers) with the [Instrument browser](/docs/beta/usage/browsers), which finds Instruments across all your installed sample libraries. A layer with no Instrument loaded shows _None_ in place of the name: click it to open the browser.

Instruments come from sample libraries, which are made with Floe's open developer tools.

---

# Legacy Parameters

> How Floe ensures backwards compatibility

When you open an older DAW project, some of Floe's controls might show a yellow badge and refuse to move. Don't worry: your sound is safe and sounds exactly as it did when you saved it.

What's happened is that a Floe update replaced some parameters with new versions. The old parameters still exist and work exactly as before, but they're hidden out of sight. While one of them is in charge, the matching control on the main UI is locked. That's what the badge means.

You have two options:

-   **Do nothing.** If you don't need to change the sound any further, leave it as it is. Floe is stable like this and sounds identical to when the project was saved.
-   **Update to the current parameters.** Do this if you want to keep shaping the sound: it unlocks the main UI and the new parameters. The update keeps the sound the same and is normally perfectly safe, but check for DAW automation first, as described [below](#updating-a-legacy-parameter).

## Why legacy parameters exist

Floe aims for perfect backwards compatibility: a preset or DAW project saved with any version of Floe loads up sounding exactly the same in every later version. To make that possible without the main interface filling up with outdated controls, Floe never deletes a parameter. When a parameter needs to change, a new one goes on the main UI and the old one moves out of sight as a "legacy" parameter that quietly keeps doing its old job.

## When does a parameter become legacy?

A parameter becomes legacy when it changes in a way that would otherwise alter how an existing project sounds. We keep this to a minimum. It can happen, though, when adding options to a menu, improving the response of a knob, or combining or simplifying controls.

In every case, the old parameter stays alive behind the scenes so your projects sound the same, and a new parameter appears on the main UI.

## Presets and DAW projects

When you load a preset, Floe usually updates any legacy values it finds by itself: it copies the equivalent value onto the new parameter and clears the legacy one. You won't see any legacy parameters, and the controls on the main UI work as normal.

When you load a DAW project, Floe can't do this automatically, because it has no way of knowing whether your DAW is automating a legacy parameter, and silently changing the target would break your automation. Instead, Floe keeps the legacy value, lets it take charge of the new parameter, and shows the yellow badge on the affected control. The _Legacy Parameters_ panel, in the menu at the top of Floe's window, lists every legacy parameter that's currently in charge.

## Locked controls

While a legacy parameter is in charge, the matching control on the main UI is greyed out and doesn't respond: moving it would do nothing, since the legacy value is what reaches the sound. Click the badge in its corner to open the _Legacy Parameters_ panel.

The control's position, and any display linked to it (such as filter curves, EQ displays or envelope shapes), shows the new parameter's own value, not the legacy value you're hearing. The sound is right, since the legacy value is the one being applied. Once you update, the display, the control and the sound all match up again.

## Updating a legacy parameter

Updating hands control from the legacy parameter to its replacement, copying across a value that sounds the same. The _Legacy Parameters_ panel has two ways to do this:

-   **Update all to current parameters** — updates every legacy parameter that's in charge at once.
-   **Update** — on each row, updates just that parameter.

Your project sounds exactly as it did before, and the control on the main UI works again.

If any DAW automation targets one of these parameters, remove or re-create that automation before updating. Floe decides whether a legacy parameter is in charge simply by checking whether it's at its default value, so as soon as the automation writes a different value, the legacy parameter takes charge again and the control locks.

The recommended order:

1.  Check your DAW for any automation lanes targeting the legacy parameter.
2.  If there is automation, delete it in your DAW. If you still want it, re-create it on the new parameter.
3.  Open the _Legacy Parameters_ panel and click _Update_ on the row, or _Update all to current parameters_.

If there's no DAW automation on a legacy parameter, you can skip step 2: updating is then completely safe.

---

# Parameters

> A list of all parameters in Floe

## Shorter parameter names

In your DAW, Floe's parameter names are long and descriptive, such as "Effect Distortion On". If your DAW shows them in a narrow space, you can switch to abbreviated names such as "Dist On": turn on _Abbreviate parameter names in DAW_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences. You might need to restart your DAW for the change to take effect.

## Parameter table

This table lists every one of Floe's parameters, for when you need to look up an ID or a detail. To learn how to use them, see the pages on [layers](/docs/beta/usage/layers), [effects](/docs/beta/usage/effects) and the rest of the Using Floe chapter.

| Module | Name | ID | Abbreviated Name | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Layer 1 | Volume | 160 | L1 Volume | The Layer Volume sets the level of this layer. The marks on the slider show the level of each sounding voice: its velocity, key range fade and any MPE volume expression. Tip: to change how velocity relates to volume, edit the velocity to volume curve on the CONFIG tab. |
| Layer 1 | Mute | 161 | L1 Mute | Mute silences this layer. Handy for hearing how the other layers sit together while you're designing a sound. A muted layer keeps running in the background exactly as if you could hear it, so when you unmute, the sound carries on seamlessly from wherever it has naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload the Instrument instead. If a layer is still audible after muting it, check whether it's also soloed: Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 1 | Solo | 162 | L1 Solo | Solo lets you hear this layer on its own. Any layer that isn't soloed goes quiet. Handy for focusing on one part of a sound while you're designing it. Silenced layers keep running in the background exactly as if you could hear them, so when you unsolo, they carry on seamlessly from wherever they have naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload their Instruments instead. If a layer has gone quiet unexpectedly, check whether another layer is soloed. And if a muted layer is still audible, that's because Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 1 | Pan | 163 | L1 Pan | Pan places this layer in the stereo field, anywhere from fully left to fully right. It uses a constant-power pan law (-3 dB at centre), so the layer stays at the same perceived loudness wherever you put it. Pan is applied after the Stereo control, so you can narrow a wide sound first and then place it as a single point. |
| Layer 1 | Detune Cents | 164 | L1 Detune Cents | Detune fine-tunes this layer's pitch in cents (100 cents is one semitone). This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. |
| Layer 1 | Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | 165 | L1 Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | Legacy layer pitch in semitones. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | Start | 167 | L1Lp Start | Set the loop start point, where the loop begins within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between here and the loop end. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | End | 168 | L1Lp End | Set the loop end point, where the loop finishes within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between the loop start and here. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | Crossfade Size | 169 | L1Lp Crossfade Size | Set the size of the loop crossfade, which blends audio across the loop point so the loop doesn't click. A small amount usually helps, especially for sustained or tonal sounds. Floe keeps the crossfade within the loop and the sample, so it shrinks automatically if you make the loop too small for it. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | Sample Start Offset | 171 | L1Lp Sample Start Offset | Change the starting point of the sample |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | Reverse On | 172 | L1Lp Reverse On | Play the Instrument's samples backwards, from the end to the start. It works in every play mode and whether looping is on or off. The waveform display flips to match, so playback always runs from left to right (unless in the reverse portion of a ping-pong loop). |
| Layer 1/Main/Volume Envelope | On | 173 | L1Vol On | Switch the volume envelope on or off. It's typically best left on. When it's off, every note plays its sample straight through to the end, however briefly you press the key. Handy for one-shot sounds that should always be heard in full. Looping is disabled while the envelope is off, since nothing would ever bring a looping note to an end. Careful: with the envelope off, notes can't be cut short, so voices pile up if you play quickly, which costs CPU. |
| Layer 1/Main/Volume Envelope | Attack | 174 | L1Vol Attack | Attack sets how long each note takes to fade in. A few milliseconds is enough to avoid clicks if you've moved the sample start point. |
| Layer 1/Main/Volume Envelope | Decay | 175 | L1Vol Decay | Decay sets how long the note takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 1/Main/Volume Envelope | Sustain | 176 | L1Vol Sustain | Sustain sets the level the note holds at while the key is down. At 0 dB, Decay has nothing to do. |
| Layer 1/Main/Volume Envelope | Release | 177 | L1Vol Release | Release sets how long the note takes to fade out after you lift the key. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | On | 178 | L1Filt On | Switch the filter on or off. It's a clean, digital-sounding state-variable filter (12 dB per octave). Every voice gets its own copy, so the filter envelope and the LFO (on the LFO tab) can sweep each note independently. Tip: for broader tone shaping, the EQ tab has a three-band equaliser. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Legacy Cutoff Frequency | 179 | L1Filt Legacy Cutoff Frequency | Legacy cutoff parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Legacy Resonance | 180 | L1Filt Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Legacy Type | 181 | L1Filt Legacy Type | Legacy filter type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Envelope Amount | 182 | L1Filt Envelope Amount | Envelope Amount sets how strongly the filter envelope (shown to the right) moves the cutoff on every note. At 0% the envelope does nothing. Turn it up and the cutoff follows the envelope's shape, rising and falling with it. Turn it down and the cutoff moves the opposite way, falling as the envelope rises. The envelope is centred on the Cutoff setting: the top half of the display pushes the cutoff above it, the bottom half pulls it below. A negative amount flips this. For example, with a low-pass filter, a long attack opens the sound up gradually at the start of each note. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Attack | 183 | L1Filt Attack | Attack sets how long the filter envelope takes to reach its peak. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Decay | 184 | L1Filt Decay | Decay sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Sustain | 185 | L1Filt Sustain | Sustain sets the level the filter envelope holds at while the key is down. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Release | 186 | L1Filt Release | Release sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall back after you lift the key. |
| Layer 1/LFO | On | 187 | L1Lfo On | Switch this layer's LFO on or off. Enable Floe's LFO (low frequency oscillator) for adding movement to a one of this layer's controls (such as the volume or filter cutoff). |
| Layer 1/LFO | Legacy Shape | 188 | L1Lfo Legacy Shape | Legacy LFO shape parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/LFO | Mode | 189 | L1Lfo Mode | Choose where the LFO starts when you play a new note. With Retrigger, every note starts the LFO from the beginning of its cycle. With Free, a new note joins in wherever this layer's sounding notes have reached, so every note modulates precisely together. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Amount | 190 | L1Lfo Amount | Amount sets how far the LFO moves its target. 0% is no movement at all and 100% is the full range for that target: silence to full level for Volume, a semitone either way for Pitch, and so on. Negative values flip the shape upside down, so a falling sawtooth becomes a rising one. For random Shapes this only makes a difference when Variation is set to one of the Identical options. The LFO display shows the shape at the current Amount. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Target (Legacy) | 191 | L1Lfo Target (Legacy) | Legacy LFO target parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | 192 | L1Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | Legacy LFO rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/LFO | Time (Hz) | 193 | L1Lfo Time (Hz) | Time sets how fast the LFO cycles, in Hz (cycles per second). Tip: for movement that stays in time with your track, switch Sync on and choose a note length instead. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Sync On | 194 | L1Lfo Sync On | Sync ties the LFO's speed to your DAW's tempo. When it's on, Time is chosen as a note length that follows the tempo; when it's off, Time is set freely in Hz. Both settings are remembered, so you can flick between them without losing either. |
| Layer 1/EQ | On | 195 | L1Eq On | Switch on this layer's three-band equaliser to shape its tone before it's mixed with the other layers. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Frequency | 196 | L1EqB1 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 1 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Resonance | 197 | L1EqB1 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Gain | 198 | L1EqB1 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Type | 199 | L1EqB1 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Frequency | 200 | L1EqB2 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 2 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Resonance | 201 | L1EqB2 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Gain | 202 | L1EqB2 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Type | 203 | L1EqB2 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Config | Legacy Velocity Mapping | 204 | L1 Legacy Velocity Mapping | Choose how MIDI velocity should affect the volume of this layer. There are 6 modes that can be selected for this parameter via the buttons on the GUI. By setting one layer to be quiet at high velocities and another layer to be quiet at low velocities you can create an instrument that sounds different based on how hard the notes are played. (0) Ignore velocity, always play full volume. (1) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at low velocity (2) Loudest at low velocity, quietist at high velocity (3) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at middle velocity and below (4) Loudest at middle velocity, quietist at both high and low velocities (5) Loudest at bottom velocity, quietist at middle velocity and above, |
| Layer 1/Config | Keytrack On | 205 | L1 Keytrack On | With Keytrack on, this layer follows the keyboard: higher keys play higher pitches. Switch it off and every key plays the sample at its recorded pitch, which might be what you want for drum hits, loops and sound effects that shouldn't be transposed. Some sample libraries may override this - marking individual samples as always or never keytracked. |
| Layer 1/Config | Legacy Monophonic On | 206 | L1 Legacy Monophonic On | Only allow one voice of each sound to play at a time |
| Layer 1/Config | MIDI Transpose On | 208 | L1 MIDI Transpose On | Transpose shifts this layer up or down in semitones by changing which samples get triggered, rather than by speeding the audio up or down. On a multi-sampled Instrument that keeps the character of the sound intact, so it's the better choice for large shifts. The key range isn't affected: you play the same keys as before, they just reach for different samples. Tip: the Pitch control at the top of the layer transposes by re-pitching the audio instead. That's the one to reach for on a single-sample Instrument, and Detune beside it covers amounts smaller than a semitone. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Loop | Loop Mode | 209 | L1Lp Loop Mode | Select the Loop Mode for this layer. Floe can loop a portion of the sound for as long as you hold a note, so even a short sample can sustain indefinitely. Some Instruments come with loop points built in, while others let you set your own on the waveform. You can also turn looping off. There's 2 modes: 'standard' wrap-around loops jump from the loop end back to the start; 'ping-pong' loops bounce back and forth, alternating playback direction. The options that are available depend on the Instrument: library authors can provide built-in loops, allow or disallow custom loops, or require that certain sounds always loop. |
| Layer 1/Config | Key Range Low | 210 | L1 Key Range Low | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 1/Config | Key Range High | 211 | L1 Key Range High | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 1/Config | Key Range Low Fade | 212 | L1 Key Range Low Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 1/Config | Key Range High Fade | 213 | L1 Key Range High Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 1/Config | Pitch Bend Range | 214 | L1 Pitch Bend Range | Pitch Bend Range sets how far the pitch wheel bends this layer, in semitones. Each layer has its own, so for example, a lead can bend a whole tone while the pad underneath can be set to zero to ignore the wheel entirely. Bending re-pitches the audio by speeding it up or slowing it down, so large bends will noticeably change the character of the sound. With MPE enabled, this governs the wheel on the master channel; the per-note bend of each individual note follows the range the controller asks for. |
| Layer 1/Config | Monophonic Mode | 215 | L1 Monophonic Mode | Monophonic decides what happens when notes on this layer overlap. Left off, the layer is polyphonic and every note you play gets a voice of its own; the other two modes hold it to one note at a time, in different ways. It's set per layer, so a monophonic lead can sit on top of a polyphonic pad in the same preset. The arpeggiator handles its own notes, so this has no effect while the arpeggiator is running on this layer. |
| Layer 1/Playback | Play Mode | 216 | L1 Play Mode | Select the Play Mode for this layer: the engine it uses to play its Instrument. Standard Playback plays each sample straight through: the playhead moves steadily from start to end, with options for looping and reversing along the way. The granular modes instead rebuild the sound from a stream of tiny snippets called grains. In Granular Playback, the point grains are drawn from moves through the sample at a rate you set with Speed, giving a time-stretch-like effect. In Granular Fixed, you place that point yourself with Position, letting you freeze on one part of the sample and explore its texture. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Length | 217 | L1Grn Length | Length sets how long each grain lasts, from a few milliseconds up to a second. Short grains chop the sound into a fine, buzzy texture that keeps little of the original's shape. Long grains preserve much more of the sample's natural character. Density and Smooth are both measured relative to Length, so changing it here changes how they feel too. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Speed | 218 | L1Grn Speed | Speed sets how fast the playhead travels through the sample in Granular Playback mode. Grains are drawn from wherever the playhead is. 100% is the sample's original speed. Turn it down to slow the sound to a crawl or stop it altogether, or up to race through at up to eight times normal speed. The playhead still respects the sample start, looping and Reverse settings. In Granular Fixed, this knob is replaced by Position. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Position | 219 | L1Grn Position | Position chooses where in the sample grains are drawn from, shown as the highlighted region on the waveform. Grains come from here for as long as you hold the note, so you can freeze on one moment of the sound and sustain it indefinitely. Tip: you can create movement with this parameter by setting the LFO's target to Grain Position, or by assigning this knob to a macro. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Density | 220 | L1Grn Density | Density sets how many grains overlap at once, relative to their Length. At 0%, each grain starts as the previous one ends, so they follow on one after another. Turning it up starts new grains sooner, stacking more and more of them on top of each other. Low values give an open texture where individual grains can be picked out. High values pile up so many grains that they smear into a thick, continuous wash. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Spread | 221 | L1Grn Spread | Spread widens the area of the sample that grains can start from. Each new grain begins somewhere between the playhead and a point up to this far past it, measured as a percentage of the whole sample. Small values keep every grain close to the playhead for a focused, precise sound. Large values scatter grains across a wide stretch of the sample. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Smooth | 222 | L1Grn Smooth | Smooth shapes the envelope of each grain: how gently it fades in and out, relative to its Length. At 0% grains start and stop abruptly, giving a hard, percussive edge. At 100% the fade-in and fade-out meet in the middle, so neighbouring grains blend into each other for a seamless texture. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Pan | 223 | L1Grn Pan | Pan randomises where each grain sits in the stereo field. Every new grain is given its own position, picked at random within the range you set here. At 0% every grain plays dead centre. At 100% grains can land anywhere from fully left to fully right, spreading the cloud from one side to the other. A quick way to create an interestingly wide stereo image. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Detune | 224 | L1Grn Detune | Detune randomises the pitch of each grain. Every new grain is nudged sharp or flat by a random amount within the range you set here. At 0% all grains play in tune. At 100% each grain can be up to a semitone sharp or flat. Small amounts thicken the sound like a chorus; larger amounts get progressively more smeared and out of tune. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Direction | 225 | L1Grn Direction | Direction gives each grain a chance of playing the opposite way to the main playhead. At 0% every grain follows the playhead's direction. At 100% each grain is equally likely to play forwards or backwards. In between, you can dial in a blend of the two for meandering, less predictable tones. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Harmony | 226 | L1Grn Harmony | Harmony gives each grain a chance of playing at a musical interval above or below the note you played, so a single note can bloom into a chord or a shimmering octave. At 0% every grain plays at the root. Turning it up shifts more of the grains, until at 100% every grain picks at random from the root and the intervals you've chosen. Choose which intervals are allowed with the Intervals menu next to this knob: pick a preset such as Octaves or Major Triad, or toggle individual semitones yourself. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Legacy Shape V2 | 227 | L1Lfo Legacy Shape V2 | Legacy LFO shape parameter (v2). Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/LFO | Target | 228 | L1Lfo Target | Choose the Target: what the LFO modulates. The modulation is applied relative to the target's current knob/slider. For example, when Volume is chosen, the movement will occur around wherever the layer's volume slider is currently set. Hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Resonance | 229 | L1Filt Resonance | Resonance emphasises the frequencies at the cutoff. At 0% the slope is smooth and rounded; at 100% it peaks by around 20 dB, without ever self-oscillating. For the band-pass, notch and band-shelving types it also narrows the band, and for Peak it sets the size of the boost. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Note Order | 230 | L1Arp Note Order | Order sets how the notes you're holding are shared out across the steps: climbing, falling, bouncing between the two, picked at random, or one of the less common shapes. Chord is the odd one out — it plays every held note together on each step, which is ideal for rhythmic stabs and percussion. Not available in Fixed Notes mode. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Trigger | 231 | L1Arp Trigger | Trigger decides what a new note does to a pattern that's already running. Free lets it carry on, so you can change chord underneath without breaking the groove. Retrigger restarts it from step 1 every time you press a note, which keeps the pattern locked to your playing. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Rate (Legacy) | 232 | L1Arp Rate (Legacy) | Legacy arpeggiator rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/Arp | Length | 233 | L1Arp Length | Length sets how many steps the pattern runs through before it loops back to the start. Steps beyond the length are hidden from the sequencer but keep their settings, so you can shorten a pattern and lengthen it again without losing anything. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Arpeggiator Mode | 234 | L1Arp Arpeggiator Mode | Choose where the steps get their notes from. Played Notes arpeggiates whatever you're holding, giving each step one of those notes in the order set by Order. Fixed Notes ignores what you play and runs a sequence of notes you've set yourself, either by dragging each step's note or by capturing a performance with the Record button. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Humanise | 235 | L1Arp Humanise | Humanise loosens the pattern up by nudging each step's timing and velocity by a random amount. A few percent takes the machine-like edge off; higher settings give a much looser, hand-played feel, which suits percussion especially well. Steps are only ever pushed later, never earlier, and never by more than a fifth of a step. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Auto Rate | 236 | L1Arp Auto Rate | Auto Rate lets Floe pick the step rate so a sliced Instrument plays close to the speed it was recorded at, rather than leaving silent gaps between slices when your host tempo is a long way from the loop's own. While it's on, the rate Floe has chosen is shown in place of the Rate menu. The multiplier shifts that choice: 2x for double speed, 0.5x for half, with Dotted and Triplet variants for a different feel. Because the choice has to land on a tempo-synced division it moves in jumps as the tempo changes, and every layer using Auto Rate jumps at the same points so they stay in the same rhythmic relationship. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Polyrate | 237 | L1Arp Polyrate | Polyrate gives each octave of the notes you're holding its own speed, so a single chord can produce several interleaving rhythms at once. The octave starting at middle C plays at the Rate you've set, and the octaves above and below scale from there by the ratio you choose. Tip: hold two notes an octave apart to hear the effect at its clearest. |
| Layer 1/Arp | One Shot | 238 | L1Arp One Shot | With One Shot on, the pattern plays through once and stops rather than looping for as long as you hold the notes. It's handy for fills and one-off flourishes, or for letting a sliced loop play through exactly once. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Resonance | 239 | L1EqB1 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Resonance | 240 | L1EqB2 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Arpeggiator | 241 | L1Arp Arpeggiator | Switch on the arpeggiator to turn the notes you hold into a rhythmic pattern locked to your host's tempo. Each step retriggers this layer's Instrument exactly as if you'd played the note yourself, so the envelopes, filter, LFOs and effects all respond as normal. Every layer has its own arpeggiator, so you can run different patterns side by side. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Shape | 242 | L1Lfo Shape | Choose the Shape of the LFO. Alongside the classics there are a few more interesting options, such as random and plucky shapes. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Type | 244 | L1EqB1 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Type | 245 | L1EqB2 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 3 | Legacy Frequency | 246 | L1EqB3 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 3 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 3 | Resonance | 247 | L1EqB3 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 3 | Gain | 248 | L1EqB3 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 3 | Type | 249 | L1EqB3 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Cutoff Frequency | 250 | L1Filt Cutoff Frequency | Cutoff Frequency sets where the filter takes effect. The filter envelope and the LFO sweep the cutoff around this value, so it's the centre of any modulation rather than the starting point. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 1 | Frequency | 251 | L1EqB1 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 2 | Frequency | 252 | L1EqB2 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 1/EQ/Band 3 | Frequency | 253 | L1EqB3 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 1/Main/Filter | Type | 254 | L1Filt Type | Select the filter type. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. |
| Layer 1 | Stereo Width | 255 | L1 Stereo Width | Stereo narrows or widens this layer's stereo image. Negative values pull it toward mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves the sound as recorded. It works by splitting the sound into mid (what both channels share) and side (what differs between them), then rebalancing the two with a constant-power crossfade. At -100% only the mid remains; at +100% only the side, so anything dead centre disappears. Mono sounds have no side, so pushing to +100% silences them. |
| Layer 1/Config | MPE Press Target | 256 | L1 MPE Press Target | Press is the channel pressure, or aftertouch, that an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows how hard you're pushing into the key once it's sounding. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Press rests at nothing and climbs from there, so it only ever adds to the destination you point it at. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before press does anything. |
| Layer 1/Config | MPE Press Amount | 257 | L1 MPE Press Amount | Amount sets how far press moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before press reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a lighter touch. |
| Layer 1/Config | MPE Slide Target | 258 | L1 MPE Slide Target | Slide is CC74, which an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows where your finger sits along the front-to-back axis of the key. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Slide rests in the middle, so it pushes the destination either side of where you've set it. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before slide does anything. |
| Layer 1/Config | MPE Slide Amount | 259 | L1 MPE Slide Amount | Amount sets how far slide moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before slide reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a smaller movement. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) | 260 | L1Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) | Time sets how long one LFO cycle lasts, as a note length at your DAW's tempo. 1/4 is a quarter note; a D on the end is dotted (one and a half times as long) and a T is triplet (two thirds as long). The LFO follows tempo changes, but it isn't locked to the bar: each cycle starts from the note, as set by Mode. |
| Layer 1/Arp | Rate | 261 | L1Arp Rate | Rate sets how long each step lasts, synced to your host's tempo. Together with Length it decides how long the whole pattern takes to come round — eight steps at 1/8 fills one bar of 4/4. The T and D suffixes are triplet and dotted divisions, useful for swung or lopsided patterns. |
| Layer 1 | Pitch Semitones | 262 | L1 Pitch Semitones | Pitch moves this layer up or down in semitones. This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. Tip: for a multisampled Instrument, you might get better results from Transpose on the CONFIG tab. It changes which samples are played rather than processing them, which can sound more natural. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Variation | 263 | L1Grn Variation | Variation decides whether each note scatters its grains differently or plays back the exact same grains every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern of grains and save it with the preset. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Seed | 264 | L1Grn Seed | Seed picks which pattern of grains repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the grains you choose are the grains everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Variation | 265 | L1Lfo Variation | Variation decides whether the random shapes move differently on each note or play back the exact same pattern every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern and save it with the preset. In Free mode, a note that joins already-sounding notes follows their pattern. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 1/LFO | Seed | 266 | L1Lfo Seed | Seed picks which random pattern repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the movement you choose is the movement everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 1/Playback/Granular | Share Grains | 267 | L1Grn Share Grains | Share Grains keeps the number of grains the same whether you play one note or a chord, so the sound keeps the same density however many notes you hold. Each grain plays from one of the held notes, weaving the chord's pitches together. At low Density you can hear the grains hop between the notes of the chord. |
| Layer 2 | Volume | 320 | L2 Volume | The Layer Volume sets the level of this layer. The marks on the slider show the level of each sounding voice: its velocity, key range fade and any MPE volume expression. Tip: to change how velocity relates to volume, edit the velocity to volume curve on the CONFIG tab. |
| Layer 2 | Mute | 321 | L2 Mute | Mute silences this layer. Handy for hearing how the other layers sit together while you're designing a sound. A muted layer keeps running in the background exactly as if you could hear it, so when you unmute, the sound carries on seamlessly from wherever it has naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload the Instrument instead. If a layer is still audible after muting it, check whether it's also soloed: Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 2 | Solo | 322 | L2 Solo | Solo lets you hear this layer on its own. Any layer that isn't soloed goes quiet. Handy for focusing on one part of a sound while you're designing it. Silenced layers keep running in the background exactly as if you could hear them, so when you unsolo, they carry on seamlessly from wherever they have naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload their Instruments instead. If a layer has gone quiet unexpectedly, check whether another layer is soloed. And if a muted layer is still audible, that's because Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 2 | Pan | 323 | L2 Pan | Pan places this layer in the stereo field, anywhere from fully left to fully right. It uses a constant-power pan law (-3 dB at centre), so the layer stays at the same perceived loudness wherever you put it. Pan is applied after the Stereo control, so you can narrow a wide sound first and then place it as a single point. |
| Layer 2 | Detune Cents | 324 | L2 Detune Cents | Detune fine-tunes this layer's pitch in cents (100 cents is one semitone). This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. |
| Layer 2 | Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | 325 | L2 Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | Legacy layer pitch in semitones. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | Start | 327 | L2Lp Start | Set the loop start point, where the loop begins within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between here and the loop end. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | End | 328 | L2Lp End | Set the loop end point, where the loop finishes within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between the loop start and here. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | Crossfade Size | 329 | L2Lp Crossfade Size | Set the size of the loop crossfade, which blends audio across the loop point so the loop doesn't click. A small amount usually helps, especially for sustained or tonal sounds. Floe keeps the crossfade within the loop and the sample, so it shrinks automatically if you make the loop too small for it. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | Sample Start Offset | 331 | L2Lp Sample Start Offset | Change the starting point of the sample |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | Reverse On | 332 | L2Lp Reverse On | Play the Instrument's samples backwards, from the end to the start. It works in every play mode and whether looping is on or off. The waveform display flips to match, so playback always runs from left to right (unless in the reverse portion of a ping-pong loop). |
| Layer 2/Main/Volume Envelope | On | 333 | L2Vol On | Switch the volume envelope on or off. It's typically best left on. When it's off, every note plays its sample straight through to the end, however briefly you press the key. Handy for one-shot sounds that should always be heard in full. Looping is disabled while the envelope is off, since nothing would ever bring a looping note to an end. Careful: with the envelope off, notes can't be cut short, so voices pile up if you play quickly, which costs CPU. |
| Layer 2/Main/Volume Envelope | Attack | 334 | L2Vol Attack | Attack sets how long each note takes to fade in. A few milliseconds is enough to avoid clicks if you've moved the sample start point. |
| Layer 2/Main/Volume Envelope | Decay | 335 | L2Vol Decay | Decay sets how long the note takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 2/Main/Volume Envelope | Sustain | 336 | L2Vol Sustain | Sustain sets the level the note holds at while the key is down. At 0 dB, Decay has nothing to do. |
| Layer 2/Main/Volume Envelope | Release | 337 | L2Vol Release | Release sets how long the note takes to fade out after you lift the key. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | On | 338 | L2Filt On | Switch the filter on or off. It's a clean, digital-sounding state-variable filter (12 dB per octave). Every voice gets its own copy, so the filter envelope and the LFO (on the LFO tab) can sweep each note independently. Tip: for broader tone shaping, the EQ tab has a three-band equaliser. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Legacy Cutoff Frequency | 339 | L2Filt Legacy Cutoff Frequency | Legacy cutoff parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Legacy Resonance | 340 | L2Filt Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Legacy Type | 341 | L2Filt Legacy Type | Legacy filter type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Envelope Amount | 342 | L2Filt Envelope Amount | Envelope Amount sets how strongly the filter envelope (shown to the right) moves the cutoff on every note. At 0% the envelope does nothing. Turn it up and the cutoff follows the envelope's shape, rising and falling with it. Turn it down and the cutoff moves the opposite way, falling as the envelope rises. The envelope is centred on the Cutoff setting: the top half of the display pushes the cutoff above it, the bottom half pulls it below. A negative amount flips this. For example, with a low-pass filter, a long attack opens the sound up gradually at the start of each note. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Attack | 343 | L2Filt Attack | Attack sets how long the filter envelope takes to reach its peak. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Decay | 344 | L2Filt Decay | Decay sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Sustain | 345 | L2Filt Sustain | Sustain sets the level the filter envelope holds at while the key is down. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Release | 346 | L2Filt Release | Release sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall back after you lift the key. |
| Layer 2/LFO | On | 347 | L2Lfo On | Switch this layer's LFO on or off. Enable Floe's LFO (low frequency oscillator) for adding movement to a one of this layer's controls (such as the volume or filter cutoff). |
| Layer 2/LFO | Legacy Shape | 348 | L2Lfo Legacy Shape | Legacy LFO shape parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/LFO | Mode | 349 | L2Lfo Mode | Choose where the LFO starts when you play a new note. With Retrigger, every note starts the LFO from the beginning of its cycle. With Free, a new note joins in wherever this layer's sounding notes have reached, so every note modulates precisely together. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Amount | 350 | L2Lfo Amount | Amount sets how far the LFO moves its target. 0% is no movement at all and 100% is the full range for that target: silence to full level for Volume, a semitone either way for Pitch, and so on. Negative values flip the shape upside down, so a falling sawtooth becomes a rising one. For random Shapes this only makes a difference when Variation is set to one of the Identical options. The LFO display shows the shape at the current Amount. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Target (Legacy) | 351 | L2Lfo Target (Legacy) | Legacy LFO target parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | 352 | L2Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | Legacy LFO rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/LFO | Time (Hz) | 353 | L2Lfo Time (Hz) | Time sets how fast the LFO cycles, in Hz (cycles per second). Tip: for movement that stays in time with your track, switch Sync on and choose a note length instead. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Sync On | 354 | L2Lfo Sync On | Sync ties the LFO's speed to your DAW's tempo. When it's on, Time is chosen as a note length that follows the tempo; when it's off, Time is set freely in Hz. Both settings are remembered, so you can flick between them without losing either. |
| Layer 2/EQ | On | 355 | L2Eq On | Switch on this layer's three-band equaliser to shape its tone before it's mixed with the other layers. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Frequency | 356 | L2EqB1 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 1 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Resonance | 357 | L2EqB1 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Gain | 358 | L2EqB1 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Type | 359 | L2EqB1 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Frequency | 360 | L2EqB2 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 2 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Resonance | 361 | L2EqB2 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Gain | 362 | L2EqB2 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Type | 363 | L2EqB2 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Config | Legacy Velocity Mapping | 364 | L2 Legacy Velocity Mapping | Choose how MIDI velocity should affect the volume of this layer. There are 6 modes that can be selected for this parameter via the buttons on the GUI. By setting one layer to be quiet at high velocities and another layer to be quiet at low velocities you can create an instrument that sounds different based on how hard the notes are played. (0) Ignore velocity, always play full volume. (1) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at low velocity (2) Loudest at low velocity, quietist at high velocity (3) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at middle velocity and below (4) Loudest at middle velocity, quietist at both high and low velocities (5) Loudest at bottom velocity, quietist at middle velocity and above, |
| Layer 2/Config | Keytrack On | 365 | L2 Keytrack On | With Keytrack on, this layer follows the keyboard: higher keys play higher pitches. Switch it off and every key plays the sample at its recorded pitch, which might be what you want for drum hits, loops and sound effects that shouldn't be transposed. Some sample libraries may override this - marking individual samples as always or never keytracked. |
| Layer 2/Config | Legacy Monophonic On | 366 | L2 Legacy Monophonic On | Only allow one voice of each sound to play at a time |
| Layer 2/Config | MIDI Transpose On | 368 | L2 MIDI Transpose On | Transpose shifts this layer up or down in semitones by changing which samples get triggered, rather than by speeding the audio up or down. On a multi-sampled Instrument that keeps the character of the sound intact, so it's the better choice for large shifts. The key range isn't affected: you play the same keys as before, they just reach for different samples. Tip: the Pitch control at the top of the layer transposes by re-pitching the audio instead. That's the one to reach for on a single-sample Instrument, and Detune beside it covers amounts smaller than a semitone. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Loop | Loop Mode | 369 | L2Lp Loop Mode | Select the Loop Mode for this layer. Floe can loop a portion of the sound for as long as you hold a note, so even a short sample can sustain indefinitely. Some Instruments come with loop points built in, while others let you set your own on the waveform. You can also turn looping off.
