There's 2 modes: 'standard' wrap-around loops jump from the loop end back to the start; 'ping-pong' loops bounce back and forth, alternating playback direction. The options that are available depend on the Instrument: library authors can provide built-in loops, allow or disallow custom loops, or require that certain sounds always loop. |
| Layer 2/Config | Key Range Low | 370 | L2 Key Range Low | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 2/Config | Key Range High | 371 | L2 Key Range High | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 2/Config | Key Range Low Fade | 372 | L2 Key Range Low Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 2/Config | Key Range High Fade | 373 | L2 Key Range High Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 2/Config | Pitch Bend Range | 374 | L2 Pitch Bend Range | Pitch Bend Range sets how far the pitch wheel bends this layer, in semitones. Each layer has its own, so for example, a lead can bend a whole tone while the pad underneath can be set to zero to ignore the wheel entirely. Bending re-pitches the audio by speeding it up or slowing it down, so large bends will noticeably change the character of the sound. With MPE enabled, this governs the wheel on the master channel; the per-note bend of each individual note follows the range the controller asks for. |
| Layer 2/Config | Monophonic Mode | 375 | L2 Monophonic Mode | Monophonic decides what happens when notes on this layer overlap. Left off, the layer is polyphonic and every note you play gets a voice of its own; the other two modes hold it to one note at a time, in different ways. It's set per layer, so a monophonic lead can sit on top of a polyphonic pad in the same preset. The arpeggiator handles its own notes, so this has no effect while the arpeggiator is running on this layer. |
| Layer 2/Playback | Play Mode | 376 | L2 Play Mode | Select the Play Mode for this layer: the engine it uses to play its Instrument. Standard Playback plays each sample straight through: the playhead moves steadily from start to end, with options for looping and reversing along the way. The granular modes instead rebuild the sound from a stream of tiny snippets called grains. In Granular Playback, the point grains are drawn from moves through the sample at a rate you set with Speed, giving a time-stretch-like effect. In Granular Fixed, you place that point yourself with Position, letting you freeze on one part of the sample and explore its texture. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Length | 377 | L2Grn Length | Length sets how long each grain lasts, from a few milliseconds up to a second. Short grains chop the sound into a fine, buzzy texture that keeps little of the original's shape. Long grains preserve much more of the sample's natural character. Density and Smooth are both measured relative to Length, so changing it here changes how they feel too. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Speed | 378 | L2Grn Speed | Speed sets how fast the playhead travels through the sample in Granular Playback mode. Grains are drawn from wherever the playhead is. 100% is the sample's original speed. Turn it down to slow the sound to a crawl or stop it altogether, or up to race through at up to eight times normal speed. The playhead still respects the sample start, looping and Reverse settings. In Granular Fixed, this knob is replaced by Position. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Position | 379 | L2Grn Position | Position chooses where in the sample grains are drawn from, shown as the highlighted region on the waveform. Grains come from here for as long as you hold the note, so you can freeze on one moment of the sound and sustain it indefinitely. Tip: you can create movement with this parameter by setting the LFO's target to Grain Position, or by assigning this knob to a macro. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Density | 380 | L2Grn Density | Density sets how many grains overlap at once, relative to their Length. At 0%, each grain starts as the previous one ends, so they follow on one after another. Turning it up starts new grains sooner, stacking more and more of them on top of each other. Low values give an open texture where individual grains can be picked out. High values pile up so many grains that they smear into a thick, continuous wash. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Spread | 381 | L2Grn Spread | Spread widens the area of the sample that grains can start from. Each new grain begins somewhere between the playhead and a point up to this far past it, measured as a percentage of the whole sample. Small values keep every grain close to the playhead for a focused, precise sound. Large values scatter grains across a wide stretch of the sample. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Smooth | 382 | L2Grn Smooth | Smooth shapes the envelope of each grain: how gently it fades in and out, relative to its Length. At 0% grains start and stop abruptly, giving a hard, percussive edge. At 100% the fade-in and fade-out meet in the middle, so neighbouring grains blend into each other for a seamless texture. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Pan | 383 | L2Grn Pan | Pan randomises where each grain sits in the stereo field. Every new grain is given its own position, picked at random within the range you set here. At 0% every grain plays dead centre. At 100% grains can land anywhere from fully left to fully right, spreading the cloud from one side to the other. A quick way to create an interestingly wide stereo image. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Detune | 384 | L2Grn Detune | Detune randomises the pitch of each grain. Every new grain is nudged sharp or flat by a random amount within the range you set here. At 0% all grains play in tune. At 100% each grain can be up to a semitone sharp or flat. Small amounts thicken the sound like a chorus; larger amounts get progressively more smeared and out of tune. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Direction | 385 | L2Grn Direction | Direction gives each grain a chance of playing the opposite way to the main playhead. At 0% every grain follows the playhead's direction. At 100% each grain is equally likely to play forwards or backwards. In between, you can dial in a blend of the two for meandering, less predictable tones. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Harmony | 386 | L2Grn Harmony | Harmony gives each grain a chance of playing at a musical interval above or below the note you played, so a single note can bloom into a chord or a shimmering octave. At 0% every grain plays at the root. Turning it up shifts more of the grains, until at 100% every grain picks at random from the root and the intervals you've chosen. Choose which intervals are allowed with the Intervals menu next to this knob: pick a preset such as Octaves or Major Triad, or toggle individual semitones yourself. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Legacy Shape V2 | 387 | L2Lfo Legacy Shape V2 | Legacy LFO shape parameter (v2). Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/LFO | Target | 388 | L2Lfo Target | Choose the Target: what the LFO modulates. The modulation is applied relative to the target's current knob/slider. For example, when Volume is chosen, the movement will occur around wherever the layer's volume slider is currently set. Hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Resonance | 389 | L2Filt Resonance | Resonance emphasises the frequencies at the cutoff. At 0% the slope is smooth and rounded; at 100% it peaks by around 20 dB, without ever self-oscillating. For the band-pass, notch and band-shelving types it also narrows the band, and for Peak it sets the size of the boost. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Note Order | 390 | L2Arp Note Order | Order sets how the notes you're holding are shared out across the steps: climbing, falling, bouncing between the two, picked at random, or one of the less common shapes. Chord is the odd one out — it plays every held note together on each step, which is ideal for rhythmic stabs and percussion. Not available in Fixed Notes mode. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Trigger | 391 | L2Arp Trigger | Trigger decides what a new note does to a pattern that's already running. Free lets it carry on, so you can change chord underneath without breaking the groove. Retrigger restarts it from step 1 every time you press a note, which keeps the pattern locked to your playing. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Rate (Legacy) | 392 | L2Arp Rate (Legacy) | Legacy arpeggiator rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/Arp | Length | 393 | L2Arp Length | Length sets how many steps the pattern runs through before it loops back to the start. Steps beyond the length are hidden from the sequencer but keep their settings, so you can shorten a pattern and lengthen it again without losing anything. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Arpeggiator Mode | 394 | L2Arp Arpeggiator Mode | Choose where the steps get their notes from. Played Notes arpeggiates whatever you're holding, giving each step one of those notes in the order set by Order. Fixed Notes ignores what you play and runs a sequence of notes you've set yourself, either by dragging each step's note or by capturing a performance with the Record button. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Humanise | 395 | L2Arp Humanise | Humanise loosens the pattern up by nudging each step's timing and velocity by a random amount. A few percent takes the machine-like edge off; higher settings give a much looser, hand-played feel, which suits percussion especially well. Steps are only ever pushed later, never earlier, and never by more than a fifth of a step. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Auto Rate | 396 | L2Arp Auto Rate | Auto Rate lets Floe pick the step rate so a sliced Instrument plays close to the speed it was recorded at, rather than leaving silent gaps between slices when your host tempo is a long way from the loop's own. While it's on, the rate Floe has chosen is shown in place of the Rate menu. The multiplier shifts that choice: 2x for double speed, 0.5x for half, with Dotted and Triplet variants for a different feel. Because the choice has to land on a tempo-synced division it moves in jumps as the tempo changes, and every layer using Auto Rate jumps at the same points so they stay in the same rhythmic relationship. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Polyrate | 397 | L2Arp Polyrate | Polyrate gives each octave of the notes you're holding its own speed, so a single chord can produce several interleaving rhythms at once. The octave starting at middle C plays at the Rate you've set, and the octaves above and below scale from there by the ratio you choose. Tip: hold two notes an octave apart to hear the effect at its clearest. |
| Layer 2/Arp | One Shot | 398 | L2Arp One Shot | With One Shot on, the pattern plays through once and stops rather than looping for as long as you hold the notes. It's handy for fills and one-off flourishes, or for letting a sliced loop play through exactly once. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Resonance | 399 | L2EqB1 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Resonance | 400 | L2EqB2 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Arpeggiator | 401 | L2Arp Arpeggiator | Switch on the arpeggiator to turn the notes you hold into a rhythmic pattern locked to your host's tempo. Each step retriggers this layer's Instrument exactly as if you'd played the note yourself, so the envelopes, filter, LFOs and effects all respond as normal. Every layer has its own arpeggiator, so you can run different patterns side by side. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Shape | 402 | L2Lfo Shape | Choose the Shape of the LFO. Alongside the classics there are a few more interesting options, such as random and plucky shapes. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Type | 404 | L2EqB1 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Type | 405 | L2EqB2 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 3 | Legacy Frequency | 406 | L2EqB3 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 3 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 3 | Resonance | 407 | L2EqB3 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 3 | Gain | 408 | L2EqB3 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 3 | Type | 409 | L2EqB3 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Cutoff Frequency | 410 | L2Filt Cutoff Frequency | Cutoff Frequency sets where the filter takes effect. The filter envelope and the LFO sweep the cutoff around this value, so it's the centre of any modulation rather than the starting point. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 1 | Frequency | 411 | L2EqB1 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 2 | Frequency | 412 | L2EqB2 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 2/EQ/Band 3 | Frequency | 413 | L2EqB3 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 2/Main/Filter | Type | 414 | L2Filt Type | Select the filter type. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. |
| Layer 2 | Stereo Width | 415 | L2 Stereo Width | Stereo narrows or widens this layer's stereo image. Negative values pull it toward mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves the sound as recorded. It works by splitting the sound into mid (what both channels share) and side (what differs between them), then rebalancing the two with a constant-power crossfade. At -100% only the mid remains; at +100% only the side, so anything dead centre disappears. Mono sounds have no side, so pushing to +100% silences them. |
| Layer 2/Config | MPE Press Target | 416 | L2 MPE Press Target | Press is the channel pressure, or aftertouch, that an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows how hard you're pushing into the key once it's sounding. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Press rests at nothing and climbs from there, so it only ever adds to the destination you point it at. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before press does anything. |
| Layer 2/Config | MPE Press Amount | 417 | L2 MPE Press Amount | Amount sets how far press moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before press reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a lighter touch. |
| Layer 2/Config | MPE Slide Target | 418 | L2 MPE Slide Target | Slide is CC74, which an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows where your finger sits along the front-to-back axis of the key. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Slide rests in the middle, so it pushes the destination either side of where you've set it. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before slide does anything. |
| Layer 2/Config | MPE Slide Amount | 419 | L2 MPE Slide Amount | Amount sets how far slide moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before slide reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a smaller movement. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) | 420 | L2Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) | Time sets how long one LFO cycle lasts, as a note length at your DAW's tempo. 1/4 is a quarter note; a D on the end is dotted (one and a half times as long) and a T is triplet (two thirds as long). The LFO follows tempo changes, but it isn't locked to the bar: each cycle starts from the note, as set by Mode. |
| Layer 2/Arp | Rate | 421 | L2Arp Rate | Rate sets how long each step lasts, synced to your host's tempo. Together with Length it decides how long the whole pattern takes to come round — eight steps at 1/8 fills one bar of 4/4. The T and D suffixes are triplet and dotted divisions, useful for swung or lopsided patterns. |
| Layer 2 | Pitch Semitones | 422 | L2 Pitch Semitones | Pitch moves this layer up or down in semitones. This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. Tip: for a multisampled Instrument, you might get better results from Transpose on the CONFIG tab. It changes which samples are played rather than processing them, which can sound more natural. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Variation | 423 | L2Grn Variation | Variation decides whether each note scatters its grains differently or plays back the exact same grains every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern of grains and save it with the preset. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Seed | 424 | L2Grn Seed | Seed picks which pattern of grains repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the grains you choose are the grains everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Variation | 425 | L2Lfo Variation | Variation decides whether the random shapes move differently on each note or play back the exact same pattern every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern and save it with the preset. In Free mode, a note that joins already-sounding notes follows their pattern. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 2/LFO | Seed | 426 | L2Lfo Seed | Seed picks which random pattern repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the movement you choose is the movement everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 2/Playback/Granular | Share Grains | 427 | L2Grn Share Grains | Share Grains keeps the number of grains the same whether you play one note or a chord, so the sound keeps the same density however many notes you hold. Each grain plays from one of the held notes, weaving the chord's pitches together. At low Density you can hear the grains hop between the notes of the chord. |
| Layer 3 | Volume | 480 | L3 Volume | The Layer Volume sets the level of this layer. The marks on the slider show the level of each sounding voice: its velocity, key range fade and any MPE volume expression. Tip: to change how velocity relates to volume, edit the velocity to volume curve on the CONFIG tab. |
| Layer 3 | Mute | 481 | L3 Mute | Mute silences this layer. Handy for hearing how the other layers sit together while you're designing a sound. A muted layer keeps running in the background exactly as if you could hear it, so when you unmute, the sound carries on seamlessly from wherever it has naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload the Instrument instead. If a layer is still audible after muting it, check whether it's also soloed: Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 3 | Solo | 482 | L3 Solo | Solo lets you hear this layer on its own. Any layer that isn't soloed goes quiet. Handy for focusing on one part of a sound while you're designing it. Silenced layers keep running in the background exactly as if you could hear them, so when you unsolo, they carry on seamlessly from wherever they have naturally got to. If you're trying to save CPU, unload their Instruments instead. If a layer has gone quiet unexpectedly, check whether another layer is soloed. And if a muted layer is still audible, that's because Solo takes priority over Mute. |
| Layer 3 | Pan | 483 | L3 Pan | Pan places this layer in the stereo field, anywhere from fully left to fully right. It uses a constant-power pan law (-3 dB at centre), so the layer stays at the same perceived loudness wherever you put it. Pan is applied after the Stereo control, so you can narrow a wide sound first and then place it as a single point. |
| Layer 3 | Detune Cents | 484 | L3 Detune Cents | Detune fine-tunes this layer's pitch in cents (100 cents is one semitone). This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. |
| Layer 3 | Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | 485 | L3 Pitch Semitones (Legacy) | Legacy layer pitch in semitones. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | Start | 487 | L3Lp Start | Set the loop start point, where the loop begins within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between here and the loop end. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | End | 488 | L3Lp End | Set the loop end point, where the loop finishes within the sample. While a note is held, playback loops between the loop start and here. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | Crossfade Size | 489 | L3Lp Crossfade Size | Set the size of the loop crossfade, which blends audio across the loop point so the loop doesn't click. A small amount usually helps, especially for sustained or tonal sounds. Floe keeps the crossfade within the loop and the sample, so it shrinks automatically if you make the loop too small for it. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | Sample Start Offset | 491 | L3Lp Sample Start Offset | Change the starting point of the sample |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | Reverse On | 492 | L3Lp Reverse On | Play the Instrument's samples backwards, from the end to the start. It works in every play mode and whether looping is on or off. The waveform display flips to match, so playback always runs from left to right (unless in the reverse portion of a ping-pong loop). |
| Layer 3/Main/Volume Envelope | On | 493 | L3Vol On | Switch the volume envelope on or off. It's typically best left on. When it's off, every note plays its sample straight through to the end, however briefly you press the key. Handy for one-shot sounds that should always be heard in full. Looping is disabled while the envelope is off, since nothing would ever bring a looping note to an end. Careful: with the envelope off, notes can't be cut short, so voices pile up if you play quickly, which costs CPU. |
| Layer 3/Main/Volume Envelope | Attack | 494 | L3Vol Attack | Attack sets how long each note takes to fade in. A few milliseconds is enough to avoid clicks if you've moved the sample start point. |
| Layer 3/Main/Volume Envelope | Decay | 495 | L3Vol Decay | Decay sets how long the note takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 3/Main/Volume Envelope | Sustain | 496 | L3Vol Sustain | Sustain sets the level the note holds at while the key is down. At 0 dB, Decay has nothing to do. |
| Layer 3/Main/Volume Envelope | Release | 497 | L3Vol Release | Release sets how long the note takes to fade out after you lift the key. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | On | 498 | L3Filt On | Switch the filter on or off. It's a clean, digital-sounding state-variable filter (12 dB per octave). Every voice gets its own copy, so the filter envelope and the LFO (on the LFO tab) can sweep each note independently. Tip: for broader tone shaping, the EQ tab has a three-band equaliser. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Legacy Cutoff Frequency | 499 | L3Filt Legacy Cutoff Frequency | Legacy cutoff parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Legacy Resonance | 500 | L3Filt Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Legacy Type | 501 | L3Filt Legacy Type | Legacy filter type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Envelope Amount | 502 | L3Filt Envelope Amount | Envelope Amount sets how strongly the filter envelope (shown to the right) moves the cutoff on every note. At 0% the envelope does nothing. Turn it up and the cutoff follows the envelope's shape, rising and falling with it. Turn it down and the cutoff moves the opposite way, falling as the envelope rises. The envelope is centred on the Cutoff setting: the top half of the display pushes the cutoff above it, the bottom half pulls it below. A negative amount flips this. For example, with a low-pass filter, a long attack opens the sound up gradually at the start of each note. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Attack | 503 | L3Filt Attack | Attack sets how long the filter envelope takes to reach its peak. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Decay | 504 | L3Filt Decay | Decay sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall to the Sustain level after the attack. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Sustain | 505 | L3Filt Sustain | Sustain sets the level the filter envelope holds at while the key is down. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Release | 506 | L3Filt Release | Release sets how long the filter envelope takes to fall back after you lift the key. |
| Layer 3/LFO | On | 507 | L3Lfo On | Switch this layer's LFO on or off. Enable Floe's LFO (low frequency oscillator) for adding movement to a one of this layer's controls (such as the volume or filter cutoff). |
| Layer 3/LFO | Legacy Shape | 508 | L3Lfo Legacy Shape | Legacy LFO shape parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/LFO | Mode | 509 | L3Lfo Mode | Choose where the LFO starts when you play a new note. With Retrigger, every note starts the LFO from the beginning of its cycle. With Free, a new note joins in wherever this layer's sounding notes have reached, so every note modulates precisely together. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Amount | 510 | L3Lfo Amount | Amount sets how far the LFO moves its target. 0% is no movement at all and 100% is the full range for that target: silence to full level for Volume, a semitone either way for Pitch, and so on. Negative values flip the shape upside down, so a falling sawtooth becomes a rising one. For random Shapes this only makes a difference when Variation is set to one of the Identical options. The LFO display shows the shape at the current Amount. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Target (Legacy) | 511 | L3Lfo Target (Legacy) | Legacy LFO target parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | 512 | L3Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | Legacy LFO rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/LFO | Time (Hz) | 513 | L3Lfo Time (Hz) | Time sets how fast the LFO cycles, in Hz (cycles per second). Tip: for movement that stays in time with your track, switch Sync on and choose a note length instead. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Sync On | 514 | L3Lfo Sync On | Sync ties the LFO's speed to your DAW's tempo. When it's on, Time is chosen as a note length that follows the tempo; when it's off, Time is set freely in Hz. Both settings are remembered, so you can flick between them without losing either. |
| Layer 3/EQ | On | 515 | L3Eq On | Switch on this layer's three-band equaliser to shape its tone before it's mixed with the other layers. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Frequency | 516 | L3EqB1 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 1 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Resonance | 517 | L3EqB1 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Gain | 518 | L3EqB1 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Legacy Type | 519 | L3EqB1 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Frequency | 520 | L3EqB2 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 2 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Resonance | 521 | L3EqB2 Legacy Resonance | Legacy resonance parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Gain | 522 | L3EqB2 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Legacy Type | 523 | L3EqB2 Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Config | Legacy Velocity Mapping | 524 | L3 Legacy Velocity Mapping | Choose how MIDI velocity should affect the volume of this layer. There are 6 modes that can be selected for this parameter via the buttons on the GUI. By setting one layer to be quiet at high velocities and another layer to be quiet at low velocities you can create an instrument that sounds different based on how hard the notes are played. (0) Ignore velocity, always play full volume. (1) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at low velocity (2) Loudest at low velocity, quietist at high velocity (3) Loudest at high velocity, quietist at middle velocity and below (4) Loudest at middle velocity, quietist at both high and low velocities (5) Loudest at bottom velocity, quietist at middle velocity and above, |
| Layer 3/Config | Keytrack On | 525 | L3 Keytrack On | With Keytrack on, this layer follows the keyboard: higher keys play higher pitches. Switch it off and every key plays the sample at its recorded pitch, which might be what you want for drum hits, loops and sound effects that shouldn't be transposed. Some sample libraries may override this - marking individual samples as always or never keytracked. |
| Layer 3/Config | Legacy Monophonic On | 526 | L3 Legacy Monophonic On | Only allow one voice of each sound to play at a time |
| Layer 3/Config | MIDI Transpose On | 528 | L3 MIDI Transpose On | Transpose shifts this layer up or down in semitones by changing which samples get triggered, rather than by speeding the audio up or down. On a multi-sampled Instrument that keeps the character of the sound intact, so it's the better choice for large shifts. The key range isn't affected: you play the same keys as before, they just reach for different samples. Tip: the Pitch control at the top of the layer transposes by re-pitching the audio instead. That's the one to reach for on a single-sample Instrument, and Detune beside it covers amounts smaller than a semitone. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Loop | Loop Mode | 529 | L3Lp Loop Mode | Select the Loop Mode for this layer. Floe can loop a portion of the sound for as long as you hold a note, so even a short sample can sustain indefinitely. Some Instruments come with loop points built in, while others let you set your own on the waveform. You can also turn looping off. There's 2 modes: 'standard' wrap-around loops jump from the loop end back to the start; 'ping-pong' loops bounce back and forth, alternating playback direction. The options that are available depend on the Instrument: library authors can provide built-in loops, allow or disallow custom loops, or require that certain sounds always loop. |
| Layer 3/Config | Key Range Low | 530 | L3 Key Range Low | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 3/Config | Key Range High | 531 | L3 Key Range High | This layer only plays within the given range of keys, letting you give each layer its own portion of the keyboard. Key Fade below softens the edges of the range, so the layer eases in and out instead of switching on abruptly. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 3/Config | Key Range Low Fade | 532 | L3 Key Range Low Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 3/Config | Key Range High Fade | 533 | L3 Key Range High Fade | Key Fade eases the layer in and out at the edges of its key range instead of letting it switch on abruptly. Both values are in semitones: the left one fades up from Range Low, the right one fades down from Range High. Give two layers overlapping fades and they crossfade into one another as you play up the keyboard. Tip: see each layer's range on the bar above the keyboard in the bottom panel. Hover it to enlarge it, and use the octave arrows beside the keyboard to scroll beyond the keys shown. |
| Layer 3/Config | Pitch Bend Range | 534 | L3 Pitch Bend Range | Pitch Bend Range sets how far the pitch wheel bends this layer, in semitones. Each layer has its own, so for example, a lead can bend a whole tone while the pad underneath can be set to zero to ignore the wheel entirely. Bending re-pitches the audio by speeding it up or slowing it down, so large bends will noticeably change the character of the sound. With MPE enabled, this governs the wheel on the master channel; the per-note bend of each individual note follows the range the controller asks for. |
| Layer 3/Config | Monophonic Mode | 535 | L3 Monophonic Mode | Monophonic decides what happens when notes on this layer overlap. Left off, the layer is polyphonic and every note you play gets a voice of its own; the other two modes hold it to one note at a time, in different ways. It's set per layer, so a monophonic lead can sit on top of a polyphonic pad in the same preset. The arpeggiator handles its own notes, so this has no effect while the arpeggiator is running on this layer. |
| Layer 3/Playback | Play Mode | 536 | L3 Play Mode | Select the Play Mode for this layer: the engine it uses to play its Instrument. Standard Playback plays each sample straight through: the playhead moves steadily from start to end, with options for looping and reversing along the way. The granular modes instead rebuild the sound from a stream of tiny snippets called grains. In Granular Playback, the point grains are drawn from moves through the sample at a rate you set with Speed, giving a time-stretch-like effect. In Granular Fixed, you place that point yourself with Position, letting you freeze on one part of the sample and explore its texture. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Length | 537 | L3Grn Length | Length sets how long each grain lasts, from a few milliseconds up to a second. Short grains chop the sound into a fine, buzzy texture that keeps little of the original's shape. Long grains preserve much more of the sample's natural character. Density and Smooth are both measured relative to Length, so changing it here changes how they feel too. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Speed | 538 | L3Grn Speed | Speed sets how fast the playhead travels through the sample in Granular Playback mode. Grains are drawn from wherever the playhead is. 100% is the sample's original speed. Turn it down to slow the sound to a crawl or stop it altogether, or up to race through at up to eight times normal speed. The playhead still respects the sample start, looping and Reverse settings. In Granular Fixed, this knob is replaced by Position. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Position | 539 | L3Grn Position | Position chooses where in the sample grains are drawn from, shown as the highlighted region on the waveform. Grains come from here for as long as you hold the note, so you can freeze on one moment of the sound and sustain it indefinitely. Tip: you can create movement with this parameter by setting the LFO's target to Grain Position, or by assigning this knob to a macro. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Density | 540 | L3Grn Density | Density sets how many grains overlap at once, relative to their Length. At 0%, each grain starts as the previous one ends, so they follow on one after another. Turning it up starts new grains sooner, stacking more and more of them on top of each other. Low values give an open texture where individual grains can be picked out. High values pile up so many grains that they smear into a thick, continuous wash. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Spread | 541 | L3Grn Spread | Spread widens the area of the sample that grains can start from. Each new grain begins somewhere between the playhead and a point up to this far past it, measured as a percentage of the whole sample. Small values keep every grain close to the playhead for a focused, precise sound. Large values scatter grains across a wide stretch of the sample. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Smooth | 542 | L3Grn Smooth | Smooth shapes the envelope of each grain: how gently it fades in and out, relative to its Length. At 0% grains start and stop abruptly, giving a hard, percussive edge. At 100% the fade-in and fade-out meet in the middle, so neighbouring grains blend into each other for a seamless texture. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Pan | 543 | L3Grn Pan | Pan randomises where each grain sits in the stereo field. Every new grain is given its own position, picked at random within the range you set here. At 0% every grain plays dead centre. At 100% grains can land anywhere from fully left to fully right, spreading the cloud from one side to the other. A quick way to create an interestingly wide stereo image. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Detune | 544 | L3Grn Detune | Detune randomises the pitch of each grain. Every new grain is nudged sharp or flat by a random amount within the range you set here. At 0% all grains play in tune. At 100% each grain can be up to a semitone sharp or flat. Small amounts thicken the sound like a chorus; larger amounts get progressively more smeared and out of tune. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Direction | 545 | L3Grn Direction | Direction gives each grain a chance of playing the opposite way to the main playhead. At 0% every grain follows the playhead's direction. At 100% each grain is equally likely to play forwards or backwards. In between, you can dial in a blend of the two for meandering, less predictable tones. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Harmony | 546 | L3Grn Harmony | Harmony gives each grain a chance of playing at a musical interval above or below the note you played, so a single note can bloom into a chord or a shimmering octave. At 0% every grain plays at the root. Turning it up shifts more of the grains, until at 100% every grain picks at random from the root and the intervals you've chosen. Choose which intervals are allowed with the Intervals menu next to this knob: pick a preset such as Octaves or Major Triad, or toggle individual semitones yourself. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Legacy Shape V2 | 547 | L3Lfo Legacy Shape V2 | Legacy LFO shape parameter (v2). Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/LFO | Target | 548 | L3Lfo Target | Choose the Target: what the LFO modulates. The modulation is applied relative to the target's current knob/slider. For example, when Volume is chosen, the movement will occur around wherever the layer's volume slider is currently set. Hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Resonance | 549 | L3Filt Resonance | Resonance emphasises the frequencies at the cutoff. At 0% the slope is smooth and rounded; at 100% it peaks by around 20 dB, without ever self-oscillating. For the band-pass, notch and band-shelving types it also narrows the band, and for Peak it sets the size of the boost. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Note Order | 550 | L3Arp Note Order | Order sets how the notes you're holding are shared out across the steps: climbing, falling, bouncing between the two, picked at random, or one of the less common shapes. Chord is the odd one out — it plays every held note together on each step, which is ideal for rhythmic stabs and percussion. Not available in Fixed Notes mode. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Trigger | 551 | L3Arp Trigger | Trigger decides what a new note does to a pattern that's already running. Free lets it carry on, so you can change chord underneath without breaking the groove. Retrigger restarts it from step 1 every time you press a note, which keeps the pattern locked to your playing. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Rate (Legacy) | 552 | L3Arp Rate (Legacy) | Legacy arpeggiator rate. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/Arp | Length | 553 | L3Arp Length | Length sets how many steps the pattern runs through before it loops back to the start. Steps beyond the length are hidden from the sequencer but keep their settings, so you can shorten a pattern and lengthen it again without losing anything. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Arpeggiator Mode | 554 | L3Arp Arpeggiator Mode | Choose where the steps get their notes from. Played Notes arpeggiates whatever you're holding, giving each step one of those notes in the order set by Order. Fixed Notes ignores what you play and runs a sequence of notes you've set yourself, either by dragging each step's note or by capturing a performance with the Record button. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Humanise | 555 | L3Arp Humanise | Humanise loosens the pattern up by nudging each step's timing and velocity by a random amount. A few percent takes the machine-like edge off; higher settings give a much looser, hand-played feel, which suits percussion especially well. Steps are only ever pushed later, never earlier, and never by more than a fifth of a step. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Auto Rate | 556 | L3Arp Auto Rate | Auto Rate lets Floe pick the step rate so a sliced Instrument plays close to the speed it was recorded at, rather than leaving silent gaps between slices when your host tempo is a long way from the loop's own. While it's on, the rate Floe has chosen is shown in place of the Rate menu. The multiplier shifts that choice: 2x for double speed, 0.5x for half, with Dotted and Triplet variants for a different feel. Because the choice has to land on a tempo-synced division it moves in jumps as the tempo changes, and every layer using Auto Rate jumps at the same points so they stay in the same rhythmic relationship. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Polyrate | 557 | L3Arp Polyrate | Polyrate gives each octave of the notes you're holding its own speed, so a single chord can produce several interleaving rhythms at once. The octave starting at middle C plays at the Rate you've set, and the octaves above and below scale from there by the ratio you choose. Tip: hold two notes an octave apart to hear the effect at its clearest. |
| Layer 3/Arp | One Shot | 558 | L3Arp One Shot | With One Shot on, the pattern plays through once and stops rather than looping for as long as you hold the notes. It's handy for fills and one-off flourishes, or for letting a sliced loop play through exactly once. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Resonance | 559 | L3EqB1 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Resonance | 560 | L3EqB2 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Arpeggiator | 561 | L3Arp Arpeggiator | Switch on the arpeggiator to turn the notes you hold into a rhythmic pattern locked to your host's tempo. Each step retriggers this layer's Instrument exactly as if you'd played the note yourself, so the envelopes, filter, LFOs and effects all respond as normal. Every layer has its own arpeggiator, so you can run different patterns side by side. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Shape | 562 | L3Lfo Shape | Choose the Shape of the LFO. Alongside the classics there are a few more interesting options, such as random and plucky shapes. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Type | 564 | L3EqB1 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Type | 565 | L3EqB2 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 3 | Legacy Frequency | 566 | L3EqB3 Legacy Frequency | Legacy band 3 frequency parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 3 | Resonance | 567 | L3EqB3 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 3 | Gain | 568 | L3EqB3 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 3 | Type | 569 | L3EqB3 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Cutoff Frequency | 570 | L3Filt Cutoff Frequency | Cutoff Frequency sets where the filter takes effect. The filter envelope and the LFO sweep the cutoff around this value, so it's the centre of any modulation rather than the starting point. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 1 | Frequency | 571 | L3EqB1 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 2 | Frequency | 572 | L3EqB2 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 3/EQ/Band 3 | Frequency | 573 | L3EqB3 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Layer 3/Main/Filter | Type | 574 | L3Filt Type | Select the filter type. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. |
| Layer 3 | Stereo Width | 575 | L3 Stereo Width | Stereo narrows or widens this layer's stereo image. Negative values pull it toward mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves the sound as recorded. It works by splitting the sound into mid (what both channels share) and side (what differs between them), then rebalancing the two with a constant-power crossfade. At -100% only the mid remains; at +100% only the side, so anything dead centre disappears. Mono sounds have no side, so pushing to +100% silences them. |
| Layer 3/Config | MPE Press Target | 576 | L3 MPE Press Target | Press is the channel pressure, or aftertouch, that an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows how hard you're pushing into the key once it's sounding. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Press rests at nothing and climbs from there, so it only ever adds to the destination you point it at. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before press does anything. |
| Layer 3/Config | MPE Press Amount | 577 | L3 MPE Press Amount | Amount sets how far press moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before press reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a lighter touch. |
| Layer 3/Config | MPE Slide Target | 578 | L3 MPE Slide Target | Slide is CC74, which an MPE controller sends on each note's own channel. On most keyboards it follows where your finger sits along the front-to-back axis of the key. Choose what it controls on this layer here, and how strongly with Amount beside it. Slide rests in the middle, so it pushes the destination either side of where you've set it. MPE has to be switched on in the Performance Controls panel before slide does anything. |
| Layer 3/Config | MPE Slide Amount | 579 | L3 MPE Slide Amount | Amount sets how far slide moves its destination, and a negative value flips the direction so the effect runs in reverse. Past 100% the destination reaches its limit before slide reaches its own, so you get the full effect from a smaller movement. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Time (Tempo Synced) | 580 | L3Lfo Time (Tempo Synced) | Time sets how long one LFO cycle lasts, as a note length at your DAW's tempo. 1/4 is a quarter note; a D on the end is dotted (one and a half times as long) and a T is triplet (two thirds as long). The LFO follows tempo changes, but it isn't locked to the bar: each cycle starts from the note, as set by Mode. |
| Layer 3/Arp | Rate | 581 | L3Arp Rate | Rate sets how long each step lasts, synced to your host's tempo. Together with Length it decides how long the whole pattern takes to come round — eight steps at 1/8 fills one bar of 4/4. The T and D suffixes are triplet and dotted divisions, useful for swung or lopsided patterns. |
| Layer 3 | Pitch Semitones | 582 | L3 Pitch Semitones | Pitch moves this layer up or down in semitones. This works by speeding up or slowing down the audio. Tip: for a multisampled Instrument, you might get better results from Transpose on the CONFIG tab. It changes which samples are played rather than processing them, which can sound more natural. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Variation | 583 | L3Grn Variation | Variation decides whether each note scatters its grains differently or plays back the exact same grains every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern of grains and save it with the preset. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Seed | 584 | L3Grn Seed | Seed picks which pattern of grains repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the grains you choose are the grains everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Variation | 585 | L3Lfo Variation | Variation decides whether the random shapes move differently on each note or play back the exact same pattern every time. Different on every note suits most sounds, while the Identical options let you capture a particular pattern and save it with the preset. In Free mode, a note that joins already-sounding notes follows their pattern. Open the menu and hover over each option for details. |
| Layer 3/LFO | Seed | 586 | L3Lfo Seed | Seed picks which random pattern repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like: it's saved with the preset, so the movement you choose is the movement everyone hears. Set Variation to one of the Identical options for this to take effect. |
| Layer 3/Playback/Granular | Share Grains | 587 | L3Grn Share Grains | Share Grains keeps the number of grains the same whether you play one note or a chord, so the sound keeps the same density however many notes you hold. Each grain plays from one of the held notes, weaving the chord's pitches together. At low Density you can hear the grains hop between the notes of the chord. |
| Effect/Distortion | Legacy Type | 3 | Dist Legacy Type | Legacy type parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |

Holding the low end in the middle keeps kicks and basslines solid, and stops them losing power on mono systems. The two bands are split with a 24 dB per octave Linkwitz-Riley crossover, so they recombine without a dip around the crossover point. |

| Effect/Reverb | Pre Low-pass Cutoff | 70 | Rvrb Pre Low-pass Cutoff | The Pre LP is a low-pass filter cutoff for rolling the highs off the signal on its way into the reverb, for a darker, more distant space. The dry signal keeps its full range. |
| Effect/Reverb | Pre High-pass Cutoff | 71 | Rvrb Pre High-pass Cutoff | The Pre HP is a high-pass filter cutoff for rolling the lows off the signal on its way into the reverb, keeping the tail clear so the bass stays tight and centred. The dry signal keeps its full range. |
| Effect/Reverb | Low-shelf Cutoff | 72 | Rvrb Low-shelf Cutoff | The Lo-Shelf sets the frequency below which the reverb tail is cut by the Lo-Gain amount. Turn Lo-Gain down to hear it work. |
| Effect/Reverb | Low Gain | 73 | Rvrb Low Gain | The Lo-Gain sets how much the reverb tail is cut below the Lo-Shelf frequency. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the low end thins out as the reverb fades - handy for stopping long tails clouding the bass. |
| Effect/Reverb | High-shelf Cutoff | 74 | Rvrb High-shelf Cutoff | The Hi-Shelf sets the frequency above which the reverb tail is cut by the Hi-Gain amount. Turn Hi-Gain down to hear it work. |
| Effect/Reverb | High Gain | 75 | Rvrb High Gain | The Hi-Gain sets how much the reverb tail is cut above the Hi-Shelf frequency. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the highs die away first, just as soft furnishings absorb them in a real room. |
| Effect/Reverb | Chorus Amount | 76 | Rvrb Chorus Amount | The Depth sets how far the reverb's reflections drift, smearing the resonances that build up in the tail. A little stops long tails ringing; more gives an obvious shimmer and movement. |
| Effect/Reverb | Chorus Frequency | 77 | Rvrb Chorus Frequency | The Mod Rate sets how quickly the drift set by Depth moves through the tail. Very slow rates give a gentle, breathing wash, while faster rates add a distinct warble. |
| Effect/Reverb | Size | 78 | Rvrb Size | The Size scales the spacing of the simulated reflections, setting how large the space feels. Small values pack them together for a boxy, coloured character; large values spread them out for something open and airy. |
| Effect/Reverb | Delay | 79 | Rvrb Delay | The Predelay holds the reverb back for a moment so the dry sound is heard on its own first. Short amounts keep the sound upfront and defined, while longer amounts push the walls further away. |
| Effect/Reverb | Mix | 80 | Rvrb Mix | Blend between the dry input and the reverb signal. |
| Effect/Reverb | On | 81 | Rvrb On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Phaser | Feedback | 82 | Phs Feedback | Feedback routes the phased signal back into the filters, sharpening the peaks and deepening the notches. Small amounts keep it as a gentle swoosh, while higher amounts give the sweep a resonant, whistling edge. |
| Effect/Phaser | Mod Rate | 83 | Phs Mod Rate | The Rate sets how quickly the peaks sweep up and down the frequency range. Slow rates give a gentle, drifting movement, while faster rates turn the sweep into a warble. |
| Effect/Phaser | Center Frequency | 84 | Phs Center Frequency | Freq sets the centre of the sweep: the frequency that the peaks and notches travel around. Keep it low for a deep, throaty movement, or raise it to place the phasing amongst the brighter harmonics. |
| Effect/Phaser | Shape | 85 | Phs Shape | Shape sets how many peaks and notches are carved into the sound. Turned down there's a single broad one for a soft, vowel-like sweep; turned up there are more of them stacked up the spectrum for a richer, more obvious phasing. |
| Effect/Phaser | Mod Depth | 86 | Phs Mod Depth | The Depth sets how far the peaks travel either side of the Freq setting. Small amounts give a narrow, shimmering movement, while larger amounts sweep across the whole spectrum. Tip: with Depth all the way down the peaks hold still, leaving a fixed colouration that you can sweep by hand with Freq. |
| Effect/Phaser | Stereo Amount | 87 | Phs Stereo Amount | Stereo offsets the left and right sweeps from each other so the movement drifts across the stereo image. At zero both channels sweep together; at maximum they sweep in opposite directions, for a wide, swirling feel. |

# Sample Libraries

> What is a Floe sample library

Sample libraries are where Floe's sounds come from: collections of mapped, playable sounds along with images, tags and other details. Without a sample library, Floe can't make any sound.

A library usually has a theme or focus. 'Music Box Suite', for example, is multi-sampled music boxes, while 'Lost Reveries' is a collection of single-sample ambient tones.

A sample library can contain [Instruments](/docs/beta/reference/instruments), impulse responses, or both. Most focus on Instruments, but some contain only impulse responses, giving the [Convolution Reverb](/docs/beta/usage/effects#convolution-reverb) new spaces and textures to work with.

You don't load a library itself. Instead, you load its Instruments into Floe's layers and its impulse responses into the Convolution Reverb. To see which libraries you have installed, open the menu at the top of Floe's window and choose _Info_.

## What's inside a library

Floe sample libraries use Floe's own open format: portable folders of audio files and configuration files, made with Floe's [developer tools](/docs/beta/develop/develop-libraries). A library's folder usually has a name like `Developer Name - Library Name`, and inside it a `Samples` subfolder and a file called `floe.lua`. Libraries can hold thousands of audio files and take up many gigabytes.

---

# Autosave

> How Floe autosaves your sound, and how to get it back

Floe saves a copy of each instance's sound every few seconds while you work, so a sound you've spent time on is never lost for good. That helps if Floe or your DAW crashes, but it's just as handy for everyday accidents: deleting the wrong track, closing a project without saving, or tweaking a sound past the point you liked it.

Autosaves are ordinary preset files. Floe only saves when something has changed, and the files are tiny, so autosaving won't slow your computer down or fill up your drive.

## Getting a sound back

1.  In the [preset box](/docs/beta/presets/loading-presets#the-preset-box), click _Load from file_.
2.  Go to Floe's autosave folder:
    -   Windows: `C:\Users\Public\Floe\Autosaves`
    -   macOS: `/Users/Shared/Floe/Autosaves`
    -   Linux: `~/Floe/Autosaves`
3.  Pick the autosave you want. Each file name holds the time and date it was saved, followed by the instance name, such as `autosave 14-32-05 Thu 2 Oct 2026 dawn-205 (4821).floe-preset`.

The autosave folder isn't one of Floe's preset folders, so autosaves don't clutter the preset browser. Once you've loaded the sound you wanted, [save it](/docs/beta/presets/saving-presets) as a normal preset to keep it.

## Instance names

Every instance of Floe has a name of its own, such as `dawn-205`. It's saved with your DAW project, so the same instance keeps its name each time you open the project. When you have several instances of Floe running, the name in an autosave's file name tells you which one it came from.

To see each instance's name in the top panel, turn on _Show instance name_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences. It's worth turning on if you often use several instances of Floe at once.

## Settings

The defaults suit most people, but you can change them on the _General_ tab of Preferences:

-   **Autosave interval (seconds)** — how often Floe checks for changes and saves.
-   **Max autosaves per instance** — how many autosaves to keep for each instance. When an instance reaches the limit, its oldest autosave is deleted to make room.
-   **Autosave delete after days** — how long to keep autosaves before deleting them.

---

# Error Reporting

> How Floe reports problems, how to send feedback, and what to do if Floe stops responding

Floe is built to be dependable for professional work. When something does go wrong, a few systems help keep your project safe and get the problem fixed quickly.

## Share feedback

If you find a bug, have an idea for a feature or just want to tell us something, use the feedback form inside Floe. Open the menu at the top of Floe's window and choose _Share Feedback_.

-   **Description** — what happened, or what you'd like. For a bug, say what you did just before it happened.
-   **Email** — optional. Add it if you'd like a reply.
-   **Include anonymous diagnostic data** — sends details about your system and Floe's state along with your message, which often makes a bug much quicker to track down.

Please do report anything that doesn't seem right. We want to know about it, and we want to fix it.

## Automatic error reports

If Floe crashes, it sends an anonymous error report. The report describes the error, the state of Floe leading up to it, and the computer it was running on. That gives us what we need to fix the bug without asking you to gather the information yourself. Floe also sends anonymous notes of when each session starts and ends, which tell us how reliably Floe is running overall.

To turn all of this off, enable _Disable anonymous error reports_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences. Floe is open source, so anyone can read the code and see exactly what's sent.

## If Floe stops responding

Floe tries never to take your DAW down with it. If it detects a serious problem, it stops itself rather than crashing the DAW: it goes silent and stops responding. Every instance of Floe in that DAW session is affected.

When this happens:

1.  Save your DAW project under a new name. That keeps the rest of your work safe without replacing your last good save, since a stopped Floe can't save its sound into the project.
2.  Restart your DAW. Floe can't start again within the same DAW session.
3.  If a sound in Floe didn't come back as you left it, recover it from an [autosave](/docs/beta/support/autosave). The [instance name](/docs/beta/support/autosave#instance-names) in each autosave's file name tells you which instance it came from.

An anonymous report of the problem is usually sent to us automatically, so we can work on a fix.

---

# FAQ

> Answers to common questions about Floe

### Can I add my own samples?

Not at the moment. Floe isn't a sampler you drop your own recordings into: it's a platform for complete, polished sample libraries, a bit like an open ROMpler. Each library comes ready to play, with its Instruments set up and presets designed around them.

We're looking into ways to expand this in the future.

If you have some programming experience, you can make your own sample libraries for Floe with its open tools: see [Library Development](/docs/beta/develop/develop-libraries).

### Does Floe load SFZ, SoundFont or other formats?

No. Floe loads sample libraries in its own format, an open format with similar ideas to SFZ that uses the Lua programming language. It also loads the older Mirage format used by some FrozenPlain libraries.

---

# Arp Tab

> Turn held notes into rhythmic patterns with each layer's own arpeggiator

The arpeggiator turns the notes you hold down into a tempo-synced rhythmic pattern. You choose how fast the steps go, the order the notes of your chord are played in, and the velocity, length, and pitch of each step.

Every [layer](/docs/beta/usage/layers) has its own arpeggiator, so you can build sounds with several rhythmic parts playing off each other: fast, high hits over slow, booming drums, say, or a melody over a pulsing bass. With a couple of arpeggiated layers, a single preset can drive a whole track.

Switch the arpeggiator on and hold a chord: you'll hear its notes play one after another in a rhythm. Each step triggers the layer's Instrument just as if you'd played the note yourself; each step runs through all the layer's usual settings, such as its play mode, volume envelope, filter and LFO.

The arpeggiator lives on each layer's _ARP_ tab. A dot on the tab shows that it's on.

![A layer's ARP tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-arp.3e2ced3e273a2a2e.png)12345

1.  **On/off and mode** — the _Arpeggiator_ switch, and a menu choosing where the steps get their notes from: _Played Notes_ or _Fixed Notes_.
2.  **Velocity bars** — one bar for each step, setting its velocity. Click and drag to change them, or drag sideways across the bars to draw a whole pattern in one go.
3.  **Step settings** — under each bar, from top to bottom, are the step number (click it to turn the step on or off), its pitch, a tie to the previous step, and its gate.
4.  **Sequence** — the step _Rate_, the pattern's _Length_, the note _Order_ and _Humanise_.
5.  **Config** — _Trigger_, _Polyrate_ and _One Shot_, plus the _Record_ button in _Fixed Notes_ mode.

While the arpeggiator is off, its controls are greyed out.

## The step sequencer

### Velocity bars

The height of each bar (2) is that step's velocity — typically, that's how loud the step is played. The taller the bar, the louder the step. Use this to accent every 4th step, for example.

`ctrl`/`cmd`\-click a bar to reset it, or `ctrl`/`cmd`\-drag across several to reset them all.

There are a few things that are good to know about velocities in Floe.

Velocity usually corresponds to volume, but how much depends on the layer's [velocity to volume curve](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#velocity-to-volume-curve) on the _CONFIG_ tab. That curve sometimes doesn't start at zero, so even the lowest bar may still be heard quietly.

Velocity can also affect more than just volume. For multi-sampled Instruments, it may select different samples to play (for example, playing a softer dynamic hit).

In _Played Notes_ mode, whilst the step's velocity is a major factor, how hard you play the note that triggers the sequence also plays a part — it scales the step velocities down. In other words, when you play the triggering note as softly as possible (MIDI velocity 1), the step velocities will be 50% as intense. When you play as hard as possible (MIDI velocity 127), the step velocities reach their full intensity. This upholds the natural way you use velocity on a keyboard. Play at full velocity to make the step velocities the only thing that matters. In _Fixed Notes_ mode, how hard you play is ignored.

### Step settings

Under each velocity bar is a column of smaller controls (3):

![The rows of step settings under the velocity bars, numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-step-settings.03a9288cde0f19a0.png)1234

1.  **Step number** — click to skip the step, leaving a gap in the pattern. A skipped step keeps its other settings, so you can bring it back later. It still ends the note before it, just as an active step would.
2.  **Pitch** — drag up or down to nudge the step's note. In _Played Notes_ mode it's an offset in semitones from whichever held note the step plays. In _Fixed Notes_ mode it's the exact note the step plays. Double-click to type a value.
3.  **Tie** — the link icon joins the step to the previous one, so they play as one longer note. Use ties to place some long notes among the short ones.
4.  **Gate** — the small knob sets how long each note lasts, as a proportion of the step. Pull it right down for short, percussive notes; at 100% the notes run into each other for a more legato feel. Remember that the volume envelope's release on the layer's _MAIN_ tab may affect what you hear.

### More step options

Right-click a velocity bar for a menu of options for that step: reset it, apply its settings to all the steps, reset all the steps, or rotate the whole pattern forwards or backwards by one step. Right-click a pitch or gate control to type a value or reset it, or to apply it to every step or reset it on every step.

When the pattern has more steps than fit across the tab, scroll sideways to see the rest; while it plays, the view follows the current step. Alternatively, click _OVERVIEW_ in the top-right corner to squeeze every step on screen at once. You can still draw velocities there, but the other step settings are hidden until you switch back.

## Sequence controls

The _SEQUENCE_ section (4) sets the shape and feel of the whole pattern:

![The arpeggiator's SEQUENCE controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-sequence.3fcc1295cec251c5.png)

-   **Rate** — how long each step lasts, as a note length at your DAW's tempo. The T and D suffixes are triplet and dotted divisions, useful for swung or lopsided patterns. Together with _Length_ it decides how long the pattern takes to come round: eight steps at 1/8 fills one bar of 4/4.
-   **Length** — how many steps the pattern runs through before it loops. Steps beyond the length are hidden but keep their settings, so you can shorten a pattern and lengthen it again without losing anything.
-   **Order** — how the notes you're holding are shared out across the steps. The options include going from lowest to highest or highest to lowest, bouncing between the two, playing at random, and some less common shapes. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. _Chord_ is the odd one out: it plays every held note together on each step, which is ideal for rhythmic stabs and percussion. Not available in _Fixed Notes_ mode.
-   **Humanise** — nudges each step's timing and velocity by a random amount, to counteract the machine-gun effect of perfectly identical steps. A few percent takes the mechanical edge off; higher settings give a much looser, hand-played feel. Steps are only ever pushed later, never earlier.

_Humanise_ works especially well with _Chord_ order: instead of every note of the chord starting at exactly the same instant, they spread out slightly, for a more natural, wider sound.

## Config controls

The _CONFIG_ section (5) sets how the pattern responds to your playing:

![The arpeggiator's CONFIG controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-config.69dfd372a93a94bf.png)

-   **Trigger** — what a new note does to a pattern that's already running. _Free_ is usually the one you want: the pattern carries on, so you can change chord underneath it without breaking the groove. _Retrigger_ restarts the pattern from the first step every time you press a note, which keeps it locked to your playing. In both modes, letting go of every key (and the sustain pedal) resets the pattern, so the next chord starts from the first step.
-   **Polyrate** — gives each octave of the notes you're holding its own speed, so one chord can produce several interweaving rhythms. The octave starting at middle C (C3) plays at the _Rate_, and the octaves above and below scale from there. _Double at octaves_ is particularly good: each octave up plays twice as fast as the one below. _3:2 at octaves_ and _4:3 at octaves_ create polyrhythms, where the octaves drift apart and meet up again. Hold two notes an octave apart to hear it most clearly.
-   **One Shot** — the pattern plays through once and stops, rather than looping for as long as you hold the notes. It's handy for fills and one-off flourishes. To play it again, release the keys and press again, or use _Retrigger_.
-   **Record** — in _Fixed Notes_ mode only; see below.

## Played Notes and Fixed Notes

The menu next to the _Arpeggiator_ switch (1) chooses where the steps get their notes from.

_Played Notes_ arpeggiates whatever you're holding. Each step plays one of your held notes, chosen by _Order_, moved up or down by the step's pitch offset.

_Fixed Notes_ ignores which notes you play, and each step plays a specific note that you set. You still hold a key to make the pattern run, but which key doesn't matter. Every step starts on C3, and you can set each one to any note by dragging its pitch.

![A layer's ARP tab in Fixed Notes mode with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-fixed-notes.3501fc38f7f26fd5.png)123

1.  **Mode** — the menu beside the _Arpeggiator_ switch, set to _Fixed Notes_.
2.  **Step notes** — each step's note, shown by name. Drag one up or down to change it.
3.  **Record** — play the pattern in from your keyboard.

It's particularly useful with a drum kit Instrument, where each key is a different drum: rather than following your chord, the pattern always plays the drums you've picked.

You can also play the pattern in with the _Record_ button (3) in the _CONFIG_ section. Click it, then play notes on your keyboard in your own time: each note you press lands on the next step. Recording stops by itself once the last step is filled, or you can click again to stop early. Only the notes are recorded; each step keeps the velocity, gate and tie you've already set. While recording, your notes play normally rather than through the pattern.

If your kick drum is on C3 and your snare on D3, for example, play C3, D3, C3, D3 for an alternating pattern.

## Sliced loops

Some Instruments are sliced loops: rhythmic loops marked up with slice points. The arpeggiator is what powers them: each slice becomes a step, so the loop plays in time with your DAW at any tempo. Because each slice is played as it was recorded, rather than being time-stretched, the loop still sounds natural even when your tempo is a long way from the one it was recorded at.

With a sliced Instrument loaded, the arpeggiator is always on, and the _ARP_ tab changes a little:

![A layer's ARP tab with a sliced Instrument loaded, with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-sliced.080368edd742cf1b.png)12

-   The _Arpeggiator_ switch, mode menu and _Length_ are hidden.
-   Each step has its velocity bar, step number and gate, but no pitch or tie: ties are set for you, so slices longer than one step play in full.
-   **Auto Rate** appears in the _SEQUENCE_ section (1). It picks the step rate for you, so the loop plays close to the speed it was recorded at rather than leaving silent gaps between slices. It's most useful when making presets: the preset keeps the same feel whether it's loaded into a 60 BPM track or a 170 BPM one. While it's on, the chosen rate is shown in place of the _Rate_ menu. The multiplier shifts that choice: _2x_ for double speed, _0.5x_ for half, with dotted and triplet variants for a different feel. Set it to _Off_ to choose the rate yourself.
-   A _SLICING_ section (2) appears. **Offset** picks which slice the pattern starts from, so you can begin part-way into the loop: an easy way to get a fresh groove out of a familiar loop. **Length** sets how many slices play before the pattern loops back to the offset, wrapping round the end of the loop if it needs to. Set it to _All_ to play every slice. Looping a short run of slices turns a long loop into a tight, repeating figure.

### Auto Rate and tempo changes

You may notice that raising the tempo sometimes makes a loop using _Auto Rate_ play slower, and lowering it can make it play faster: for example, a loop can feel faster at 147 BPM than at 148 BPM. That's because _Auto Rate_ aims to play the loop at roughly the speed it was recorded at, where it sounds most natural, with the fewest silent gaps or overlaps between slices. It can only choose from the tempo-synced note lengths, so when the tempo moves far enough from the loop's own speed, it switches to whichever note length is now closer. Every layer using _Auto Rate_ switches at the same tempos, so they stay in the same rhythmic relationship.

## Good to know

-   The pattern starts the moment you press the first key, and runs whether or not your DAW is playing. It follows your DAW's tempo, but it isn't lined up to its bars and beats.
-   The sustain pedal counts as holding notes, so it keeps the pattern running.
-   The layer's [key range](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) applies to the notes the arpeggiator plays, not the keys you hold. In _Played Notes_ mode a step whose note lands outside the range is silent.
-   The [_Monophonic_](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab) setting has no effect while the arpeggiator is running.
