-   In _Free_ mode with _Chord_ order, press the notes of a chord at the same moment. If one arrives slightly late, the first step plays without it, and it joins on the next step. When playing from your DAW, quantising the recorded notes lines them up so every step plays the whole chord.
-   Right-click the _ARP_ tab to copy and paste the whole arpeggiator, steps included, to another layer.

---

# Browsers

> How to find and load presets, Instruments and impulse responses with Floe's browsers.

The browsers help you find the right items quickly, without scrolling through long lists. Think of them as supercharged drop-down menus.

There are three browsers, and they all work the same way. Each one opens when you click the name of the item it loads:

-   **Preset browser** — click the preset's name in the [top panel](/docs/beta/usage/top-panel), which is there on every page.
-   **Instrument browser** — click the Instrument name at the top of a layer, on the [_Layers_](/docs/beta/usage/layers#layer-header) page.
-   **IR browser** — click the IR name in the [Convolution Reverb](/docs/beta/usage/effects#convolution-reverb) effect, on the _Effects_ page.

![Layer 1's Instrument browser, open beneath its selector, with its regions numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-browse.73d96a92f8a5fdb2.png)12345

1.  **Items** — the light panel on the left lists everything you can load. Click one to load it.
2.  **Narrowing down** — the dark panel on the right is for narrowing down the list on the left, such as to one sample library or one tag.
3.  **Selector** — the box you clicked to open the browser. It stays usable while the browser is open.
4.  **Navigation** — step back and forth through the pages of the right-hand panel.
5.  **Mode** — switch the right-hand panel between browse mode and [filter mode](#filter-mode).

## Loading items

Click an item (1) to load it. The browser stays open, so you can try one sound after another, playing as you go. Once you've loaded something, the browser closes by itself as soon as you move the mouse away from it. You can also double-click an item to load it and close the browser in one go, or close it at any time by clicking outside it or pressing `escape`.

While the browser is open, the selector you clicked (3) can still be used: previous, next, random and unload, where it has them.

Hover over an item for a moment to see more about it, such as its description.

## Favourites

If there are items you keep coming back to, mark them as favourites. Hover over an item and click the next to its name. The star stays lit to show it's a favourite. To see only your favourites, click the in the toolbar at the bottom of the list. Click it again to see everything. Favourites are shared by every instance of Floe, so anything you star in one project is there in the next.

## The list of items

The left panel (1) starts off showing everything, and shrinks as you narrow it down with the right panel.

Beneath the list, a line of italic text says what you're looking at, such as _Showing all instruments_. As you narrow things down it changes to match, such as _Showing from Lost Reveries_. Each part of it that narrows the list has a : click one to remove it.

At the very bottom is a small toolbar:

-   — jump to the item that's currently loaded. The right panel jumps to where it came from, too.
-   — show only your favourites.
-   — search. As you type, the list shows only the items containing your text. `ctrl`+`F` (`cmd`+`F` on macOS) opens it too.

## Narrowing down

The right panel (2) has pages that you click through to narrow down the list. In the Instrument browser, for example, you might click _Libraries_, then a particular sample library. The list on the left then shows only that library's Instruments. Numbers in brackets, such as _(26)_, show how many items each option holds.

The first page offers two ways in. _Browse by collection_ narrows down by where items come from. _Browse by attribute_ narrows down by their properties, such as their tags or who made them.

As you click through the pages, a trail of the pages you've visited builds up at the bottom of the panel (4) — a bit like a web browser. Click any step to jump back to it, or click to go back to the first page. The and arrows step back and forth.

## Right-click menus

Right-click items in the browsers for options to do with their files:

-   **A preset** — open the folder it's in, make it your [default preset](/docs/beta/presets/loading-presets#default-preset), or send it to the bin.
-   **A preset bank or folder** — open it in your file manager, or uninstall it.
-   **A sample library** — open its folder, or uninstall it. See [Uninstalling](/docs/beta/installation/uninstalling).

## Keyboard navigation

You can use the browsers from your computer keyboard. The focused item gets a blue outline, which appears once you press an arrow key.

-   `up`/`down` move through the list.
-   `enter` clicks the focused item.
-   `tab` moves between the left and right panels.
-   `left`/`right` move along the trail at the bottom of the right panel.
-   `ctrl`+`F` (`cmd`+`F` on macOS) opens the search.
-   `home`/`end` jump to the start or end of the list.
-   `ctrl`+`up`/`down` (`cmd` on macOS) jump to the previous or next folder.
-   `page up`/`page down` jump 8 items at a time.

## Filter mode

Browse mode, where you click through one page at a time, is all most people need. When you know exactly what you're after, filter mode goes further: it lets you combine several ways of narrowing down at once, such as showing only Instruments tagged _ambient_ from one particular sample library.

Switch to it with the button (5), and back to browse mode with .

![The Instrument browser in filter mode, with its regions numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-full.89de4f11b56240f7.png)1234

1.  **Filters** — every option in one tree, rather than pages to click through. Click a to open a section, then click the options you want.
2.  **Summary** — what's currently showing. Click the next to a filter to remove it.
3.  **Mode** — switch between browse mode and filter mode.
4.  **Matching** — choose how your filters combine.

The list on the left updates as soon as you click an option.

Choose how the filters combine with the button next to the mode switch (4):

![The One, Match all and Match any menu](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-menu.5ef644a9f8155d92.png)

-   **Match all (AND)** — the one you'll usually want. Only items that match every selected filter are shown, so the more filters you choose, the shorter the list gets. Filters that would leave nothing to show are greyed out, so you don't hit dead ends.
-   **Match any (OR)** — items that match any of the selected filters are shown, so the more filters you choose, the longer the list gets.
-   **One** — only one filter at a time, like browse mode but with the tree layout.

Filter mode has its own search, at the bottom of the right panel, for finding a filter in the tree, such as the _aggressive_ tag.

Filter mode pairs well with the random button: narrow the list down to the kind of sound you're after, then jump around within it for inspiration. See [Randomisation](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation).

## Tips

-   The previous, next and random buttons ( ) always stay within the list you've narrowed down to, whether the browser is open or closed. On the _Perform_ page and in the top panel, the preset arrows follow the preset browser in the same way.
-   Drag the bottom-right corner of a browser to resize it. To make room for longer names, drag the line where the two panels meet. Double-click either to reset it.
-   Each layer's Instrument browser remembers its own settings. On the _Layers_ page, set up each one the way you like, perhaps the first narrowed to the _bass_ tag and the second to _keys_. Then click the button that randomises every layer, and each one jumps to a random Instrument within its own selection.

---

# Config Tab

> How a layer responds to your playing, including key ranges, pitch bend, velocity and MPE

The _CONFIG_ tab sets how the layer responds to your playing: which keys it uses, and how it follows velocity, pitch bend and MPE controllers.

![A layer's CONFIG tab](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-config.499578f75666d12d.png)1234567

1.  **Transpose** — shift the layer in semitones by changing which samples are triggered, rather than re-pitching the audio as _Pitch_ in the [layer header](/docs/beta/usage/layers#layer-header) does. On a multi-sampled Instrument this keeps the character of the sound intact, so it's the better choice for large shifts. You still play the same keys; they just reach for different samples.
2.  **Pitch Bend Range** — how far the pitch wheel bends this layer, in semitones. Each layer has its own, so one layer can bend a whole tone while another ignores the wheel entirely.
3.  **Keytrack** — with it on, higher keys play higher pitches. Switch it off and every key plays the sample at its recorded pitch, which suits drum hits, loops and sound effects. Some libraries mark particular samples as always or never keytracked.
4.  **Monophonic** — what happens when notes overlap. _Off_ is polyphonic: every note gets its own voice. _Retrigger_ plays one note at a time, with each new note releasing the previous one. _Latch_ holds on to the first note, ignoring any new ones, until you let go of every key: useful for drones and textures. Because it's per layer, one layer can play one note at a time while another stays polyphonic. While the layer's [arpeggiator](/docs/beta/usage/arp-tab) is on, this setting has no effect.
5.  **MPE** — choose what an MPE controller's press (channel pressure) and slide (CC74) control on this layer, such as volume, filter cutoff, timbre or LFO amount, and by how much. Negative amounts reverse the response. MPE must be switched on in the Performance Controls panel first. See [MIDI](/docs/beta/usage/midi#mpe) for details.
6.  **Key Range** and **Key Fade** — give the layer its own portion of the keyboard, with soft edges if you like.
7.  **Velocity to volume curve** — how hard you play turns into how loud each note sounds. Steepen the curve for a wider dynamic range, or flatten it to even out your playing. When you play, a red line shows where your note landed.

## Key ranges

Key ranges let you split the keyboard into zones, with each layer responding to specific keys. Use them to split the keyboard, stack zones on top of each other, or crossfade smoothly from one sound to another as you play up the keys.

### Setting up key ranges

_Key Range_ is the lowest and highest note the layer plays, and _Key Fade_ is how many semitones it takes to fade in at the bottom of the range, and to fade out at the top. Drag a value up or down, click its arrows ( ), or double-click to type it in (a note name, for the range).

![Key range controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-controls.8f042068dc69b686.png)

Fades are what make smooth transitions possible: overlap two layers' ranges by a few notes, fade the lower layer out and the upper layer in across the overlap, and one sound crossfades into the other as you play up the keyboard.

To play a different part of a multi-sampled Instrument's mapping, use _Transpose_ on the same tab. It shifts which samples are triggered, so higher or lower samples play, while the layer's _Pitch_ re-pitches the audio by speeding it up or slowing it down. _Transpose_ doesn't move the key range itself.

### Key range display

A bar above the keyboard at the bottom of the interface shows which keys trigger each layer, with colours corresponding to each layer. Only layers with an Instrument loaded appear. The bar is hidden when every layer uses the full keyboard range (C-2 to G8), unless an Instrument has named ranges (see below).

![Key range display above the keyboard](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-bars.bccf7ecc8a586a01.png)

On the _Layers_ and _Effects_ pages, the keyboard shows a section of the full 128 keys: use the [octave controls](/docs/beta/usage/keyboard) to scroll it, and the bar scrolls with it. The _Perform_ page shows a wider, fixed stretch of nine octaves. Vertical lines mark where each range starts and ends, and small chevrons show when a range carries on past the visible keys. Fades show as gradients on the bars: the more transparent, the quieter.

Hover over the display to see an enlarged view with more detail. An Instrument can also have named ranges, such as the name of the sound on each key, or each group of drums in a kit. They appear as thicker capsules, labelled in the enlarged view.

![Enlarged key range view with named ranges, fades, and off-screen chevrons](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-enlarged.631825e6f15b2f25.png)

## Velocity to volume curve

Each layer has its own _velocity to volume curve_, which shapes how hard you play (MIDI velocity) into the volume of each note.

![Velocity to volume curve editor](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/velocity-curve.7a4bb3dd5dc53a7e.png)

### How the curve works

The horizontal axis is velocity — far left is the softest possible velocity (MIDI value 1), far right is the hardest (MIDI value 127). The vertical axis is the resulting note volume. When you play a note, a red indicator appears at its velocity position on the curve so you can see where you're playing.

While notes are sounding, each active voice also gets a red line on the layer's volume slider, showing the level that voice is playing at, once the curve, any [key range](#key-ranges) fade and any MPE volume expression are taken into account.

A straight line from bottom-left to top-right gives a natural response: the harder you play, the louder the note.

Move, add or remove points, or reshape the curve between them, to change this relationship: make soft playing louder than it would be naturally, cap the volume of hard hits, or create a non-linear response that emphasises a particular dynamic range.

The curve pictured above is one example. The softest notes stay quiet, the volume climbs steeply as you play a little harder, then it levels off so the hardest hits can't get much louder.

Setting different curves across the three layers also opens up creative sound design — for example, fading one layer in as you play harder while another fades out.

By default the curve doesn't start at zero, so even the softest notes still make a quiet sound. Drag the left-most point down to the bottom if you want the softest notes to be silent.

### Velocity and multi-sampled Instruments

While not directly related to this curve, it's worth noting that velocity does more than just control volume. For multi-sampled Instruments that contain separate velocity layers, a note's velocity also selects _which_ sample is played — not just how loud it is. A low-velocity note on a piano, for instance, plays the soft-velocity samples (with their distinct tone and character) rather than a quieter version of the hard-hit samples.

### Editing the curve

-   **Double-click** anywhere on the curve to add a control point (up to 8 in total)
-   **Drag control points** to move them
-   **Drag between points** to adjust curve shape
-   **Double-click a point** to remove it
-   **Shift-drag** for finer control
-   **`ctrl`/`cmd`\-click** a point to reset its height, or between points to reset that stretch's shape
-   **Right-click** to add or remove points, copy and paste the curve between layers, or reset it

---

# Controls

> How to use Floe's knobs, sliders, menus and graphs

Almost everything you shape is done with knobs and sliders, and they all work the same way.

## Knobs and sliders

-   **Drag** — click and drag up or right to increase the value, down or left to decrease it. Use whichever direction feels natural.
-   **Fine adjustment** — hold `shift` while dragging for four times finer control. You can press or release `shift` mid-drag.
-   **Reset** — `ctrl`\-click (`cmd`\-click on macOS) to return the control to its default value.
-   **Type a value** — double-click to type an exact number. You can typically use abbreviations like `2k` instead of 2000 Hz.
-   **More options** — right-click for a menu of extra actions (see below).

When you hover over a control it lights up, and its current value appears below it. Pause on it for a moment and a short description appears too, with a reminder of these shortcuts underneath. Both are adjustable in the preferences: _Show tooltips_ turns the descriptions off, and turning off _Instant value readouts_ makes the value appear only after a moment or while you're dragging.

Sometimes controls are greyed out — showing it currently has no effect; such as a filter knob while the filter is switched off.

### Reading a knob

A knob shows its value in two places: the line on the dial, and the coloured arc around the edge.

These 2 aspects can differ when a [macro](/docs/beta/usage/macros) is controlling the knob. The dial shows the knob's own setting, the one you drag. The coloured arc shows the value you actually hear once the macros have been applied. Hover over the knob to see both readouts.

![The Filter effect's controls, with a macro moving its Cutoff knob](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/knob.ed9ee6bd141faee8.png)

Here, a macro is raising the Filter's _Cutoff_. The dial points to where the knob is set, while the arc reaches further round, to the cutoff you hear.

## The right-click menu

![The right-click menu of the Filter effect's Cutoff knob](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/knob-menu.2b32dcce31cfb5f2.png)

Right-click any knob or slider for extra actions, including:

-   **Copy Value** and **Paste Value** — carry a setting from one control to another.
-   **Enter Value** — type an exact value, the same as double-clicking.
-   **Reset Value to Default** — the same as `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click.
-   **Reset Value to "…" state** — appears when you've loaded a preset, and names it. It returns just this control to how the preset had it.
-   **MIDI CC Learn** — link the control to a knob or fader on your MIDI controller. See [MIDI](/docs/beta/usage/midi#midi-cc).

Some controls add their own shortcuts. A layer's _Pitch_, for example, has _+1 Octave_ and _\-1 Octave_, and _Detune_ can fold whole semitones into _Pitch_.

Many sections have a right-click menu of their own too. Right-click a layer's tab, an envelope or an effect to copy, paste or reset the whole section at once: a quick way to give two layers the same filter settings, for example.

## Menus, buttons and number fields

-   **Menus** — click to open the list of options. The arrows either side, and , step to the previous or next option, which is a quick way to audition them. Hover over an option in the open menu to see what it does.
-   **Buttons** — click to switch on or off. Most can be right-clicked for more options.
-   **Number fields**, such as a layer's _Pitch_ — drag them like a knob, double-click to type, or use the arrows beside them ( ).

Menus reset to their default with `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click, just like knobs.

## Graphs

Envelopes, filters and EQs have graphs with points you can drag directly. Dragging a point is simply another way of moving the knobs beneath it. Everything above still applies: `shift` for fine adjustment, `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click to reset, double-click to type.

Hover over a point to see exactly what it controls. On a filter point, for example, moving left and right changes the cutoff, and moving up and down changes the resonance. On some points, such as the EQ bands, the mouse wheel adjusts the resonance.

## Undo

Every change you make can be undone. Use the _Undo_ and _Redo_ buttons in the [top panel](/docs/beta/usage/top-panel#buttons) to step back and forth through your edits.

---

# Effects Page

> How to use Floe's effects rack, and details of each effect

![Floe's window with the EFFECTS page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-effects.73801094172d2026.png)

The _Effects_ page is where you colour the whole sound. The three [layers](/docs/beta/usage/layers) are mixed together and then passed through a single rack of effects, from top to bottom. Use them lightly to add some space or warmth, or push much further with heavy distortion, filtering and modulation to take the sound somewhere new. There's 12 effects available. Each can be used once in the rack, in whatever order you like.

![Floe's Effects page with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effects.39fc87a1ccda5330.png)12345

1.  **Switchboard** — every effect listed in order, each on its own card. Tick a card's checkbox to add that effect to the rack.
2.  **Rack** — the effects that are in use, with their controls.
3.  **Effect name** — drag it to move the effect up or down the chain. Right-click for more options.
4.  **Mix, remove and bypass** — _Mix_ sets how much of the effect you hear, removes the effect from the rack, and bypasses it.
5.  **All-effect buttons** — these act on the whole rack at once: randomise , bypass all , and remove all .

### Adding and removing effects

The switchboard (1) lists every effect. Those in the rack are shown brightly with a ticked checkbox; the rest are dimmed.

-   **Add an effect** by ticking its checkbox. Doing so will add it to the rack, and the rack will scroll to show it.
-   **Remove an effect** by unticking its checkbox, or clicking next to its _Mix_ knob (4). Removing an effect doesn't reset its controls, it will be the same if you re-add it later.
-   **Jump to an effect** by clicking its card anywhere other than the checkbox. The rack will scroll to show it, with a brief flash so you can spot it.

### Bypassing effects

Bypassing an effect lets the sound pass straight through it while it stays in the rack, ready to switch back on. It's the easiest way to hear exactly what an effect is contributing. A bypassed effect is greyed out and uses no CPU.

Click next to an effect's _Mix_ knob (4), or the coloured light at the left of its switchboard card, to bypass it. Click again to switch it back on.

The button at the top right of the page (5) bypasses every effect in the rack at once, so you can hear your layers without any processing. Click it again to switch them all back on.

### Changing the order

The effects run from top to bottom, and the order can make a big difference: a reverb after a distortion gives a clean tail on a gritty sound, while a reverb before it distorts the tail too.

Drag an effect's name (3) up or down the rack to move it. You can also drag the cards in the switchboard: hover over a card and a grip appears to show it can be moved. Because the switchboard also shows the effects that aren't in the rack, after some reordering the effects in use can end up scattered among the unused ones. Right-click the switchboard and choose _Tidy FX Order_ to group the effects in the rack at the top, without changing their order.

### Mix

Every effect has a _Mix_ knob (4). It blends the sound going into the effect with the effect's output. At 100% you hear only the effect's output; turn it down to bring back more of the unprocessed sound. It's a quick way to set an effect's strength without changing its other settings: a touch of reverb, gentle distortion, or parallel compression, say.

### The all-effect buttons

The buttons at the top right of the page (5) act on the whole rack:

-   **Randomise** — randomly puts each effect in or takes it out of the rack, and shuffles the order. The effects' settings aren't changed. It's a quick way to stumble on combinations you'd never have reached for. Use _Undo_ from the top panel if you don't like the result. For bigger changes, including new settings, try the [Random Variation](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation) strip on the _Perform_ page.
-   **Bypass all** — deactivates all effects.
-   **Remove all** — removes every effect from the rack.

### Copying, pasting and resetting

Right-click an effect's name in the rack or its card in the switchboard for a menu to:

-   **Copy and paste one effect** — copy an effect's settings, then paste them onto the same effect on another preset.
-   **Copy and paste the whole rack** — copy every effect, its order and its settings, then paste them all at once to a new preset.
-   **Reset** — return the effect's settings to their defaults.

Copying works between presets: copy from one, load another, and paste. Right-click an empty part of the switchboard or rack for the whole-rack options, and to paste a single copied effect.

## Distortion

![The Distortion effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-distortion.a583b9946e316265.png)

Distortion adds harmonics to a sound, anything from gentle tape warmth to outright destruction. Choose a character from the _Type_ menu, then set how hard you push it with the _Drive_ knob. That's the whole workflow; everything else is there to shape the result. The display on the left passes a sine wave through your current settings, so you can see how each type and setting reshapes it.

It runs with 4× oversampling and is anti-aliased to stay clean and musical. It also has built-in gain compensation to keep the level steady as you turn up _Drive_ or _Punish_. For the Legacy types, you opt in to this with the _Auto Gain_ switch; for the other types it's always on.

-   **Type** — the character of the distortion. See below.
-   **Drive** — how hard the sound is pushed into the distortion, and the main control for how much distortion you hear. Each step of the knob adds a similar amount. For the Mangle types it also moves the effect itself, so the character changes as well as the intensity.
-   **Punish** — stacks extra distortion stages after the first, each driven harder than the last, like an amp cascading its gain stages. Turn it up for a denser, grittier, more compressed drive that holds its character as notes decay.
-   **Tilt EQ** — shifts the tone going into the distortion. Turn it up to saturate the highs for a brighter result, or down to push the lows for a warmer, fatter drive.
-   **Gain** — a flat level adjustment to the distorted sound, before _Mix_ blends it with the unprocessed sound. It's separate from the automatic gain compensation.
-   **Auto Gain** — for the Legacy types, holds the loudness steady as you turn up _Drive_. For the other types it's always on.

The types are grouped into two families in the menu. _Bite_ types saturate and thicken the sound, from clean warmth to hard clipping:

-   **Tape** — warm and smooth. Rounds off the loud peaks while quieter passages and tails stay clean.
-   **Valve** — rich, even harmonics that stay musical however hard you push, instead of collapsing into a harsh square.
-   **Overdrive** — pedal-style grit with a threshold. A note cleans up as it decays, and playing harder brings the bite in.
-   **Hard Clip** — clean, aggressive brickwall clipping.
-   **Octave** — adds a hard octave-up edge, then saturates. It squares up on hot notes and follows their dynamics.

_Mangle_ types are more extreme, tearing the sound apart and adding new tones rather than just thickening it:

-   **Bitcrush** — lo-fi digital crunch, made by lowering the effective sample rate. More _Drive_ means coarser and grittier.
-   **Ring Mod** — multiplies the sound by a low oscillator for clangorous, metallic, bell-like tones. _Drive_ raises the oscillator's pitch and deepens the effect.
-   **Sine Fold** — folds the wave through a sine curve for interesting, chaotic harmonics.
-   **Warp** — an asymmetric shaper that bends the wave lopsidedly into a gritty, off-kilter drive.
-   **Wavefolder** — folds the peaks back on themselves for bright, metallic harmonics.

The Legacy types are the original distortion algorithms, kept so that older presets and projects sound the same. They load with _Auto Gain_ off to keep their original level; turn it on to give them the same steady loudness as the other types.

## Bit Crush

![The Bit Crush effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-bit-crush.eb0ae0d0c3717f57.png)

Bit Crush is a lo-fi effect that degrades the sound in two ways: lowering the sample rate for ringing, metallic aliasing, and lowering the bit depth for gritty noise. The display shows a preview of the crushing applied to a rising test signal. Both controls start at full quality, so turn them down to hear the effect.

-   **Bits** — lowers the bit depth, adding a gritty digital noise that's most obvious in quiet passages and tails. At the lowest settings quiet sounds crush to silence, so feed the effect a strong signal.
-   **Samp Rate** — lowers the sample rate by holding each sample for longer. Lower rates fold high frequencies back down into ringing, metallic aliasing: the sound of early samplers and retro hardware.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

## Compressor

![The Compressor effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-compressor.5a5d0c835f3f6c23.png)

The compressor shapes the dynamics of the sound, evening out the difference between its loud and quiet parts. It has two types, each with its own character.

-   **Type** — _Modern_ is precise, and gives you the _Attack_ and _Release_ knobs. _Vintage_ has a bit more character, and sets its attack and release for you.
-   **Threshold** — the level the sound has to rise above before it's compressed.
-   **Ratio** — how strongly the sound is compressed once it's above the threshold. Higher ratios compress more, and above about 2:1 the pumping becomes much more noticeable.
-   **Attack** and **Release** (_Modern_ only) — how quickly the compressor responds to a rise in level, and how quickly it recovers after the level drops.
-   **Gain** — adjusts the level after compression.
-   **Auto Gain** (_Vintage_ only) — automatically adjusts the level so the sound stays consistently loud however hard it's compressed.

Three meters show what the compressor is doing: _In_ is the incoming level, with a marker at the threshold; _GR_ (gain reduction) is how much it's turning the sound down; and _Out_ is the final level.

## Filter

![The Filter effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-filter.6e299e9ebedef899.png)

The Filter cuts away part of the frequency range, or boosts or dips it. It's a single filter across the whole mix; each layer also has its own filter for shaping notes individually (see [Layers](/docs/beta/usage/main-tab#filter)).

-   **Type** — the shape of the filter, such as low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peak or shelf. The low-pass and high-pass types come in 12 and 24 dB per octave slopes.
-   **Cutoff** — where the filter does its work: where the low-pass and high-pass filters roll off from, the centre of the band for band-pass and notch, or the corner for the shelves.
-   **Reso** — resonance, which emphasises the frequencies right at the cutoff, adding a peak there on the low-pass and high-pass filters. For band-pass and notch it narrows the band, for peak it tightens the boost, and for the shelves it steepens the corner.
-   **Gain** — how far the peak and shelf types boost or cut. It only appears for those types.

## Stereo Widen

![The Stereo Widen effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-stereo-widen.689f9c85db9c28f0.png)

Stereo Widen narrows the sound towards mono or spreads it out wider. Each layer also has its own _Stereo_ control, if you want to widen just one of them.

-   **Mode** — how the widening is done. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each.
    -   _Balanced_ keeps the loudness the same wherever _Width_ is set. It's the one to reach for by default.
    -   _Bass Mono_ widens in the same way, but keeps everything below the _Bass Mono_ frequency in the centre.
    -   _Legacy_ is the widening from older versions of Floe, kept so that existing presets sound as they always did. It gets louder as _Width_ goes up.
-   **Width** — negative values pull the sound towards mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves it as it is. It works by rebalancing the mid (what both channels share) against the side (what differs between them). At the far left only the mid is left; at the far right only the side is left, so anything dead centre disappears.
-   **Bass Mono** (_Bass Mono_ mode only) — the frequency below which the sound is kept in the centre. Holding the low end in the middle keeps kicks and basslines solid, and stops them losing power on mono systems. The split uses a 24 dB per octave Linkwitz-Riley crossover, so the two bands recombine without a dip around the crossover point.

## Chorus

![The Chorus effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-chorus.3bdf4b0fca3fc2fe.png)

The Chorus thickens the sound by layering it with delayed copies that drift in pitch. Gentle settings add a subtle shimmer and movement, while deeper settings give an obvious, tape-like wobble.

-   **Rate** — how quickly the pitch drifts up and down. Low settings give a gentle swelling movement, while turning it up gives a quicker, shimmering warble.
-   **Depth** — how far the pitch drifts away from the original. Small amounts thicken the sound, while larger amounts give an obvious wobble. At zero, the delayed copies are still there, adding a static colouration.
-   **High-pass** — removes low frequencies from the chorused copies, leaving the unprocessed sound untouched. Raise it to keep the bass tight and free from movement.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

## Reverb

![The Reverb effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-reverb.3ca4505d77aaecb2.png)

The Reverb simulates the reflections of a real space, from a small, tight room to a vast hall that takes many seconds to fade. It can also modulate its tail for a shimmering, moving sound.

-   **Pre LP** and **Pre HP** — low-pass and high-pass filters on the sound going into the reverb. _Pre LP_ rolls off the highs for a darker, more distant space. _Pre HP_ rolls off the lows, keeping the tail clear so the bass stays tight and centred. The unprocessed sound keeps its full range.
-   **Lo-Shelf** and **Lo-Gain** — cut the reverb's tail below the _Lo-Shelf_ frequency by the _Lo-Gain_ amount. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the low end thins out as the reverb fades: handy for stopping long tails clouding the bass. Turn _Lo-Gain_ down to hear it work.
-   **Hi-Shelf** and **Hi-Gain** — the same for the highs, so they die away first, just as soft furnishings absorb them in a real room.
-   **Decay** — how long the tail takes to fade away once a sound stops. It holds steady whatever the _Size_, so you can choose the length of the reverb and the character of the space separately.
-   **Size** — how large the space feels. Small values pack the reflections together for a boxy, coloured character; large values spread them out for something open and airy.
-   **Predelay** — holds the reverb back for a moment so the unprocessed sound is heard on its own first. Short amounts keep the sound upfront and defined, while longer amounts push the walls further away.
-   **Mod Rate** and **Depth** — make the reflections drift, smearing the resonances that build up in the tail. A little _Depth_ stops long tails ringing; more gives an obvious shimmer and movement. _Mod Rate_ sets how quickly the drift moves: keep it low for a gentle, breathing wash, or turn it up for a quicker, more distinct warble.

## Delay

![The Delay effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-delay.e6e66ebc5fbfc868.png)

The Delay is a stereo echo. You can set the left and right times separately, either freely or synced to tempo, bounce the repeats between the speakers with the ping-pong modes, and thin them out with a filter as they fade.

-   **Time L** and **Time R** — the gap between the repeats in the left and right channels. With _Tempo Sync_ off, they're set freely in milliseconds. Very short times stop sounding like separate echoes and become a metallic, resonant tone instead.
-   **Tempo Sync** — sets the times as note lengths that follow your DAW's tempo, keeping the repeats in time with your track.
-   **Feedback** — how long the echoes trail on for. Low amounts give a handful of repeats, while high amounts carry on long after the note has gone. It works by feeding each repeat back in to make the next one.
-   **Mode** — how the repeats move around the stereo image:
    -   _Mono_ — both channels repeat at the _Time L_ setting, so the echoes sit where the original sound sits in the stereo image. _Time R_ is unused.
    -   _Stereo_ — each channel has its own delay, so setting _Time L_ and _Time R_ apart spreads the repeats across the stereo image.
    -   _Ping-pong_ — the sound is summed to the centre, and the repeats then bounce from one side to the other, with _Time L_ and _Time R_ setting how long each half of the bounce lasts.
    -   _Mid ping-pong_ — the repeats bounce from side to side as in _Ping-pong_, but the sound keeps its stereo image on the way in. Choose _Ping-pong_ for the clearest left-right bounce, especially from a wide sound, and _Mid ping-pong_ when you want the echoes to keep some of the original's width.
-   **Filter** and **Spread** — a band-pass filter the repeats run through, leaving the unprocessed sound untouched. _Filter_ sets the centre of the band and _Spread_ its width. Wide open, the repeats stay close to the original sound; narrowed, they squeeze towards the _Filter_ frequency. The filter sits inside the feedback loop, so every repeat is filtered again and the echoes thin out as they fade.

## Convolution Reverb

![The Convolution Reverb effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-convolution-reverb.80934c27d68d6c02.png)

The Convolution Reverb gets all its character from an impulse response (IR): a recording of how a space or object responds to sound. Floe's IRs are chosen for character. Some are realistic spaces, but most are stranger: textures and resonances that can transform a sound, making this as much a sound-design tool as a reverb.

-   **Impulse** — click the IR's name to choose one in the [IR browser](/docs/beta/usage/browsers). The arrows beside it, and , step to the previous or next IR, and jumps to a random one. All three follow the filters you've set in the IR browser. unloads the IR. There's no reverb until one is loaded.
-   **High-pass** — rolls off the low end of the reverb to avoid muddy bass, before the _Mix_ blend.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

Floe always has its own built-in IRs, and some sample libraries add more.

## Phaser

![The Phaser effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-phaser.440718747662cf50.png)

The Phaser sweeps a series of peaks and notches through the sound, giving it the classic swooshing, jet-like motion. Gentle settings add a subtle sense of movement to sustained sounds, while faster or more resonant ones become an unmistakable whoosh.

-   **Freq** — the centre of the sweep. Keep it low for a deep, throaty movement, or raise it to place the phasing amongst the brighter harmonics.
-   **Feedback** — sharpens the peaks and deepens the notches. Small amounts keep it a gentle swoosh, while higher amounts give the sweep a resonant, whistling edge.
-   **Shape** — how many peaks and notches there are. Turned down, there's a single broad one for a soft, vowel-like sweep; turned up, there are more of them for a richer, more obvious phasing.
-   **Rate** — how quickly the peaks sweep up and down. Low settings give a gentle, drifting movement, while turning it up makes the sweep a warble.
-   **Depth** — how far the peaks travel either side of _Freq_. Small amounts give a narrow, shimmering movement, while larger amounts sweep across the whole spectrum. With _Depth_ all the way down, the peaks hold still, leaving a fixed colouration that you can sweep by hand with _Freq_.
-   **Stereo** — offsets the left and right sweeps from each other so the movement drifts across the stereo image. At zero both channels sweep together; at maximum they sweep in opposite directions, for a wide, swirling feel.

## EQ

![The EQ effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-eq.65bb6b6d6747ec42.png)

The EQ is a three-band equaliser for lifting or taming parts of the frequency range, from broad tonal shaping to surgical cuts. Each layer also has its own EQ (see [Layers](/docs/beta/usage/eq-tab)).

The graph shows the combined effect of all three bands. Drag a band's handle to move it, scroll over it to change its resonance, or right-click it to change its type or copy and paste the whole band. The three bands have identical controls:

-   **Type** — a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a low-pass or high-pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum.
-   **Freq** — where the band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter.
-   **Reso** — how tightly the band is focused. For peaks and notches it's the width, from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen their corner, and the pass filters to add a peak at the cutoff.
-   **Gain** — how far the band boosts or cuts. Only the peak and shelf types use it.

## Limiter

![The Limiter effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-limiter.411ca416265c7bf3.png)

The limiter is a brickwall limiter: it holds your output firmly below a maximum level, whether you just want to catch stray peaks or push the overall level up without clipping. It's usually best placed last in the rack, so it catches everything above it.

-   **Gain** — drives the sound harder into the limiter. The harder you push, the more it's limited, making the sound louder and denser.
-   **Ceiling** — the level the output is never allowed to go above. Leave a small safety margin below 0 dB, giving headroom for whatever comes after Floe.

Three meters show what the limiter is doing: _In_ is the incoming level, _GR_ (gain reduction) is how much it's turning the sound down, and _Out_ is the final level.

It's a true-peak limiter, so the _Ceiling_ is a reliable maximum for the output. It looks a fraction of a millisecond ahead in the audio so it can react before a peak arrives. The delay is so small (0.5 ms) that Floe absorbs it rather than asking your DAW to compensate for it, so you don't need to do anything about it.

Thanks to that short lookahead, the limiter is fast and transparent for moderate amounts of limiting. Push it hard and there's less room for the gain change to ramp smoothly, so you may start to hear it colour or slightly distort the sound. If that happens, back off the _Gain_ or raise the _Ceiling_ a little.

---

# EQ Tab

> Shape a layer's tone with its three-band equaliser

The _EQ_ tab has a three-band equaliser for shaping the layer's tone before it's mixed with the other layers.

![A layer's EQ tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-eq.9ddfe3af1923a2ab.png)123

1.  **On/off** — switch the EQ on or off. A dot on the _EQ_ tab shows that it's on.
2.  **EQ graph** — shows the combined effect of all three bands. Drag a band's point to move it, use your mouse scroll wheel over it to change its resonance, or right-click it to change its type or copy and paste the whole band. For band types without a gain control, dragging up and down changes the resonance.
3.  **Bands** — the three bands have identical controls:
    -   **Type** — a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum.
    -   **Freq** — where the band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter.
    -   **Reso** — how tightly the band is focused. For peaks and notches it's the width; shelves use it to steepen their corner, and pass filters to add a peak at the cutoff.
    -   **Gain** — how far the band boosts or cuts. Only the peak and shelf types use it.

---

# Keyboard

> The on-screen keyboard in Floe's bottom panel, and what it shows about the notes and voices playing

The bottom panel of Floe's window is home to the on-screen keyboard. It's there on every page, and it's a quick way to see which notes are coming in, how many voices each one is playing, and which keys play which layer. You can click it to play notes too.

![The bottom panel on the Layers page, with a chord held on the keyboard](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/keyboard.65449d5b30f4e02c.png)12345

1.  **Tabs** — _PLAY_ shows the keyboard and macros. _MACROS_ shows the panel where you [set up the macros](/docs/beta/usage/macros#making-your-own-macros).
2.  **Macros** — the four macro knobs, the same ones as on the _Perform_ page. A greyed-out macro has nothing linked to it. See [Macros](/docs/beta/usage/macros).
3.  **Key range bars** — which keys play each layer, shown when any layer is limited to part of the keyboard.
4.  **Keys** — held notes light up, and red marks along the top show the voices sounding on each note.
5.  **Octave** — scroll the keyboard up or down to see a different part of the note range.

On the _Perform_ page, the bottom panel is simpler: there are no tabs, macros or octave controls, and the keyboard stretches across the whole panel to show nine octaves at once.

## Playing notes

Click a key to play it. Where you click sets the velocity: near the top of the key for the softest note, lower down for harder. A clicked note plays just like a note from your MIDI keyboard, so the layers' key ranges, the arpeggiator and everything else apply as usual.

Throughout the UI we label middle C (MIDI note 60) as C3. But some DAWs call that note C4.

## What the keyboard shows

The keys light up when you play, whether that's from your MIDI keyboard, your DAW, or a click, on any MIDI channel.

The red marks along the top of a key show the voices currently sounding on that note. A note can have more than one voice, such as one for each layer, and the mark gets stronger the more voices there are. Marks often linger after you let go, because each voice plays on through the release of its [volume envelope](/docs/beta/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope).

If you've set a _Reset keyswitch_ in [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls), that key has a blue marker along its bottom edge. See [Reproducibility](/docs/beta/usage/reproducibility).

## Key range bars

When a layer is limited to part of the keyboard, the bars above the keys (3) show which keys trigger each layer, with a separate colour for each layer. Hover over them for an enlarged view that names each layer's Instrument. See [Key range display](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-range-display) for everything the bars show, and [Key ranges](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) for how to set ranges up.

---

# Layers Page

> How to build and shape sounds with Floe's three layers

![Floe's window with the LAYERS page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-layers.cf24954b099e9572.png)

Floe is built around three layers, each holding a sound of its own, playing together as one.

For each layer, you pick a sound source, its _Instrument_, then shape it further with envelopes, filters, an LFO, looping and more.

A sound can use a single layer or blend two or three together. The LAYERS page is where you control all aspects of these identical layers.

## How sound flows through the engine

When you play a note, all three layers play at once (unless a layer is limited to a [key range](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-ranges)). Each is processed on its own, then the three are mixed together and sent through the [effects rack](/docs/beta/usage/effects) and the master volume. A layer with no Instrument is simply silent.

## The layer layout

![Floe's Layers page with the parts of a layer numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layers.b8bae924c810b253.png)1234

1.  **Layer header** — the layer's Instrument and its mixing controls, always visible.
2.  **Tabs** — switch between the layer's groups of controls: _PLAYBACK_, _MAIN_, _LFO_, _EQ_, _ARP_ and _CONFIG_. A dot on the _EQ_, _LFO_ or _ARP_ tab shows that it's switched on.
3.  **Tab controls** — the controls for the selected tab. Each tab has its own chapter. You can right-click these to copy, paste or reset all of its settings at once. It's a quick way to give two layers the same configuration.
4.  **All-layer buttons** — these act on all three layers together. loads a random Instrument into every layer, with each layer following its own Instrument browser filters (see [Randomisation](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation)). clears every layer.

## Layer header

![A layer's header with its controls numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-top-controls.2543928912c17947.png)123456

1.  **Instrument selector** — shows the layer's Instrument. Click it to open the [Instrument browser](/docs/beta/usage/browsers) and choose a different one. Right-click for more options: unload the Instrument, copy and paste the Instrument or the whole layer, or swap this layer with the one to its left or right (macro assignments move with a swapped layer).
2.  **Instrument navigation** — the arrows step to the previous or next Instrument, and jumps to a random one: a quick way to audition sounds without opening the browser. They follow the filters you've set in the Instrument browser, so they only move between the Instruments that match. unloads the Instrument, leaving the layer empty and silent.
3.  **Mute and Solo** — _Mute_ silences this layer, and _Solo_ lets you hear it on its own. Silenced layers keep running in the background, so if you unmute or unsolo them they carry on seamlessly from wherever they've got to. To save CPU, unload the Instrument instead. It's simplest to just use either Solo or Mute across the layers, not both — if you do mix them, Solo is prioritised over Mute.
4.  **Volume** — the layer's level, with its level meter alongside. While notes are sounding, red marks on the slider show the level of each voice. A voice's level depends on its velocity, where it falls in a [key range](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) fade, and any MPE volume expression.
5.  **Pan and Stereo** — _Pan_ places the layer anywhere from left to right. It uses a constant-power pan law (-3 dB at centre), so the layer keeps the same perceived loudness wherever you put it. _Stereo_ narrows or widens the layer: negative values pull it toward mono, positive values push it wider. Pan comes after Stereo, so you can narrow a wide sound and then place it as a single point. A mono sound has nothing to widen, so pushing it to maximum stereo width silences it.
6.  **Detune and Pitch** — _Pitch_ moves the layer up or down in semitones, and _Detune_ fine-tunes it in cents (hundredths of a semitone). Both work by speeding up or slowing down the audio. Right-click _Pitch_ to jump up or down an octave. Right-click _Detune_ and choose _Fold into Pitch_ to move any whole semitones from _Detune_ into _Pitch_, leaving the overall tuning unchanged. For a multi-sampled Instrument, _Transpose_ on the [CONFIG tab](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab) may sound more natural.

See [Controls](/docs/beta/usage/controls) for the ways to adjust knobs, sliders and number fields.

## The tabs

Below the header, each layer's controls are grouped into six tabs. Each has its own chapter:

-   [**PLAYBACK**](/docs/beta/usage/playback-tab) — how the layer plays its samples: play mode, sample start, reverse, [granular synthesis](/docs/beta/usage/playback-tab#granular-synthesis) and [looping](/docs/beta/usage/playback-tab#looping).
-   [**MAIN**](/docs/beta/usage/main-tab) — the [volume envelope](/docs/beta/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope) and [filter](/docs/beta/usage/main-tab#filter).
-   [**LFO**](/docs/beta/usage/lfo-tab) — add movement to various aspects.
-   [**EQ**](/docs/beta/usage/eq-tab) — a three-band equaliser to shape the layer's tone.
-   [**ARP**](/docs/beta/usage/arp-tab) — the arpeggiator, which turns held notes into rhythmic patterns.
-   [**CONFIG**](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab) — how the layer responds to your playing: transpose, pitch bend, keytracking, monophonic, MPE, [key ranges](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) and the velocity curve.

Right-click a tab to copy, paste or reset all of its settings at once. Copy a tab on one layer and paste it into another to give both layers the same settings, or reset a tab to start it afresh.

![The menu that opens when you right-click a layer's MAIN tab](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-tab-menu.43085b4dca75ff1e.png)

---

# LFO Tab

> Add movement to a layer by modulating its volume, filter, pan, pitch or grain position

Use the LFO (low frequency oscillator) to add movement to the sound, modulating one of the layer's controls such as its volume or filter cutoff.

![A layer's LFO tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-lfo.dee1730f34b4599a.png)1234

1.  **On/off** — switch the LFO on or off. A dot on the _LFO_ tab shows that it's on.
2.  **LFO display** — a live preview of the LFO's shape and speed. Drag it left and right to change _Time_, and up and down to change _Amount_.
3.  **Target, Shape and Mode**:
    -   **Target** — what the LFO moves: _Volume_, _Filter_, _Pan_, _Pitch_ or _Grain Position_. The movement happens around the target's current setting. Some targets need their feature switched on first: for example, the filter must be on for the _Filter_ target, and the play mode must be _Granular Fixed_ for _Grain Position_.
    -   **Shape** — the LFO's waveform. Alongside the classic shapes there are random and plucky ones.
    -   **Variation** — appears when a random shape (_Random Steps_ or _Random Glide_) is selected. It allows you to remove the element of chance from random movement. _Different on every note_ gives each note a fresh random pattern. _Identical on all notes_ plays exactly the same pattern every time, chosen by the **Seed** number: try a few until you find a movement you like. It's saved with the preset, so everyone hears the same movement. _Identical on each key_ gives each key its own repeatable pattern. In _Free_ mode, a note that joins already-sounding notes follows their pattern. The Seed works because the random steps follow a sequence of numbers that only looks random: the Seed is where that sequence starts. Learn more about seeds and reproducibility on the [Reproducibility](/docs/beta/usage/reproducibility) page.
    -   **Mode** — with _Retrigger_, every note starts the LFO from the beginning of its cycle. With _Free_, a new note joins in wherever the layer's sounding notes have reached, so all the notes move together.
4.  **Amount and Time**:
    -   **Amount** — how far the LFO moves its target. Negative values flip the shape upside down. If MPE press or slide is routed to the LFO amount (see the [CONFIG tab](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab)), red marks show each voice's current amount.
    -   **Time** — how long each cycle lasts. With _Sync_ on, it's a note length at your DAW's tempo, such as 1/4; a D means dotted and a T means triplet. With _Sync_ off, it's a speed in Hz.
    -   **Sync** — tie the LFO to your DAW's tempo. Both the synced and free _Time_ settings are remembered, so you can switch between them without losing either.

---

# Macros

> Shape a sound with knobs that move several controls at once, and make your own

A macro is a knob that moves other controls for you. Floe has four of them, and each can be linked to up to six controls anywhere in Floe, each by its own amount.

![The four macro knobs in the bottom panel, each named for what it does in the preset](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/macros-play.33614f920333aa4e.png)

Preset authors use macros in two main ways. Sometimes a macro simply brings forward one control that matters a lot for this particular sound, tuned to a useful range, so you don't have to go looking for it. Other times it moves several controls together to create something that feels like a brand-new control made for the preset. A macro called _Surge_ might push up a distortion's drive, open a low-pass filter and thicken a granular texture, all with one turn.

Each macro has a name, chosen by whoever made the preset, that hints at what it does. Not every preset uses all four.

## Playing with macros

The macro knobs appear on the [_Perform_](/docs/beta/usage/perform) page, and on the _PLAY_ tab of the bottom panel when you're on the [_Layers_](/docs/beta/usage/layers) or [_Effects_](/docs/beta/usage/effects) page. They're the same four knobs in both places. A greyed-out macro isn't linked to anything, so it does nothing.

Your MIDI keyboard's mod wheel is linked to the first macro, so you can shape the sound as you play. You can change this, and link the other macros to knobs or faders on your controller, in the [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls) panel. Macros are also handy for automation in your DAW: one lane can move several controls at once.

When a macro moves a knob, the knob's coloured arc separates from its dial. The dial shows the knob's own setting; the arc shows the value you actually hear. See [Controls](/docs/beta/usage/controls).

## Making your own macros

Macros aren't only for preset authors. Once you're comfortable designing your own sounds, a macro or two can give your own presets a few expressive controls that shape the sound exactly the way you want, ready for your MIDI controller or DAW automation. The first macro is a good one to start with, since your mod wheel already moves it.

To set up macros, go to the _Layers_ or _Effects_ page and click the _MACROS_ tab on the left of the bottom panel. Each macro's knob is shown alongside its settings.

![The MACROS tab of the bottom panel, showing the first macro with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/macros.dda7e4e0ecfb2b8a.png)123

1.  **Destination knobs** — one blue knob for each control the macro is linked to, setting how far the macro moves it.
2.  **Add destination** — link another control to the macro.
3.  **Name** — click to rename the macro.

_Linking controls, setting their amounts, and renaming a macro_

### Linking a control

1.  **Click** next to the macro (2). Every control you can link to gets a blue plus icon of its own, across the whole window.
2.  **Hover** over one of them. A line joins it to the macro, with a note of what's about to be connected.
3.  **Click** to make the link. A new blue destination knob (1) appears next to the macro. To cancel instead, press `escape` or click somewhere empty.

You can link knobs, sliders and number fields. You can also link the handles you drag around, such as the points on the envelopes and the EQ graph, or the loop points on the waveform.

### Setting the amount

There are two kinds of knob here, and they do different jobs. The macro knob is the one you play: turning it moves every control linked to it at once. Each blue destination knob (1) is one you set and then leave alone: it decides how far the macro moves its one control, anywhere from a subtle nudge to a sweep across the control's whole range. A new link starts at zero, so the macro does nothing to that control until you change it.

The easiest way to set it is to turn the macro all the way up, then drag the destination knob while you play. Watch the linked control's coloured arc move, and listen until it sounds right.

-   **Right of centre** — the control goes up as the macro goes up.
-   **Left of centre** — the control goes down as the macro goes up.

The destination knob isn't linear: more of its travel is given to small amounts, so they're easier to set precisely.

Hover over a destination knob to see what it's linked to. It also shows the control's value right now, and what it will be with the macro at 0% and at 100%. Rest the cursor there for a moment and Floe draws a line to the linked control, scrolling it into view if needed.

Double-click a destination knob to type an amount, or right-click it for more options: copy and paste the amount between destinations, type a value, reset it to zero, invert it, or edit its range.

### Editing the range

Instead of setting an amount, you can set the two values the control moves between, in the control's own units: a filter sweeping from 200 Hz to 2 kHz, say. Right-click a destination knob and choose _Edit Range…_. The popup has two knobs:

-   **Macro at 0%** — the control's value when the macro is fully down.
-   **Macro at 100%** — the control's value when the macro is fully up.

Each knob changes only its own end, so you can raise the bottom of a filter sweep without changing where it ends up. While you hold either knob, you hear the sound as it would be with the macro at that end, though the macro itself doesn't move. Play some notes as you drag to find exactly the right values.

Changing an end also changes what you hear with the macro where it is now. To keep the current sound, tick _Move (macro name) to keep this value_: Floe moves the macro to whichever position gives the control the value it has now. Everything else the macro controls moves with it.

### How a macro moves a control

A macro moves a control relative to the control's own setting. With the macro at 0%, the control is exactly where you set it, and turning the macro up adds the amount on top. So adjusting the control itself shifts the whole sweep up or down.

If more than one macro is linked to the same control, their movements add together. A control can never go beyond its normal range, however far the macros push it.

### Removing a link

Hover over a destination knob and a red appears beneath it. Click it to remove the link. The control keeps its own setting; it just stops following the macro.

### Naming macros

Click the name (3) and type a new one. Choose a name that says what the macro does to the sound, such as _Brightness_ or _Swell_. The name is saved with the preset and labels the macro knob everywhere it appears.

### Copying, swapping and resetting

Right-click a macro knob for these options, alongside the usual ones for any knob:

-   **Copy Macro** and **Paste Macro** — copy a macro's value, name and links onto another macro.
-   **Swap with Left** and **Swap with Right** — exchange the macro with its neighbour, along with its value, name and links. This doesn't move MIDI CC assignments or DAW automation, though.
-   **Reset Macro to Default** — start the macro afresh, with no links and its original name. The next option resets it to how it was in the loaded preset instead.

### Legacy destinations

A yellow on a destination knob means it's linked to a [legacy parameter](/docs/beta/reference/legacy-parameters). These are kept so older DAW projects still work, and you'll only hear the macro move it while the legacy override is active. Legacy destinations can't use _Edit Range…_.

---

# Main Tab

> Shape each note's volume and tone over time with a layer's volume envelope and filter

The _MAIN_ tab shapes how each note's volume and tone change over time, using the volume envelope and the filter.

![A layer's MAIN tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-main.86776d3fc54ab4a0.png)1234

1.  **Volume envelope** — its switch and graph.
2.  **Filter** — its switch and graph.
3.  **Filter controls** — _Type_, _Cut_, _Res_ and _Env_.
4.  **Filter envelope** — shapes how the cutoff moves over time.

## Volume envelope

-   **On/off** — the volume envelope is typically best left on. If you turn it off every note plays its sample straight through to the end, however briefly you press the key: handy for one-shot sounds that should always be heard in full. Looping is disabled while the envelope is off. And since notes can't be cut short, voices can pile up and use a lot of CPU if you play quickly.
-   **Envelope graph** — drag its three points to shape each note's volume over time: the first sets the _Attack_, the second the _Decay_ and _Sustain_ together, and the third the _Release_.

## Filter

Each note gets its own filter, so the filter envelope and the LFO can sweep every note independently. It's a clean, digital-sounding state-variable filter (12 dB per octave). For broader tone shaping, see the [EQ tab](/docs/beta/usage/eq-tab).

-   **On/off** — switch the filter on or off.
-   **Filter graph** — shows the filter's response. Drag the point left and right to set the cutoff, and up and down for the resonance.
-   **Type** — choose the kind of filter, such as low-pass, high-pass or band-pass. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each.
-   **Cut** — the cutoff frequency, where the filter takes effect. The filter envelope and LFO move the cutoff around this setting. If MPE press or slide is routed to the filter (see the [CONFIG tab](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab)), red marks show each voice's current cutoff.
-   **Res** — resonance, which emphasises the frequencies around the cutoff. It never self-oscillates. For the band-pass, notch and band-shelving types it also narrows the band, and for the peak type it sets the size of the boost.
-   **Env** — how strongly the filter envelope moves the cutoff on each note. At the centre it does nothing. Turn it up and the cutoff rises and falls with the envelope; turn it down and the cutoff moves the opposite way. With a low-pass filter, for example, a long attack opens the sound up gradually as each note begins.
-   **Filter envelope** — works like the volume envelope, shaping how the cutoff moves over time, scaled by _Env_.

---

# MIDI

> Information about MIDI control in Floe

Floe responds to MIDI the way you'd expect from a software instrument: notes and velocity, the sustain pedal and pitch wheel, CC controllers mapped to its parameters, and MPE for expressive controllers.

-   **Velocity** — how hard you play sets each note's volume, shaped by each layer's [velocity to volume curve](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab#velocity-to-volume-curve) on its _CONFIG_ tab. On multi-sampled Instruments with velocity layers, it also picks which samples play.
-   **Sustain pedal** — CC-64 holds notes after you release the keys, until you lift the pedal, just like a piano's sustain pedal.
-   **Pitch wheel** — how far it bends is set per layer with _Pitch Bend Range_ on the layer's [_CONFIG_ tab](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab), so one layer can bend a whole tone while another underneath it stays put. A range of 0 disables pitch bend for that layer.
-   **All Notes Off and All Sound Off** — the channel messages that DAWs and controllers send to stop stuck notes. All Notes Off (CC-123) releases every note on that channel, including sustained ones, so they fade out naturally; All Sound Off (CC-120) silences them immediately.

## MIDI CC

All automatable parameters can be assigned to a MIDI CC, so you can move them with the knobs and faders on your MIDI controller.

### Creating a mapping

Right-click a parameter (a knob or slider anywhere on the UI) and select _MIDI CC Learn_, then move the dial on your MIDI controller that you want to assign. To remove a mapping, right-click the parameter and select _Remove MIDI CC_ (followed by the CC number). A mapped CC works on any MIDI channel.

You can also add and remove mappings from the [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls) panel, which lists every mapping on the current instance in one place.

![MIDI CC tab of the Performance Controls panel](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/midi-cc.2063ddce6cec1071.png)

### Default mappings

Unless you have changed your default Performance Controls, these mappings will be assigned:

-   **CC 1 (Modwheel)** — Macro 1
-   **CC 7** — Master Volume
-   **CC 11** — Master Timbre

### How mappings are saved

MIDI CC mappings are part of the [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls) system. They apply only to the current instance of Floe, but you can set up a default configuration that all new instances start with. Presets never touch them, so you can browse presets without your settings changing each time.

## MPE

MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE) lets compatible controllers, such as the Seaboard, LinnStrument, Osmose and Haken Continuum, shape each note independently.

To switch it on, open the [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls) panel with in the top panel, click the _MPE_ tab, and tick _MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression)_.

![The MPE tab of the Performance Controls panel](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/mpe.2d6bff66cf1a9aa7.png)

Once it's on, each note responds to the standard MPE per-note messages:

-   **Glide**: pitch bend on a note's channel bends just that note, following the MPE ±48-semitone convention (or whatever range your controller negotiates). The master channel's pitch wheel still bends everything, using each layer's pitch bend range parameter.
-   **Press**: each note's channel pressure (aftertouch).
-   **Slide**: each note's CC74.

Choose what press and slide control for each layer with the _MPE_ button on its [_CONFIG_ tab](/docs/beta/usage/config-tab). Each has a target (_Volume_, _Filter_, _Timbre_ or _LFO Amount_) and an amount. The amount can be negative to invert the response, or beyond 100% to reach the full effect with a smaller gesture.

With the _Volume_ target, press brings each note up to the level of the layer's _Volume_ slider, and slide works like a fader for each note, topping out at the slider's level. So until you apply expression, notes play quieter than the slider. The _Filter_, _Timbre_ and _LFO Amount_ targets nudge a setting for each note individually: _Filter_ moves the layer's filter cutoff, _Timbre_ the master _Timbre_ control, and _LFO Amount_ the layer's LFO _Amount_. Press adds to the setting, while slide can move it either way, with its centre position leaving it unchanged.

The _MPE smoothing_ setting in the [Performance Controls](/docs/beta/usage/performance-controls) panel sets how gradually press and slide respond: lower is more responsive, higher is smoother.

While notes are sounding, each active voice gets a red line on whichever control press or slide is routed to — the filter cutoff knob, the LFO Amount knob, or the master Timbre knob in the top panel — so you can see the expression from each voice.

The MPE Configuration Message for zone setup is supported too, and a sustain pedal on a zone's master channel sustains the whole zone.

CLAP note expressions (per-note pitch, pressure, and brightness) work the same way in supporting hosts regardless of the MPE setting.

---

# Perform Page

> The distraction-free page for exploring presets and variations

![Floe's window with the PERFORM page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-perform.2da3c92ed66c142e.png)

The _Perform_ page is a good place to start when you're getting to know a sample library and its presets. It shows the artwork in full, and gathers the controls you'll reach for most often into one uncluttered panel.

Most of the controls here also appear elsewhere in the interface. They're the same controls, so a change on one page shows up on the other.

When you're ready to go deeper, everything else can be found on the [_Layers_](/docs/beta/usage/layers) and [_Effects_](/docs/beta/usage/effects) pages.

![Floe's Perform page and top panel with their controls numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/perform.a40ff59a2509fcb3.png)12345678910

1.  **Preset box** — in the top panel. Click it to open the preset browser.
2.  **Preset** — the name of the current preset's sample library, with the preset's name beneath it. The arrows either side, and , step to the previous or next preset, just like the arrows in the top panel.
3.  **Folder** — the folder the preset lives in, which usually tells you what kind of sound it is.
4.  **Macros** — four knobs set up to shape this particular sound.
5.  **Layers** — the Instrument on each of the three layers, with its mute, solo and volume controls.
6.  **Random variation** — click the strip for a fresh take on the preset.
7.  **Compare** — switch between the preset as it was loaded and your changes.
8.  **Description** — more about the preset, from its author or written automatically by Floe.
9.  **Hide panel** — hides the panel so you can see the artwork in full. The arrow only appears when you hover just above the panel.
10.  **Keyboard** — lights up with the notes you play, and you can click it to play notes too. See [Keyboard](/docs/beta/usage/keyboard).

## Choosing presets

The arrows (2) are the quickest way to audition presets: play a few notes, click an arrow, and play again. To look through them by folder or tag, click the preset name in the top panel (1) to open the preset browser. See [Loading Presets](/docs/beta/presets/loading-presets) for more ways to find presets.

Once you change anything, the preset's name is marked _(modified)_.

## Macros

Use the macros (4) to shape the preset to your liking. Each one is tuned to move one or more settings in a musical way, and the knob's name hints at what it does. A greyed-out macro isn't used by the preset. By default, your mod wheel is linked to the first macro, so you can shape the sound as you play. See also [Macros](/docs/beta/usage/macros) and [MIDI](/docs/beta/usage/midi).

## Layers

Each preset is built from up to three layers (5). Not every preset uses all three. For each active layer you'll see:

-   **Instrument** — the name of the layer's Instrument, with the folder it comes from in italics. Click it to open the [Instrument browser](/docs/beta/usage/browsers) and choose a different one.
-   **Waveform** — a picture of the Instrument's sound.
-   **Mute and Solo** — _M_ silences the layer, and _S_ lets you hear it on its own. Try each layer in turn to hear what it adds to the whole.
-   **Volume** — the slider sets the layer's level, with its level meter alongside.

For everything else a layer can do, switch to the [_Layers_](/docs/beta/usage/layers) page.

## Random variation

Click anywhere on the _Random Variation_ strip (6) for a fresh take on the preset. Where you click sets how far it strays. Towards the left gives gentle, related tweaks; towards the right gets wilder, with Instruments swapped, layers added and effects changed. Hover over the strip to see how big a change you'll get. The button at its left edge rolls another variation at the same amount as last time.

Every variation starts from the preset as you loaded it, so you can keep clicking without drifting ever further away. _Undo_ in the top panel steps back through them. When you find one you like, save it as a preset to keep it. See [Randomisation](/docs/beta/usage/randomisation).

## Compare

Once you've changed something, the _Original/Modified_ switch (7) lets you flick between the preset as it was last loaded or saved and your changed version. It's an easy way to check that your changes really are an improvement. If you edit anything while you're listening to the original, that edit replaces your modified version, but you can always get it back with _Undo_.

## Description

The description tells you about the preset, such as any unusual tuning or tips for playing it. The top panel shows its opening, usually a summary of the sound, and the rest continues here (8).

If the whole description fits in the top panel, Floe fills this space with a generated summary of the preset instead.

## Seeing the artwork in full

Hover just above the panel, in the middle, and a small arrow appears (9). Click it to hide the panel and see the artwork uncovered. Click the arrow again to bring the panel back.

---

# Performance Controls

> The Performance Controls panel — MIDI CC mappings, MPE, Reproducibility, and Profiles

The _Performance Controls_ panel is where you set up how Floe responds to your playing and your controllers. Open it with in the top panel, or from the main menu.

![The Performance Controls panel with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/performance-controls.2063ddce6cec1071.png)123

1.  **Profiles menu** — load and save profiles. It reads _Profiles_ until you load one, and then shows that profile's name.
2.  **Settings for new instances** — make this panel's settings the ones new instances start with.
3.  **Tabs**:
    -   **MIDI CC** — every [MIDI CC mapping](/docs/beta/usage/midi#midi-cc) on this instance. Remove one with its button, or click _Add_ to create one by choosing a CC number and a parameter, as an alternative to right-clicking a knob and using _MIDI CC Learn_.
    -   **Reproducibility** — the _Seed_ and reset settings that make Floe's random elements play back the same every time. See [Reproducibility](/docs/beta/usage/reproducibility).
    -   **MPE** — switch on [MPE](/docs/beta/usage/midi#mpe) for expressive controllers, and set how smoothly per-note expression responds.

## Scope

Everything in this panel belongs to the current instance rather than being a global preference. When you save your DAW project, these settings are saved with it, so the next time you open the project you can perform it the same way. Different instances in the same project can each have their own settings. However, loading a _preset_ leaves it untouched, meaning you can audition presets without disturbing your performance setup.

## Settings for new instances

Each Floe instance has its own performance controls, but you can choose what new instances start with: their MIDI CC mappings, MPE, and Reproducibility settings. Set the panel up the way you like, then click _Make default_ (2), just below the panel's title. The reset button beside it does the reverse, returning this instance to your defaults. Both only appear when the current settings differ from your defaults; otherwise a _Default for new instances_ label shows in their place.

For example, say your keyboard has a fader that you always want on the second macro. Assign it once with _MIDI CC Learn_, click _Make default_, and every new instance you add from then on starts with that fader ready to go. Instances already in your projects keep their own settings.

Floe's own defaults include some common MIDI CC mappings, such as the mod wheel (CC1) to the first macro. See [MIDI](/docs/beta/usage/midi#default-mappings) for the full list.

## Profiles

A profile is a named, saved bundle of the panel's settings, like a save file for this Performance Controls. Profiles are useful when you switch between MIDI controllers regularly: save one profile per controller, then switch between them as you swap hardware.

Open the _Profiles_ menu (1) at the top-right of the panel to:

-   Load a profile, applying it to the current instance immediately. This is a one-shot copy, not a persistent link: further changes to the instance don't affect the saved profile unless you save over it.
-   Save the current settings as a new profile.
-   Overwrite, rename, or delete an existing profile.

Once a profile is loaded, the menu shows its name, with an asterisk when you've changed the settings since.

---

# Playback Tab
