| Effect/StereoWiden | Width | 21 | Ster Width | Width narrows or widens the stereo image. Negative values pull the sound towards mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves it as it is. It rebalances the mid (what both channels share) against the side (what differs between them), so at -100% only the mid is left, and at +100% only the side, which makes anything dead centre disappear. Tip: each layer has its own Stereo control if you want to widen just one of them. |
| Effect/StereoWiden | On | 22 | Ster On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Chorus | Rate | 23 | Chr Rate | The Rate sets how quickly the pitch drifts up and down. Slow rates give a gentle swelling movement, while faster rates become a shimmering warble. |
| Effect/Chorus | Legacy High-pass | 24 | Chr Legacy High-pass | Legacy high-pass parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Chorus | Depth | 25 | Chr Depth | The Depth sets how far the pitch drifts away from the original. Small amounts thicken the sound, while larger amounts give an obvious, tape-like wobble. At zero, the delayed copies are still there, adding a static colouration. |
| Effect/Chorus | Legacy Wet | 26 | Chr Legacy Wet | Legacy processed-signal volume. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Chorus | Legacy Dry | 27 | Chr Legacy Dry | Legacy unprocessed-signal volume. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Chorus | On | 28 | Chr On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Filter | Resonance | 29 | Filt Resonance | Resonance emphasises the frequencies right at the cutoff, adding a peak there on the pass filters. For Band-pass and Notch it narrows the band, for Peak it tightens the boost, and for the shelves it steepens the corner. |
| Effect/Filter | Gain | 30 | Filt Gain | Gain sets how far the Peak and shelf types boost or cut around the cutoff. |
| Effect/StereoWiden | Mode | 31 | Ster Mode | Mode sets how the widening is done. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. |
| Effect/StereoWiden | Bass Mono | 32 | Ster Bass Mono | Bass Mono sets the point below which the sound is summed to the centre. Holding the low end in the middle keeps kicks and basslines solid, and stops them losing power on mono systems. The two bands are split with a 24 dB per octave Linkwitz-Riley crossover, so they recombine without a dip around the crossover point. |
| Effect/Compressor | Type | 33 | Comp Type | The compressor algorithm to use. The Vintage type has a bit of character, and automatically sets the attack and release. The Modern type offers more precision. |
| Effect/Compressor | Attack | 34 | Comp Attack | How quickly the compressor responds to a rise in level. |
| Effect/Compressor | Release | 35 | Comp Release | How quickly the compressor recovers after the level drops. |
| Effect/Compressor | Mix | 36 | Comp Mix | Blend between the dry input and the compressed signal. |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | Legacy High-pass | 65 | Conv Legacy High-pass | Legacy high-pass parameter. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | Legacy Wet | 66 | Conv Legacy Wet | Legacy processed-signal volume. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | Legacy Dry | 67 | Conv Legacy Dry | Legacy unprocessed-signal volume. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | On | 68 | Conv On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Reverb | Decay Time | 69 | Rvrb Decay Time | The Decay Time sets how long the tail takes to fade away once a sound stops. It holds steady whatever the Size, so you can choose the length of the reverb and the character of the space separately. |
| Effect/Reverb | Pre Low-pass Cutoff | 70 | Rvrb Pre Low-pass Cutoff | The Pre LP is a low-pass filter cutoff for rolling the highs off the signal on its way into the reverb, for a darker, more distant space. The dry signal keeps its full range. |
| Effect/Reverb | Pre High-pass Cutoff | 71 | Rvrb Pre High-pass Cutoff | The Pre HP is a high-pass filter cutoff for rolling the lows off the signal on its way into the reverb, keeping the tail clear so the bass stays tight and centred. The dry signal keeps its full range. |
| Effect/Reverb | Low-shelf Cutoff | 72 | Rvrb Low-shelf Cutoff | The Lo-Shelf sets the frequency below which the reverb tail is cut by the Lo-Gain amount. Turn Lo-Gain down to hear it work. |
| Effect/Reverb | Low Gain | 73 | Rvrb Low Gain | The Lo-Gain sets how much the reverb tail is cut below the Lo-Shelf frequency. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the low end thins out as the reverb fades - handy for stopping long tails clouding the bass. |
| Effect/Reverb | High-shelf Cutoff | 74 | Rvrb High-shelf Cutoff | The Hi-Shelf sets the frequency above which the reverb tail is cut by the Hi-Gain amount. Turn Hi-Gain down to hear it work. |
| Effect/Reverb | High Gain | 75 | Rvrb High Gain | The Hi-Gain sets how much the reverb tail is cut above the Hi-Shelf frequency. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the highs die away first, just as soft furnishings absorb them in a real room. |
| Effect/Reverb | Chorus Amount | 76 | Rvrb Chorus Amount | The Depth sets how far the reverb's reflections drift, smearing the resonances that build up in the tail. A little stops long tails ringing; more gives an obvious shimmer and movement. |
| Effect/Reverb | Chorus Frequency | 77 | Rvrb Chorus Frequency | The Mod Rate sets how quickly the drift set by Depth moves through the tail. Very slow rates give a gentle, breathing wash, while faster rates add a distinct warble. |
| Effect/Reverb | Size | 78 | Rvrb Size | The Size scales the spacing of the simulated reflections, setting how large the space feels. Small values pack them together for a boxy, coloured character; large values spread them out for something open and airy. |
| Effect/Reverb | Delay | 79 | Rvrb Delay | The Predelay holds the reverb back for a moment so the dry sound is heard on its own first. Short amounts keep the sound upfront and defined, while longer amounts push the walls further away. |
| Effect/Reverb | Mix | 80 | Rvrb Mix | Blend between the dry input and the reverb signal. |
| Effect/Reverb | On | 81 | Rvrb On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Phaser | Feedback | 82 | Phs Feedback | Feedback routes the phased signal back into the filters, sharpening the peaks and deepening the notches. Small amounts keep it as a gentle swoosh, while higher amounts give the sweep a resonant, whistling edge. |
| Effect/Phaser | Mod Rate | 83 | Phs Mod Rate | The Rate sets how quickly the peaks sweep up and down the frequency range. Slow rates give a gentle, drifting movement, while faster rates turn the sweep into a warble. |
| Effect/Phaser | Center Frequency | 84 | Phs Center Frequency | Freq sets the centre of the sweep: the frequency that the peaks and notches travel around. Keep it low for a deep, throaty movement, or raise it to place the phasing amongst the brighter harmonics. |
| Effect/Phaser | Shape | 85 | Phs Shape | Shape sets how many peaks and notches are carved into the sound. Turned down there's a single broad one for a soft, vowel-like sweep; turned up there are more of them stacked up the spectrum for a richer, more obvious phasing. |
| Effect/Phaser | Mod Depth | 86 | Phs Mod Depth | The Depth sets how far the peaks travel either side of the Freq setting. Small amounts give a narrow, shimmering movement, while larger amounts sweep across the whole spectrum. Tip: with Depth all the way down the peaks hold still, leaving a fixed colouration that you can sweep by hand with Freq. |
| Effect/Phaser | Stereo Amount | 87 | Phs Stereo Amount | Stereo offsets the left and right sweeps from each other so the movement drifts across the stereo image. At zero both channels sweep together; at maximum they sweep in opposite directions, for a wide, swirling feel. |
| Effect/Phaser | Mix | 88 | Phs Mix | Blend between the dry input and the phased signal. |
| Effect/Phaser | On | 89 | Phs On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Delay | Mode | 90 | Dly Mode | Mode sets how the repeats move around the stereo image. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. |
| Effect/Delay | Filter Cutoff | 91 | Dly Filter Cutoff | Filter sets the centre of a band-pass that the repeats run through, with Spread setting how wide that band is. The dry signal is left untouched. It sits inside the feedback loop, so every repeat is filtered again and the echoes thin out as they fade. |
| Effect/Delay | Filter Spread | 92 | Dly Filter Spread | Spread sets how wide the repeats' filter band is. Wide open leaves them close to the original sound; narrowed, they squeeze towards the Filter frequency, losing a little more of the top and bottom ends with every pass. |
| Effect/Delay | Time Left (ms) | 93 | Dly Time Left (ms) | The gap between the repeats in the left channel, set freely in milliseconds. Tip: very short times stop sounding like separate echoes and become a metallic, resonant tone instead. |
| Effect/Delay | Legacy Time Right (ms) | 94 | Dly Legacy Time Right (ms) | The gap between the repeats in the right channel, set freely in milliseconds. It's unused in Mono mode, where both channels follow Time L. |
| Effect/Delay | Time Left (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | 95 | Dly Time Left (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | Legacy left delay time. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Delay | Time Right (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | 96 | Dly Time Right (Tempo Synced) (Legacy) | Legacy right delay time. Kept for backwards-compatibility with DAW automation |
| Effect/Delay | On | 97 | Dly On | Enable Tempo Sync to set the delay times as note lengths that follow the host's tempo, keeping the repeats in time with your track. With it off, the times are dialled in freely in milliseconds. |
| Effect/Delay | Mix | 98 | Dly Mix | Blend between the dry input and the delayed signal. |
| Effect/Delay | On | 99 | Dly On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/Delay | Feedback | 100 | Dly Feedback | Feedback sets how long the echoes trail on for: low amounts give a handful of repeats, while high amounts carry on long after the note has gone. It works by feeding each repeat back in to make the next one. |
| Effect/Filter | Type | 105 | Filt Type | Select the filter type. Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf bring in the Gain knob, letting you boost as well as cut. |
| Effect/Filter | Cutoff Frequency | 106 | Filt Cutoff Frequency | Cutoff sets where the filter does its work: the point the pass filters roll off from, the centre of the band for Band-pass and Notch, or the corner for the shelves. |
| Effect/Chorus | High-pass | 107 | Chr High-pass | Remove low frequencies from the chorused copies. The dry signal is unaffected. Raise this to keep the bass tight and free from movement. |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | High-pass | 108 | Conv High-pass | Use the high-pass to roll off the low end of the reverb to avoid muddy bass. It applies to the reverbed signal alone, before the Mix blend. |
| Effect/Bitcrush | Mix | 109 | Bitc Mix | Blend between the dry input and the bitcrushed signal. |
| Effect/Bitcrush | Output | 110 | Bitc Output | Output level after the mix. |
| Effect/Chorus | Mix | 111 | Chr Mix | Blend between the dry input and the chorused signal. |
| Effect/Chorus | Output | 112 | Chr Output | Output level after the mix. |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | Mix | 113 | Conv Mix | Blend between the dry input and the reverb signal. |
| Effect/Convolution Reverb | Output | 114 | Conv Output | The effect's output level, applied after the Mix blend. |
| Effect/Distortion | Mix | 115 | Dist Mix | Blend between the dry input and the distorted signal. Backing it off keeps the clarity of the original sound with the distortion sitting underneath it. |
| Effect/StereoWiden | Mix | 116 | Ster Mix | Blend between the dry input and the stereo-widened signal. |
| Effect/Filter | Mix | 117 | Filt Mix | Blend between the dry input and the filtered signal. |
| Effect/Compressor | Threshold | 118 | Comp Threshold | The threshold that the audio has to pass above before the compression should start taking place. |
| Effect/Compressor | Ratio | 119 | Comp Ratio | The intensity of compression (high ratios mean more compression). Above around 2:1 begins to make the pumping effect much more noticable. |
| Effect/EQ | On | 120 | Eq On | Enable/disable this effect. |
| Effect/EQ | Mix | 121 | Eq Mix | Blend between the dry input and the equalised signal. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 1 | Type | 122 | EqB1 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 1 | Frequency | 123 | EqB1 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 1 | Resonance | 124 | EqB1 Resonance | Resonance sets how tightly the band is focused. For the Peak and Notch types it's the width, going from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen the transition at their corner, and the pass filters use it to add a peak at the cutoff. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 1 | Gain | 125 | EqB1 Gain | Gain sets how far this band boosts or cuts at its frequency. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use Gain. The notch and pass filters always cut by their own fixed shape, so with those the knob is inactive. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 2 | Type | 126 | EqB2 Type | Choose the shape of this band: a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum. Only the Peak, Low-shelf and High-shelf types use the Gain knob; with the others it's inactive. |
| Effect/EQ/Band 2 | Frequency | 127 | EqB2 Frequency | Frequency sets where this band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter. |

| Effect/Limiter | On | 140 | Lmtr On | Enable/disable this effect. |

Presets made before Floe had this switch load with it off, so they sound just as they were made. |
| Effect/Distortion | Punish | 149 | Dist Punish | Punish stacks extra distortion stages after the first, each one driven harder than the last, for a denser, grittier, more compressed edge. Drive sets how hard the signal hits the first stage; Punish sets how much is piled on top. |

# Sample Libraries

> What is a Floe sample library

Sample libraries are where Floe's sounds come from: collections of mapped, playable sounds along with images, tags and other details. Without a sample library, Floe can't make any sound.

A library usually has a theme or focus. 'Music Box Suite', for example, is multi-sampled music boxes, while 'Lost Reveries' is a collection of single-sample ambient tones.

A sample library can contain [Instruments](/docs/reference/instruments), impulse responses, or both. Most focus on Instruments, but some contain only impulse responses, giving the [Convolution Reverb](/docs/usage/effects#convolution-reverb) new spaces and textures to work with.

You don't load a library itself. Instead, you load its Instruments into Floe's layers and its impulse responses into the Convolution Reverb. To see which libraries you have installed, open the menu at the top of Floe's window and choose _Info_.

## What's inside a library

Floe sample libraries use Floe's own open format: portable folders of audio files and configuration files, made with Floe's [developer tools](/docs/develop/develop-libraries). A library's folder usually has a name like `Developer Name - Library Name`, and inside it a `Samples` subfolder and a file called `floe.lua`. Libraries can hold thousands of audio files and take up many gigabytes.

---

# Autosave

> How Floe autosaves your sound, and how to get it back

Floe saves a copy of each instance's sound every few seconds while you work, so a sound you've spent time on is never lost for good. That helps if Floe or your DAW crashes, but it's just as handy for everyday accidents: deleting the wrong track, closing a project without saving, or tweaking a sound past the point you liked it.

Autosaves are ordinary preset files. Floe only saves when something has changed, and the files are tiny, so autosaving won't slow your computer down or fill up your drive.

## Getting a sound back

1.  In the [preset box](/docs/presets/loading-presets#the-preset-box), click _Load from file_.
2.  Go to Floe's autosave folder:
    -   Windows: `C:\Users\Public\Floe\Autosaves`
    -   macOS: `/Users/Shared/Floe/Autosaves`
    -   Linux: `~/Floe/Autosaves`
3.  Pick the autosave you want. Each file name holds the time and date it was saved, followed by the instance name, such as `autosave 14-32-05 Thu 2 Oct 2026 dawn-205 (4821).floe-preset`.

The autosave folder isn't one of Floe's preset folders, so autosaves don't clutter the preset browser. Once you've loaded the sound you wanted, [save it](/docs/presets/saving-presets) as a normal preset to keep it.

## Instance names

Every instance of Floe has a name of its own, such as `dawn-205`. It's saved with your DAW project, so the same instance keeps its name each time you open the project. When you have several instances of Floe running, the name in an autosave's file name tells you which one it came from.

To see each instance's name in the top panel, turn on _Show instance name_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences. It's worth turning on if you often use several instances of Floe at once.

## Settings

The defaults suit most people, but you can change them on the _General_ tab of Preferences:

-   **Autosave interval (seconds)** — how often Floe checks for changes and saves.
-   **Max autosaves per instance** — how many autosaves to keep for each instance. When an instance reaches the limit, its oldest autosave is deleted to make room.
-   **Autosave delete after days** — how long to keep autosaves before deleting them.

---

# Error Reporting

> How Floe reports problems, how to send feedback, and what to do if Floe stops responding

Floe is built to be dependable for professional work. When something does go wrong, a few systems help keep your project safe and get the problem fixed quickly.

## Share feedback

If you find a bug, have an idea for a feature or just want to tell us something, use the feedback form inside Floe. Open the menu at the top of Floe's window and choose _Share Feedback_.

-   **Description** — what happened, or what you'd like. For a bug, say what you did just before it happened.
-   **Email** — optional. Add it if you'd like a reply.
-   **Include anonymous diagnostic data** — sends details about your system and Floe's state along with your message, which often makes a bug much quicker to track down.

Please do report anything that doesn't seem right. We want to know about it, and we want to fix it.

## Automatic error reports

If Floe crashes, it sends an anonymous error report. The report describes the error, the state of Floe leading up to it, and the computer it was running on. That gives us what we need to fix the bug without asking you to gather the information yourself. Floe also sends anonymous notes of when each session starts and ends, which tell us how reliably Floe is running overall.

To turn all of this off, enable _Disable anonymous error reports_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences. Floe is open source, so anyone can read the code and see exactly what's sent.

## If Floe stops responding

Floe tries never to take your DAW down with it. If it detects a serious problem, it stops itself rather than crashing the DAW: it goes silent and stops responding. Every instance of Floe in that DAW session is affected.

When this happens:

1.  Save your DAW project under a new name. That keeps the rest of your work safe without replacing your last good save, since a stopped Floe can't save its sound into the project.
2.  Restart your DAW. Floe can't start again within the same DAW session.
3.  If a sound in Floe didn't come back as you left it, recover it from an [autosave](/docs/support/autosave). The [instance name](/docs/support/autosave#instance-names) in each autosave's file name tells you which instance it came from.

An anonymous report of the problem is usually sent to us automatically, so we can work on a fix.

---

# FAQ

> Answers to common questions about Floe

### Can I add my own samples?

Not at the moment. Floe isn't a sampler you drop your own recordings into: it's a platform for complete, polished sample libraries, a bit like an open ROMpler. Each library comes ready to play, with its Instruments set up and presets designed around them.

We're looking into ways to expand this in the future.

If you have some programming experience, you can make your own sample libraries for Floe with its open tools: see [Library Development](/docs/develop/develop-libraries).

### Does Floe load SFZ, SoundFont or other formats?

No. Floe loads sample libraries in its own format, an open format with similar ideas to SFZ that uses the Lua programming language. It also loads the older Mirage format used by some FrozenPlain libraries.

---

# Arp Tab

> Turn held notes into rhythmic patterns with each layer's own arpeggiator

The arpeggiator turns the notes you hold down into a tempo-synced rhythmic pattern. You choose how fast the steps go, the order the notes of your chord are played in, and the velocity, length, and pitch of each step.

Every [layer](/docs/usage/layers) has its own arpeggiator, so you can build sounds with several rhythmic parts playing off each other: fast, high hits over slow, booming drums, say, or a melody over a pulsing bass. With a couple of arpeggiated layers, a single preset can drive a whole track.

Switch the arpeggiator on and hold a chord: you'll hear its notes play one after another in a rhythm. Each step triggers the layer's Instrument just as if you'd played the note yourself; each step runs through all the layer's usual settings, such as its play mode, volume envelope, filter and LFO.

The arpeggiator lives on each layer's _ARP_ tab. A dot on the tab shows that it's on.

![A layer's ARP tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-arp.3e2ced3e273a2a2e.png)12345

1.  **On/off and mode** — the _Arpeggiator_ switch, and a menu choosing where the steps get their notes from: _Played Notes_ or _Fixed Notes_.
2.  **Velocity bars** — one bar for each step, setting its velocity. Click and drag to change them, or drag sideways across the bars to draw a whole pattern in one go.
3.  **Step settings** — under each bar, from top to bottom, are the step number (click it to turn the step on or off), its pitch, a tie to the previous step, and its gate.
4.  **Sequence** — the step _Rate_, the pattern's _Length_, the note _Order_ and _Humanise_.
5.  **Config** — _Trigger_, _Polyrate_ and _One Shot_, plus the _Record_ button in _Fixed Notes_ mode.

While the arpeggiator is off, its controls are greyed out.

## The step sequencer

### Velocity bars

The height of each bar (2) is that step's velocity — typically, that's how loud the step is played. The taller the bar, the louder the step. Use this to accent every 4th step, for example.

`ctrl`/`cmd`\-click a bar to reset it, or `ctrl`/`cmd`\-drag across several to reset them all.

There are a few things that are good to know about velocities in Floe.

Velocity usually corresponds to volume, but how much depends on the layer's [velocity to volume curve](/docs/usage/config-tab#velocity-to-volume-curve) on the _CONFIG_ tab. That curve sometimes doesn't start at zero, so even the lowest bar may still be heard quietly.

Velocity can also affect more than just volume. For multi-sampled Instruments, it may select different samples to play (for example, playing a softer dynamic hit).

In _Played Notes_ mode, whilst the step's velocity is a major factor, how hard you play the note that triggers the sequence also plays a part — it scales the step velocities down. In other words, when you play the triggering note as softly as possible (MIDI velocity 1), the step velocities will be 50% as intense. When you play as hard as possible (MIDI velocity 127), the step velocities reach their full intensity. This upholds the natural way you use velocity on a keyboard. Play at full velocity to make the step velocities the only thing that matters. In _Fixed Notes_ mode, how hard you play is ignored.

### Step settings

Under each velocity bar is a column of smaller controls (3):

![The rows of step settings under the velocity bars, numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-step-settings.03a9288cde0f19a0.png)1234

1.  **Step number** — click to skip the step, leaving a gap in the pattern. A skipped step keeps its other settings, so you can bring it back later. It still ends the note before it, just as an active step would.
2.  **Pitch** — drag up or down to nudge the step's note. In _Played Notes_ mode it's an offset in semitones from whichever held note the step plays. In _Fixed Notes_ mode it's the exact note the step plays. Double-click to type a value.
3.  **Tie** — the link icon joins the step to the previous one, so they play as one longer note. Use ties to place some long notes among the short ones.
4.  **Gate** — the small knob sets how long each note lasts, as a proportion of the step. Pull it right down for short, percussive notes; at 100% the notes run into each other for a more legato feel. Remember that the volume envelope's release on the layer's _MAIN_ tab may affect what you hear.

### More step options

Right-click a velocity bar for a menu of options for that step: reset it, apply its settings to all the steps, reset all the steps, or rotate the whole pattern forwards or backwards by one step. Right-click a pitch or gate control to type a value or reset it, or to apply it to every step or reset it on every step.

When the pattern has more steps than fit across the tab, scroll sideways to see the rest; while it plays, the view follows the current step. Alternatively, click _OVERVIEW_ in the top-right corner to squeeze every step on screen at once. You can still draw velocities there, but the other step settings are hidden until you switch back.

## Sequence controls

The _SEQUENCE_ section (4) sets the shape and feel of the whole pattern:

![The arpeggiator's SEQUENCE controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-sequence.3fcc1295cec251c5.png)

-   **Rate** — how long each step lasts, as a note length at your DAW's tempo. The T and D suffixes are triplet and dotted divisions, useful for swung or lopsided patterns. Together with _Length_ it decides how long the pattern takes to come round: eight steps at 1/8 fills one bar of 4/4.
-   **Length** — how many steps the pattern runs through before it loops. Steps beyond the length are hidden but keep their settings, so you can shorten a pattern and lengthen it again without losing anything.
-   **Order** — how the notes you're holding are shared out across the steps. The options include going from lowest to highest or highest to lowest, bouncing between the two, playing at random, and some less common shapes. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each. _Chord_ is the odd one out: it plays every held note together on each step, which is ideal for rhythmic stabs and percussion. Not available in _Fixed Notes_ mode.
-   **Humanise** — nudges each step's timing and velocity by a random amount, to counteract the machine-gun effect of perfectly identical steps. A few percent takes the mechanical edge off; higher settings give a much looser, hand-played feel. Steps are only ever pushed later, never earlier.

_Humanise_ works especially well with _Chord_ order: instead of every note of the chord starting at exactly the same instant, they spread out slightly, for a more natural, wider sound.

## Config controls

The _CONFIG_ section (5) sets how the pattern responds to your playing:

![The arpeggiator's CONFIG controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-config.69dfd372a93a94bf.png)

-   **Trigger** — what a new note does to a pattern that's already running. _Free_ is usually the one you want: the pattern carries on, so you can change chord underneath it without breaking the groove. _Retrigger_ restarts the pattern from the first step every time you press a note, which keeps it locked to your playing. In both modes, letting go of every key (and the sustain pedal) resets the pattern, so the next chord starts from the first step.
-   **Polyrate** — gives each octave of the notes you're holding its own speed, so one chord can produce several interweaving rhythms. The octave starting at middle C (C3) plays at the _Rate_, and the octaves above and below scale from there. _Double at octaves_ is particularly good: each octave up plays twice as fast as the one below. _3:2 at octaves_ and _4:3 at octaves_ create polyrhythms, where the octaves drift apart and meet up again. Hold two notes an octave apart to hear it most clearly.
-   **One Shot** — the pattern plays through once and stops, rather than looping for as long as you hold the notes. It's handy for fills and one-off flourishes. To play it again, release the keys and press again, or use _Retrigger_.
-   **Record** — in _Fixed Notes_ mode only; see below.

## Played Notes and Fixed Notes

The menu next to the _Arpeggiator_ switch (1) chooses where the steps get their notes from.

_Played Notes_ arpeggiates whatever you're holding. Each step plays one of your held notes, chosen by _Order_, moved up or down by the step's pitch offset.

_Fixed Notes_ ignores which notes you play, and each step plays a specific note that you set. You still hold a key to make the pattern run, but which key doesn't matter. Every step starts on C3, and you can set each one to any note by dragging its pitch.

![A layer's ARP tab in Fixed Notes mode with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-fixed-notes.3501fc38f7f26fd5.png)123

1.  **Mode** — the menu beside the _Arpeggiator_ switch, set to _Fixed Notes_.
2.  **Step notes** — each step's note, shown by name. Drag one up or down to change it.
3.  **Record** — play the pattern in from your keyboard.

It's particularly useful with a drum kit Instrument, where each key is a different drum: rather than following your chord, the pattern always plays the drums you've picked.

You can also play the pattern in with the _Record_ button (3) in the _CONFIG_ section. Click it, then play notes on your keyboard in your own time: each note you press lands on the next step. Recording stops by itself once the last step is filled, or you can click again to stop early. Only the notes are recorded; each step keeps the velocity, gate and tie you've already set. While recording, your notes play normally rather than through the pattern.

If your kick drum is on C3 and your snare on D3, for example, play C3, D3, C3, D3 for an alternating pattern.

## Sliced loops

Some Instruments are sliced loops: rhythmic loops marked up with slice points. The arpeggiator is what powers them: each slice becomes a step, so the loop plays in time with your DAW at any tempo. Because each slice is played as it was recorded, rather than being time-stretched, the loop still sounds natural even when your tempo is a long way from the one it was recorded at.

With a sliced Instrument loaded, the arpeggiator is always on, and the _ARP_ tab changes a little:

![A layer's ARP tab with a sliced Instrument loaded, with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/arp-sliced.080368edd742cf1b.png)12

-   The _Arpeggiator_ switch, mode menu and _Length_ are hidden.
-   Each step has its velocity bar, step number and gate, but no pitch or tie: ties are set for you, so slices longer than one step play in full.
-   **Auto Rate** appears in the _SEQUENCE_ section (1). It picks the step rate for you, so the loop plays close to the speed it was recorded at rather than leaving silent gaps between slices. It's most useful when making presets: the preset keeps the same feel whether it's loaded into a 60 BPM track or a 170 BPM one. While it's on, the chosen rate is shown in place of the _Rate_ menu. The multiplier shifts that choice: _2x_ for double speed, _0.5x_ for half, with dotted and triplet variants for a different feel. Set it to _Off_ to choose the rate yourself.
-   A _SLICING_ section (2) appears. **Offset** picks which slice the pattern starts from, so you can begin part-way into the loop: an easy way to get a fresh groove out of a familiar loop. **Length** sets how many slices play before the pattern loops back to the offset, wrapping round the end of the loop if it needs to. Set it to _All_ to play every slice. Looping a short run of slices turns a long loop into a tight, repeating figure.

### Auto Rate and tempo changes

You may notice that raising the tempo sometimes makes a loop using _Auto Rate_ play slower, and lowering it can make it play faster: for example, a loop can feel faster at 147 BPM than at 148 BPM. That's because _Auto Rate_ aims to play the loop at roughly the speed it was recorded at, where it sounds most natural, with the fewest silent gaps or overlaps between slices. It can only choose from the tempo-synced note lengths, so when the tempo moves far enough from the loop's own speed, it switches to whichever note length is now closer. Every layer using _Auto Rate_ switches at the same tempos, so they stay in the same rhythmic relationship.

## Good to know

-   The pattern starts the moment you press the first key, and runs whether or not your DAW is playing. It follows your DAW's tempo, but it isn't lined up to its bars and beats.
-   The sustain pedal counts as holding notes, so it keeps the pattern running.
-   The layer's [key range](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) applies to the notes the arpeggiator plays, not the keys you hold. In _Played Notes_ mode a step whose note lands outside the range is silent.
-   The [_Monophonic_](/docs/usage/config-tab) setting has no effect while the arpeggiator is running.
-   In _Free_ mode with _Chord_ order, press the notes of a chord at the same moment. If one arrives slightly late, the first step plays without it, and it joins on the next step. When playing from your DAW, quantising the recorded notes lines them up so every step plays the whole chord.
-   Right-click the _ARP_ tab to copy and paste the whole arpeggiator, steps included, to another layer.

---

# Browsers

> How to find and load presets, Instruments and impulse responses with Floe's browsers.

The browsers help you find the right items quickly, without scrolling through long lists. Think of them as supercharged drop-down menus.

There are three browsers, and they all work the same way. Each one opens when you click the name of the item it loads:

-   **Preset browser** — click the preset's name in the [top panel](/docs/usage/top-panel), which is there on every page.
-   **Instrument browser** — click the Instrument name at the top of a layer, on the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers#layer-header) page.
-   **IR browser** — click the IR name in the [Convolution Reverb](/docs/usage/effects#convolution-reverb) effect, on the _Effects_ page.

![Layer 1's Instrument browser, open beneath its selector, with its regions numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-browse.73d96a92f8a5fdb2.png)12345

1.  **Items** — the light panel on the left lists everything you can load. Click one to load it.
2.  **Narrowing down** — the dark panel on the right is for narrowing down the list on the left, such as to one sample library or one tag.
3.  **Selector** — the box you clicked to open the browser. It stays usable while the browser is open.
4.  **Navigation** — step back and forth through the pages of the right-hand panel.
5.  **Mode** — switch the right-hand panel between browse mode and [filter mode](#filter-mode).

## Loading items

Click an item (1) to load it. The browser stays open, so you can try one sound after another, playing as you go. Once you've loaded something, the browser closes by itself as soon as you move the mouse away from it. You can also double-click an item to load it and close the browser in one go, or close it at any time by clicking outside it or pressing `escape`.

While the browser is open, the selector you clicked (3) can still be used: previous, next, random and unload, where it has them.

Hover over an item for a moment to see more about it, such as its description.

## Favourites

If there are items you keep coming back to, mark them as favourites. Hover over an item and click the next to its name. The star stays lit to show it's a favourite. To see only your favourites, click the in the toolbar at the bottom of the list. Click it again to see everything. Favourites are shared by every instance of Floe, so anything you star in one project is there in the next.

## The list of items

The left panel (1) starts off showing everything, and shrinks as you narrow it down with the right panel.

Beneath the list, a line of italic text says what you're looking at, such as _Showing all instruments_. As you narrow things down it changes to match, such as _Showing from Lost Reveries_. Each part of it that narrows the list has a : click one to remove it.

At the very bottom is a small toolbar:

-   — jump to the item that's currently loaded. The right panel jumps to where it came from, too.
-   — show only your favourites.
-   — search. As you type, the list shows only the items containing your text. `ctrl`+`F` (`cmd`+`F` on macOS) opens it too.

## Narrowing down

The right panel (2) has pages that you click through to narrow down the list. In the Instrument browser, for example, you might click _Libraries_, then a particular sample library. The list on the left then shows only that library's Instruments. Numbers in brackets, such as _(26)_, show how many items each option holds.

The first page offers two ways in. _Browse by collection_ narrows down by where items come from. _Browse by attribute_ narrows down by their properties, such as their tags or who made them.

As you click through the pages, a trail of the pages you've visited builds up at the bottom of the panel (4) — a bit like a web browser. Click any step to jump back to it, or click to go back to the first page. The and arrows step back and forth.

## Right-click menus

Right-click items in the browsers for options to do with their files:

-   **A preset** — open the folder it's in, make it your [default preset](/docs/presets/loading-presets#default-preset), or send it to the bin.
-   **A preset bank or folder** — open it in your file manager, or uninstall it.
-   **A sample library** — open its folder, or uninstall it. See [Uninstalling](/docs/installation/uninstalling).

## Keyboard navigation

You can use the browsers from your computer keyboard. The focused item gets a blue outline, which appears once you press an arrow key.

-   `up`/`down` move through the list.
-   `enter` clicks the focused item.
-   `tab` moves between the left and right panels.
-   `left`/`right` move along the trail at the bottom of the right panel.
-   `ctrl`+`F` (`cmd`+`F` on macOS) opens the search.
-   `home`/`end` jump to the start or end of the list.
-   `ctrl`+`up`/`down` (`cmd` on macOS) jump to the previous or next folder.
-   `page up`/`page down` jump 8 items at a time.

## Filter mode

Browse mode, where you click through one page at a time, is all most people need. When you know exactly what you're after, filter mode goes further: it lets you combine several ways of narrowing down at once, such as showing only Instruments tagged _ambient_ from one particular sample library.

Switch to it with the button (5), and back to browse mode with .

![The Instrument browser in filter mode, with its regions numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-full.89de4f11b56240f7.png)1234

1.  **Filters** — every option in one tree, rather than pages to click through. Click a to open a section, then click the options you want.
2.  **Summary** — what's currently showing. Click the next to a filter to remove it.
3.  **Mode** — switch between browse mode and filter mode.
4.  **Matching** — choose how your filters combine.

The list on the left updates as soon as you click an option.

Choose how the filters combine with the button next to the mode switch (4):

![The One, Match all and Match any menu](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/browser-menu.5ef644a9f8155d92.png)

-   **Match all (AND)** — the one you'll usually want. Only items that match every selected filter are shown, so the more filters you choose, the shorter the list gets. Filters that would leave nothing to show are greyed out, so you don't hit dead ends.
-   **Match any (OR)** — items that match any of the selected filters are shown, so the more filters you choose, the longer the list gets.
-   **One** — only one filter at a time, like browse mode but with the tree layout.

Filter mode has its own search, at the bottom of the right panel, for finding a filter in the tree, such as the _aggressive_ tag.

Filter mode pairs well with the random button: narrow the list down to the kind of sound you're after, then jump around within it for inspiration. See [Randomisation](/docs/usage/randomisation).

## Tips

-   The previous, next and random buttons ( ) always stay within the list you've narrowed down to, whether the browser is open or closed. On the _Perform_ page and in the top panel, the preset arrows follow the preset browser in the same way.
-   Drag the bottom-right corner of a browser to resize it. To make room for longer names, drag the line where the two panels meet. Double-click either to reset it.
-   Each layer's Instrument browser remembers its own settings. On the _Layers_ page, set up each one the way you like, perhaps the first narrowed to the _bass_ tag and the second to _keys_. Then click the button that randomises every layer, and each one jumps to a random Instrument within its own selection.

---

# Config Tab

> How a layer responds to your playing, including key ranges, pitch bend, velocity and MPE

The _CONFIG_ tab sets how the layer responds to your playing: which keys it uses, and how it follows velocity, pitch bend and MPE controllers.

![A layer's CONFIG tab](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-config.499578f75666d12d.png)1234567

1.  **Transpose** — shift the layer in semitones by changing which samples are triggered, rather than re-pitching the audio as _Pitch_ in the [layer header](/docs/usage/layers#layer-header) does. On a multi-sampled Instrument this keeps the character of the sound intact, so it's the better choice for large shifts. You still play the same keys; they just reach for different samples.
2.  **Pitch Bend Range** — how far the pitch wheel bends this layer, in semitones. Each layer has its own, so one layer can bend a whole tone while another ignores the wheel entirely.
3.  **Keytrack** — with it on, higher keys play higher pitches. Switch it off and every key plays the sample at its recorded pitch, which suits drum hits, loops and sound effects. Some libraries mark particular samples as always or never keytracked.
4.  **Monophonic** — what happens when notes overlap. _Off_ is polyphonic: every note gets its own voice. _Retrigger_ plays one note at a time, with each new note releasing the previous one. _Latch_ holds on to the first note, ignoring any new ones, until you let go of every key: useful for drones and textures. Because it's per layer, one layer can play one note at a time while another stays polyphonic. While the layer's [arpeggiator](/docs/usage/arp-tab) is on, this setting has no effect.
5.  **MPE** — choose what an MPE controller's press (channel pressure) and slide (CC74) control on this layer, such as volume, filter cutoff, timbre or LFO amount, and by how much. Negative amounts reverse the response. MPE must be switched on in the Performance Controls panel first. See [MIDI](/docs/usage/midi#mpe) for details.
6.  **Key Range** and **Key Fade** — give the layer its own portion of the keyboard, with soft edges if you like.
7.  **Velocity to volume curve** — how hard you play turns into how loud each note sounds. Steepen the curve for a wider dynamic range, or flatten it to even out your playing. When you play, a red line shows where your note landed.

## Key ranges

Key ranges let you split the keyboard into zones, with each layer responding to specific keys. Use them to split the keyboard, stack zones on top of each other, or crossfade smoothly from one sound to another as you play up the keys.

### Setting up key ranges

_Key Range_ is the lowest and highest note the layer plays, and _Key Fade_ is how many semitones it takes to fade in at the bottom of the range, and to fade out at the top. Drag a value up or down, click its arrows ( ), or double-click to type it in (a note name, for the range).

![Key range controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-controls.8f042068dc69b686.png)

Fades are what make smooth transitions possible: overlap two layers' ranges by a few notes, fade the lower layer out and the upper layer in across the overlap, and one sound crossfades into the other as you play up the keyboard.

To play a different part of a multi-sampled Instrument's mapping, use _Transpose_ on the same tab. It shifts which samples are triggered, so higher or lower samples play, while the layer's _Pitch_ re-pitches the audio by speeding it up or slowing it down. _Transpose_ doesn't move the key range itself.

### Key range display

A bar above the keyboard at the bottom of the interface shows which keys trigger each layer, with colours corresponding to each layer. Only layers with an Instrument loaded appear. The bar is hidden when every layer uses the full keyboard range (C-2 to G8), unless an Instrument has named ranges (see below).

![Key range display above the keyboard](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-bars.bccf7ecc8a586a01.png)

On the _Layers_ and _Effects_ pages, the keyboard shows a section of the full 128 keys: use the [octave controls](/docs/usage/keyboard) to scroll it, and the bar scrolls with it. The _Perform_ page shows a wider, fixed stretch of nine octaves. Vertical lines mark where each range starts and ends, and small chevrons show when a range carries on past the visible keys. Fades show as gradients on the bars: the more transparent, the quieter.

Hover over the display to see an enlarged view with more detail. An Instrument can also have named ranges, such as the name of the sound on each key, or each group of drums in a kit. They appear as thicker capsules, labelled in the enlarged view.

![Enlarged key range view with named ranges, fades, and off-screen chevrons](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/key-range-enlarged.631825e6f15b2f25.png)

## Velocity to volume curve

Each layer has its own _velocity to volume curve_, which shapes how hard you play (MIDI velocity) into the volume of each note.

![Velocity to volume curve editor](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/velocity-curve.7a4bb3dd5dc53a7e.png)

### How the curve works

The horizontal axis is velocity — far left is the softest possible velocity (MIDI value 1), far right is the hardest (MIDI value 127). The vertical axis is the resulting note volume. When you play a note, a red indicator appears at its velocity position on the curve so you can see where you're playing.

While notes are sounding, each active voice also gets a red line on the layer's volume slider, showing the level that voice is playing at, once the curve, any [key range](#key-ranges) fade and any MPE volume expression are taken into account.

A straight line from bottom-left to top-right gives a natural response: the harder you play, the louder the note.

Move, add or remove points, or reshape the curve between them, to change this relationship: make soft playing louder than it would be naturally, cap the volume of hard hits, or create a non-linear response that emphasises a particular dynamic range.

The curve pictured above is one example. The softest notes stay quiet, the volume climbs steeply as you play a little harder, then it levels off so the hardest hits can't get much louder.

Setting different curves across the three layers also opens up creative sound design — for example, fading one layer in as you play harder while another fades out.

By default the curve doesn't start at zero, so even the softest notes still make a quiet sound. Drag the left-most point down to the bottom if you want the softest notes to be silent.

### Velocity and multi-sampled Instruments

While not directly related to this curve, it's worth noting that velocity does more than just control volume. For multi-sampled Instruments that contain separate velocity layers, a note's velocity also selects _which_ sample is played — not just how loud it is. A low-velocity note on a piano, for instance, plays the soft-velocity samples (with their distinct tone and character) rather than a quieter version of the hard-hit samples.

### Editing the curve

-   **Double-click** anywhere on the curve to add a control point (up to 8 in total)
-   **Drag control points** to move them
-   **Drag between points** to adjust curve shape
-   **Double-click a point** to remove it
-   **Shift-drag** for finer control
-   **`ctrl`/`cmd`\-click** a point to reset its height, or between points to reset that stretch's shape
-   **Right-click** to add or remove points, copy and paste the curve between layers, or reset it

---

# Controls

> How to use Floe's knobs, sliders, menus and graphs

Almost everything you shape is done with knobs and sliders, and they all work the same way.

## Knobs and sliders

-   **Drag** — click and drag up or right to increase the value, down or left to decrease it. Use whichever direction feels natural.
-   **Fine adjustment** — hold `shift` while dragging for four times finer control. You can press or release `shift` mid-drag.
-   **Reset** — `ctrl`\-click (`cmd`\-click on macOS) to return the control to its default value.
-   **Type a value** — double-click to type an exact number. You can typically use abbreviations like `2k` instead of 2000 Hz.
-   **More options** — right-click for a menu of extra actions (see below).

When you hover over a control it lights up, and its current value appears below it. Pause on it for a moment and a short description appears too, with a reminder of these shortcuts underneath. Both are adjustable in the preferences: _Show tooltips_ turns the descriptions off, and turning off _Instant value readouts_ makes the value appear only after a moment or while you're dragging.

Sometimes controls are greyed out — showing it currently has no effect; such as a filter knob while the filter is switched off.

### Reading a knob

A knob shows its value in two places: the line on the dial, and the coloured arc around the edge.

These 2 aspects can differ when a [macro](/docs/usage/macros) is controlling the knob. The dial shows the knob's own setting, the one you drag. The coloured arc shows the value you actually hear once the macros have been applied. Hover over the knob to see both readouts.

![The Filter effect's controls, with a macro moving its Cutoff knob](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/knob.ed9ee6bd141faee8.png)

Here, a macro is raising the Filter's _Cutoff_. The dial points to where the knob is set, while the arc reaches further round, to the cutoff you hear.

## The right-click menu

![The right-click menu of the Filter effect's Cutoff knob](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/knob-menu.2b32dcce31cfb5f2.png)

Right-click any knob or slider for extra actions, including:

-   **Copy Value** and **Paste Value** — carry a setting from one control to another.
-   **Enter Value** — type an exact value, the same as double-clicking.
-   **Reset Value to Default** — the same as `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click.
-   **Reset Value to "…" state** — appears when you've loaded a preset, and names it. It returns just this control to how the preset had it.
-   **MIDI CC Learn** — link the control to a knob or fader on your MIDI controller. See [MIDI](/docs/usage/midi#midi-cc).

Some controls add their own shortcuts. A layer's _Pitch_, for example, has _+1 Octave_ and _\-1 Octave_, and _Detune_ can fold whole semitones into _Pitch_.

Many sections have a right-click menu of their own too. Right-click a layer's tab, an envelope or an effect to copy, paste or reset the whole section at once: a quick way to give two layers the same filter settings, for example.

## Menus, buttons and number fields

-   **Menus** — click to open the list of options. The arrows either side, and , step to the previous or next option, which is a quick way to audition them. Hover over an option in the open menu to see what it does.
-   **Buttons** — click to switch on or off. Most can be right-clicked for more options.
-   **Number fields**, such as a layer's _Pitch_ — drag them like a knob, double-click to type, or use the arrows beside them ( ).

Menus reset to their default with `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click, just like knobs.

## Graphs

Envelopes, filters and EQs have graphs with points you can drag directly. Dragging a point is simply another way of moving the knobs beneath it. Everything above still applies: `shift` for fine adjustment, `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click to reset, double-click to type.

Hover over a point to see exactly what it controls. On a filter point, for example, moving left and right changes the cutoff, and moving up and down changes the resonance. On some points, such as the EQ bands, the mouse wheel adjusts the resonance.

## Undo

Every change you make can be undone. Use the _Undo_ and _Redo_ buttons in the [top panel](/docs/usage/top-panel#buttons) to step back and forth through your edits.

---

# Effects Page

> How to use Floe's effects rack, and details of each effect

![Floe's window with the EFFECTS page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-effects.73801094172d2026.png)

The _Effects_ page is where you colour the whole sound. The three [layers](/docs/usage/layers) are mixed together and then passed through a single rack of effects, from top to bottom. Use them lightly to add some space or warmth, or push much further with heavy distortion, filtering and modulation to take the sound somewhere new. There's 12 effects available. Each can be used once in the rack, in whatever order you like.

![Floe's Effects page with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effects.39fc87a1ccda5330.png)12345

1.  **Switchboard** — every effect listed in order, each on its own card. Tick a card's checkbox to add that effect to the rack.
2.  **Rack** — the effects that are in use, with their controls.
3.  **Effect name** — drag it to move the effect up or down the chain. Right-click for more options.
4.  **Mix, remove and bypass** — _Mix_ sets how much of the effect you hear, removes the effect from the rack, and bypasses it.
5.  **All-effect buttons** — these act on the whole rack at once: randomise , bypass all , and remove all .

### Adding and removing effects

The switchboard (1) lists every effect. Those in the rack are shown brightly with a ticked checkbox; the rest are dimmed.

-   **Add an effect** by ticking its checkbox. Doing so will add it to the rack, and the rack will scroll to show it.
-   **Remove an effect** by unticking its checkbox, or clicking next to its _Mix_ knob (4). Removing an effect doesn't reset its controls, it will be the same if you re-add it later.
-   **Jump to an effect** by clicking its card anywhere other than the checkbox. The rack will scroll to show it, with a brief flash so you can spot it.

### Bypassing effects

Bypassing an effect lets the sound pass straight through it while it stays in the rack, ready to switch back on. It's the easiest way to hear exactly what an effect is contributing. A bypassed effect is greyed out and uses no CPU.

Click next to an effect's _Mix_ knob (4), or the coloured light at the left of its switchboard card, to bypass it. Click again to switch it back on.

The button at the top right of the page (5) bypasses every effect in the rack at once, so you can hear your layers without any processing. Click it again to switch them all back on.

### Changing the order

The effects run from top to bottom, and the order can make a big difference: a reverb after a distortion gives a clean tail on a gritty sound, while a reverb before it distorts the tail too.

Drag an effect's name (3) up or down the rack to move it. You can also drag the cards in the switchboard: hover over a card and a grip appears to show it can be moved. Because the switchboard also shows the effects that aren't in the rack, after some reordering the effects in use can end up scattered among the unused ones. Right-click the switchboard and choose _Tidy FX Order_ to group the effects in the rack at the top, without changing their order.

### Mix

Every effect has a _Mix_ knob (4). It blends the sound going into the effect with the effect's output. At 100% you hear only the effect's output; turn it down to bring back more of the unprocessed sound. It's a quick way to set an effect's strength without changing its other settings: a touch of reverb, gentle distortion, or parallel compression, say.

### The all-effect buttons

The buttons at the top right of the page (5) act on the whole rack:

-   **Randomise** — randomly puts each effect in or takes it out of the rack, and shuffles the order. The effects' settings aren't changed. It's a quick way to stumble on combinations you'd never have reached for. Use _Undo_ from the top panel if you don't like the result. For bigger changes, including new settings, try the [Random Variation](/docs/usage/randomisation) strip on the _Perform_ page.
-   **Bypass all** — deactivates all effects.
-   **Remove all** — removes every effect from the rack.

### Copying, pasting and resetting

Right-click an effect's name in the rack or its card in the switchboard for a menu to:

-   **Copy and paste one effect** — copy an effect's settings, then paste them onto the same effect on another preset.
-   **Copy and paste the whole rack** — copy every effect, its order and its settings, then paste them all at once to a new preset.
-   **Reset** — return the effect's settings to their defaults.

Copying works between presets: copy from one, load another, and paste. Right-click an empty part of the switchboard or rack for the whole-rack options, and to paste a single copied effect.

## Distortion

![The Distortion effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-distortion.a583b9946e316265.png)

Distortion adds harmonics to a sound, anything from gentle tape warmth to outright destruction. Choose a character from the _Type_ menu, then set how hard you push it with the _Drive_ knob. That's the whole workflow; everything else is there to shape the result. The display on the left passes a sine wave through your current settings, so you can see how each type and setting reshapes it.

It runs with 4× oversampling and is anti-aliased to stay clean and musical. It also has built-in gain compensation to keep the level steady as you turn up _Drive_ or _Punish_. For the Legacy types, you opt in to this with the _Auto Gain_ switch; for the other types it's always on.

-   **Type** — the character of the distortion. See below.
-   **Drive** — how hard the sound is pushed into the distortion, and the main control for how much distortion you hear. Each step of the knob adds a similar amount. For the Mangle types it also moves the effect itself, so the character changes as well as the intensity.
-   **Punish** — stacks extra distortion stages after the first, each driven harder than the last, like an amp cascading its gain stages. Turn it up for a denser, grittier, more compressed drive that holds its character as notes decay.
-   **Tilt EQ** — shifts the tone going into the distortion. Turn it up to saturate the highs for a brighter result, or down to push the lows for a warmer, fatter drive.
-   **Gain** — a flat level adjustment to the distorted sound, before _Mix_ blends it with the unprocessed sound. It's separate from the automatic gain compensation.
-   **Auto Gain** — for the Legacy types, holds the loudness steady as you turn up _Drive_. For the other types it's always on.

The types are grouped into two families in the menu. _Bite_ types saturate and thicken the sound, from clean warmth to hard clipping:

-   **Tape** — warm and smooth. Rounds off the loud peaks while quieter passages and tails stay clean.
-   **Valve** — rich, even harmonics that stay musical however hard you push, instead of collapsing into a harsh square.
-   **Overdrive** — pedal-style grit with a threshold. A note cleans up as it decays, and playing harder brings the bite in.
-   **Hard Clip** — clean, aggressive brickwall clipping.
-   **Octave** — adds a hard octave-up edge, then saturates. It squares up on hot notes and follows their dynamics.

_Mangle_ types are more extreme, tearing the sound apart and adding new tones rather than just thickening it:

-   **Bitcrush** — lo-fi digital crunch, made by lowering the effective sample rate. More _Drive_ means coarser and grittier.
-   **Ring Mod** — multiplies the sound by a low oscillator for clangorous, metallic, bell-like tones. _Drive_ raises the oscillator's pitch and deepens the effect.
-   **Sine Fold** — folds the wave through a sine curve for interesting, chaotic harmonics.
-   **Warp** — an asymmetric shaper that bends the wave lopsidedly into a gritty, off-kilter drive.
-   **Wavefolder** — folds the peaks back on themselves for bright, metallic harmonics.

The Legacy types are the original distortion algorithms, kept so that older presets and projects sound the same. They load with _Auto Gain_ off to keep their original level; turn it on to give them the same steady loudness as the other types.

## Bit Crush

![The Bit Crush effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-bit-crush.eb0ae0d0c3717f57.png)

Bit Crush is a lo-fi effect that degrades the sound in two ways: lowering the sample rate for ringing, metallic aliasing, and lowering the bit depth for gritty noise. The display shows a preview of the crushing applied to a rising test signal. Both controls start at full quality, so turn them down to hear the effect.

-   **Bits** — lowers the bit depth, adding a gritty digital noise that's most obvious in quiet passages and tails. At the lowest settings quiet sounds crush to silence, so feed the effect a strong signal.
-   **Samp Rate** — lowers the sample rate by holding each sample for longer. Lower rates fold high frequencies back down into ringing, metallic aliasing: the sound of early samplers and retro hardware.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

## Compressor

![The Compressor effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-compressor.5a5d0c835f3f6c23.png)

The compressor shapes the dynamics of the sound, evening out the difference between its loud and quiet parts. It has two types, each with its own character.

-   **Type** — _Modern_ is precise, and gives you the _Attack_ and _Release_ knobs. _Vintage_ has a bit more character, and sets its attack and release for you.
-   **Threshold** — the level the sound has to rise above before it's compressed.
-   **Ratio** — how strongly the sound is compressed once it's above the threshold. Higher ratios compress more, and above about 2:1 the pumping becomes much more noticeable.
-   **Attack** and **Release** (_Modern_ only) — how quickly the compressor responds to a rise in level, and how quickly it recovers after the level drops.
-   **Gain** — adjusts the level after compression.
-   **Auto Gain** (_Vintage_ only) — automatically adjusts the level so the sound stays consistently loud however hard it's compressed.

Three meters show what the compressor is doing: _In_ is the incoming level, with a marker at the threshold; _GR_ (gain reduction) is how much it's turning the sound down; and _Out_ is the final level.

## Filter

![The Filter effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-filter.6e299e9ebedef899.png)

The Filter cuts away part of the frequency range, or boosts or dips it. It's a single filter across the whole mix; each layer also has its own filter for shaping notes individually (see [Layers](/docs/usage/main-tab#filter)).

-   **Type** — the shape of the filter, such as low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peak or shelf. The low-pass and high-pass types come in 12 and 24 dB per octave slopes.
-   **Cutoff** — where the filter does its work: where the low-pass and high-pass filters roll off from, the centre of the band for band-pass and notch, or the corner for the shelves.
-   **Reso** — resonance, which emphasises the frequencies right at the cutoff, adding a peak there on the low-pass and high-pass filters. For band-pass and notch it narrows the band, for peak it tightens the boost, and for the shelves it steepens the corner.
-   **Gain** — how far the peak and shelf types boost or cut. It only appears for those types.

## Stereo Widen

![The Stereo Widen effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-stereo-widen.689f9c85db9c28f0.png)

Stereo Widen narrows the sound towards mono or spreads it out wider. Each layer also has its own _Stereo_ control, if you want to widen just one of them.

-   **Mode** — how the widening is done. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each.
    -   _Balanced_ keeps the loudness the same wherever _Width_ is set. It's the one to reach for by default.
    -   _Bass Mono_ widens in the same way, but keeps everything below the _Bass Mono_ frequency in the centre.
    -   _Legacy_ is the widening from older versions of Floe, kept so that existing presets sound as they always did. It gets louder as _Width_ goes up.
-   **Width** — negative values pull the sound towards mono, positive values push it wider, and 0% leaves it as it is. It works by rebalancing the mid (what both channels share) against the side (what differs between them). At the far left only the mid is left; at the far right only the side is left, so anything dead centre disappears.
-   **Bass Mono** (_Bass Mono_ mode only) — the frequency below which the sound is kept in the centre. Holding the low end in the middle keeps kicks and basslines solid, and stops them losing power on mono systems. The split uses a 24 dB per octave Linkwitz-Riley crossover, so the two bands recombine without a dip around the crossover point.

## Chorus

![The Chorus effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-chorus.3bdf4b0fca3fc2fe.png)

The Chorus thickens the sound by layering it with delayed copies that drift in pitch. Gentle settings add a subtle shimmer and movement, while deeper settings give an obvious, tape-like wobble.

-   **Rate** — how quickly the pitch drifts up and down. Low settings give a gentle swelling movement, while turning it up gives a quicker, shimmering warble.
-   **Depth** — how far the pitch drifts away from the original. Small amounts thicken the sound, while larger amounts give an obvious wobble. At zero, the delayed copies are still there, adding a static colouration.
-   **High-pass** — removes low frequencies from the chorused copies, leaving the unprocessed sound untouched. Raise it to keep the bass tight and free from movement.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

## Reverb

![The Reverb effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-reverb.3ca4505d77aaecb2.png)

The Reverb simulates the reflections of a real space, from a small, tight room to a vast hall that takes many seconds to fade. It can also modulate its tail for a shimmering, moving sound.

-   **Pre LP** and **Pre HP** — low-pass and high-pass filters on the sound going into the reverb. _Pre LP_ rolls off the highs for a darker, more distant space. _Pre HP_ rolls off the lows, keeping the tail clear so the bass stays tight and centred. The unprocessed sound keeps its full range.
-   **Lo-Shelf** and **Lo-Gain** — cut the reverb's tail below the _Lo-Shelf_ frequency by the _Lo-Gain_ amount. The cut builds up as the tail recirculates, so the low end thins out as the reverb fades: handy for stopping long tails clouding the bass. Turn _Lo-Gain_ down to hear it work.
-   **Hi-Shelf** and **Hi-Gain** — the same for the highs, so they die away first, just as soft furnishings absorb them in a real room.
-   **Decay** — how long the tail takes to fade away once a sound stops. It holds steady whatever the _Size_, so you can choose the length of the reverb and the character of the space separately.
-   **Size** — how large the space feels. Small values pack the reflections together for a boxy, coloured character; large values spread them out for something open and airy.
-   **Predelay** — holds the reverb back for a moment so the unprocessed sound is heard on its own first. Short amounts keep the sound upfront and defined, while longer amounts push the walls further away.
-   **Mod Rate** and **Depth** — make the reflections drift, smearing the resonances that build up in the tail. A little _Depth_ stops long tails ringing; more gives an obvious shimmer and movement. _Mod Rate_ sets how quickly the drift moves: keep it low for a gentle, breathing wash, or turn it up for a quicker, more distinct warble.

## Delay

![The Delay effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-delay.e6e66ebc5fbfc868.png)

The Delay is a stereo echo. You can set the left and right times separately, either freely or synced to tempo, bounce the repeats between the speakers with the ping-pong modes, and thin them out with a filter as they fade.

-   **Time L** and **Time R** — the gap between the repeats in the left and right channels. With _Tempo Sync_ off, they're set freely in milliseconds. Very short times stop sounding like separate echoes and become a metallic, resonant tone instead.
-   **Tempo Sync** — sets the times as note lengths that follow your DAW's tempo, keeping the repeats in time with your track.
-   **Feedback** — how long the echoes trail on for. Low amounts give a handful of repeats, while high amounts carry on long after the note has gone. It works by feeding each repeat back in to make the next one.
-   **Mode** — how the repeats move around the stereo image:
    -   _Mono_ — both channels repeat at the _Time L_ setting, so the echoes sit where the original sound sits in the stereo image. _Time R_ is unused.
    -   _Stereo_ — each channel has its own delay, so setting _Time L_ and _Time R_ apart spreads the repeats across the stereo image.
    -   _Ping-pong_ — the sound is summed to the centre, and the repeats then bounce from one side to the other, with _Time L_ and _Time R_ setting how long each half of the bounce lasts.
    -   _Mid ping-pong_ — the repeats bounce from side to side as in _Ping-pong_, but the sound keeps its stereo image on the way in. Choose _Ping-pong_ for the clearest left-right bounce, especially from a wide sound, and _Mid ping-pong_ when you want the echoes to keep some of the original's width.
-   **Filter** and **Spread** — a band-pass filter the repeats run through, leaving the unprocessed sound untouched. _Filter_ sets the centre of the band and _Spread_ its width. Wide open, the repeats stay close to the original sound; narrowed, they squeeze towards the _Filter_ frequency. The filter sits inside the feedback loop, so every repeat is filtered again and the echoes thin out as they fade.

## Convolution Reverb

![The Convolution Reverb effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-convolution-reverb.80934c27d68d6c02.png)

The Convolution Reverb gets all its character from an impulse response (IR): a recording of how a space or object responds to sound. Floe's IRs are chosen for character. Some are realistic spaces, but most are stranger: textures and resonances that can transform a sound, making this as much a sound-design tool as a reverb.

-   **Impulse** — click the IR's name to choose one in the [IR browser](/docs/usage/browsers). The arrows beside it, and , step to the previous or next IR, and jumps to a random one. All three follow the filters you've set in the IR browser. unloads the IR. There's no reverb until one is loaded.
-   **High-pass** — rolls off the low end of the reverb to avoid muddy bass, before the _Mix_ blend.
-   **Output** — the level after the _Mix_ blend.

Floe always has its own built-in IRs, and some sample libraries add more.

## Phaser

![The Phaser effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-phaser.440718747662cf50.png)

The Phaser sweeps a series of peaks and notches through the sound, giving it the classic swooshing, jet-like motion. Gentle settings add a subtle sense of movement to sustained sounds, while faster or more resonant ones become an unmistakable whoosh.

-   **Freq** — the centre of the sweep. Keep it low for a deep, throaty movement, or raise it to place the phasing amongst the brighter harmonics.
-   **Feedback** — sharpens the peaks and deepens the notches. Small amounts keep it a gentle swoosh, while higher amounts give the sweep a resonant, whistling edge.
-   **Shape** — how many peaks and notches there are. Turned down, there's a single broad one for a soft, vowel-like sweep; turned up, there are more of them for a richer, more obvious phasing.
-   **Rate** — how quickly the peaks sweep up and down. Low settings give a gentle, drifting movement, while turning it up makes the sweep a warble.
-   **Depth** — how far the peaks travel either side of _Freq_. Small amounts give a narrow, shimmering movement, while larger amounts sweep across the whole spectrum. With _Depth_ all the way down, the peaks hold still, leaving a fixed colouration that you can sweep by hand with _Freq_.
-   **Stereo** — offsets the left and right sweeps from each other so the movement drifts across the stereo image. At zero both channels sweep together; at maximum they sweep in opposite directions, for a wide, swirling feel.

## EQ

![The EQ effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-eq.65bb6b6d6747ec42.png)

The EQ is a three-band equaliser for lifting or taming parts of the frequency range, from broad tonal shaping to surgical cuts. Each layer also has its own EQ (see [Layers](/docs/usage/eq-tab)).

The graph shows the combined effect of all three bands. Drag a band's handle to move it, scroll over it to change its resonance, or right-click it to change its type or copy and paste the whole band. The three bands have identical controls:

-   **Type** — a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a low-pass or high-pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum.
-   **Freq** — where the band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter.
-   **Reso** — how tightly the band is focused. For peaks and notches it's the width, from broad and gentle to tight and focused. The shelves use it to steepen their corner, and the pass filters to add a peak at the cutoff.
-   **Gain** — how far the band boosts or cuts. Only the peak and shelf types use it.

## Limiter

![The Limiter effect at its default settings](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/effect-limiter.411ca416265c7bf3.png)

The limiter is a brickwall limiter: it holds your output firmly below a maximum level, whether you just want to catch stray peaks or push the overall level up without clipping. It's usually best placed last in the rack, so it catches everything above it.

-   **Gain** — drives the sound harder into the limiter. The harder you push, the more it's limited, making the sound louder and denser.
-   **Ceiling** — the level the output is never allowed to go above. Leave a small safety margin below 0 dB, giving headroom for whatever comes after Floe.

Three meters show what the limiter is doing: _In_ is the incoming level, _GR_ (gain reduction) is how much it's turning the sound down, and _Out_ is the final level.

It's a true-peak limiter, so the _Ceiling_ is a reliable maximum for the output. It looks a fraction of a millisecond ahead in the audio so it can react before a peak arrives. The delay is so small (0.5 ms) that Floe absorbs it rather than asking your DAW to compensate for it, so you don't need to do anything about it.

Thanks to that short lookahead, the limiter is fast and transparent for moderate amounts of limiting. Push it hard and there's less room for the gain change to ramp smoothly, so you may start to hear it colour or slightly distort the sound. If that happens, back off the _Gain_ or raise the _Ceiling_ a little.

---

# EQ Tab

> Shape a layer's tone with its three-band equaliser

The _EQ_ tab has a three-band equaliser for shaping the layer's tone before it's mixed with the other layers.

![A layer's EQ tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-eq.9ddfe3af1923a2ab.png)123

1.  **On/off** — switch the EQ on or off. A dot on the _EQ_ tab shows that it's on.
2.  **EQ graph** — shows the combined effect of all three bands. Drag a band's point to move it, use your mouse scroll wheel over it to change its resonance, or right-click it to change its type or copy and paste the whole band. For band types without a gain control, dragging up and down changes the resonance.
3.  **Bands** — the three bands have identical controls:
    -   **Type** — a peak or shelf for boosting and cutting, a notch for removing a narrow slice, or a pass filter for rolling off one end of the spectrum.
    -   **Freq** — where the band does its work: the centre of a peak or notch, the corner of a shelf, or the cutoff of a pass filter.
    -   **Reso** — how tightly the band is focused. For peaks and notches it's the width; shelves use it to steepen their corner, and pass filters to add a peak at the cutoff.
    -   **Gain** — how far the band boosts or cuts. Only the peak and shelf types use it.
