# Keyboard

> The on-screen keyboard in Floe's bottom panel, and what it shows about the notes and voices playing

The bottom panel of Floe's window is home to the on-screen keyboard. It's there on every page, and it's a quick way to see which notes are coming in, how many voices each one is playing, and which keys play which layer. You can click it to play notes too.

![The bottom panel on the Layers page, with a chord held on the keyboard](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/keyboard.65449d5b30f4e02c.png)12345

1.  **Tabs** — _PLAY_ shows the keyboard and macros. _MACROS_ shows the panel where you [set up the macros](/docs/usage/macros#making-your-own-macros).
2.  **Macros** — the four macro knobs, the same ones as on the _Perform_ page. A greyed-out macro has nothing linked to it. See [Macros](/docs/usage/macros).
3.  **Key range bars** — which keys play each layer, shown when any layer is limited to part of the keyboard.
4.  **Keys** — held notes light up, and red marks along the top show the voices sounding on each note.
5.  **Octave** — scroll the keyboard up or down to see a different part of the note range.

On the _Perform_ page, the bottom panel is simpler: there are no tabs, macros or octave controls, and the keyboard stretches across the whole panel to show nine octaves at once.

## Playing notes

Click a key to play it. Where you click sets the velocity: near the top of the key for the softest note, lower down for harder. A clicked note plays just like a note from your MIDI keyboard, so the layers' key ranges, the arpeggiator and everything else apply as usual.

Throughout the UI we label middle C (MIDI note 60) as C3. But some DAWs call that note C4.

## What the keyboard shows

The keys light up when you play, whether that's from your MIDI keyboard, your DAW, or a click, on any MIDI channel.

The red marks along the top of a key show the voices currently sounding on that note. A note can have more than one voice, such as one for each layer, and the mark gets stronger the more voices there are. Marks often linger after you let go, because each voice plays on through the release of its [volume envelope](/docs/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope).

If you've set a _Reset keyswitch_ in [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls), that key has a blue marker along its bottom edge. See [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility).

## Key range bars

When a layer is limited to part of the keyboard, the bars above the keys (3) show which keys trigger each layer, with a separate colour for each layer. Hover over them for an enlarged view that names each layer's Instrument. See [Key range display](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-range-display) for everything the bars show, and [Key ranges](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) for how to set ranges up.

---

# Layers Page

> How to build and shape sounds with Floe's three layers

![Floe's window with the LAYERS page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-layers.cf24954b099e9572.png)

Floe is built around three layers, each holding a sound of its own, playing together as one.

For each layer, you pick a sound source, its _Instrument_, then shape it further with envelopes, filters, an LFO, looping and more.

A sound can use a single layer or blend two or three together. The LAYERS page is where you control all aspects of these identical layers.

## How sound flows through the engine

When you play a note, all three layers play at once (unless a layer is limited to a [key range](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-ranges)). Each is processed on its own, then the three are mixed together and sent through the [effects rack](/docs/usage/effects) and the master volume. A layer with no Instrument is simply silent.

## The layer layout

![Floe's Layers page with the parts of a layer numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layers.b8bae924c810b253.png)1234

1.  **Layer header** — the layer's Instrument and its mixing controls, always visible.
2.  **Tabs** — switch between the layer's groups of controls: _PLAYBACK_, _MAIN_, _LFO_, _EQ_, _ARP_ and _CONFIG_. A dot on the _EQ_, _LFO_ or _ARP_ tab shows that it's switched on.
3.  **Tab controls** — the controls for the selected tab. Each tab has its own chapter. You can right-click these to copy, paste or reset all of its settings at once. It's a quick way to give two layers the same configuration.
4.  **All-layer buttons** — these act on all three layers together. loads a random Instrument into every layer, with each layer following its own Instrument browser filters (see [Randomisation](/docs/usage/randomisation)). clears every layer.

## Layer header

![A layer's header with its controls numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-top-controls.2543928912c17947.png)123456

1.  **Instrument selector** — shows the layer's Instrument. Click it to open the [Instrument browser](/docs/usage/browsers) and choose a different one. Right-click for more options: unload the Instrument, copy and paste the Instrument or the whole layer, or swap this layer with the one to its left or right (macro assignments move with a swapped layer).
2.  **Instrument navigation** — the arrows step to the previous or next Instrument, and jumps to a random one: a quick way to audition sounds without opening the browser. They follow the filters you've set in the Instrument browser, so they only move between the Instruments that match. unloads the Instrument, leaving the layer empty and silent.
3.  **Mute and Solo** — _Mute_ silences this layer, and _Solo_ lets you hear it on its own. Silenced layers keep running in the background, so if you unmute or unsolo them they carry on seamlessly from wherever they've got to. To save CPU, unload the Instrument instead. It's simplest to just use either Solo or Mute across the layers, not both — if you do mix them, Solo is prioritised over Mute.
4.  **Volume** — the layer's level, with its level meter alongside. While notes are sounding, red marks on the slider show the level of each voice. A voice's level depends on its velocity, where it falls in a [key range](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) fade, and any MPE volume expression.
5.  **Pan and Stereo** — _Pan_ places the layer anywhere from left to right. It uses a constant-power pan law (-3 dB at centre), so the layer keeps the same perceived loudness wherever you put it. _Stereo_ narrows or widens the layer: negative values pull it toward mono, positive values push it wider. Pan comes after Stereo, so you can narrow a wide sound and then place it as a single point. A mono sound has nothing to widen, so pushing it to maximum stereo width silences it.
6.  **Detune and Pitch** — _Pitch_ moves the layer up or down in semitones, and _Detune_ fine-tunes it in cents (hundredths of a semitone). Both work by speeding up or slowing down the audio. Right-click _Pitch_ to jump up or down an octave. Right-click _Detune_ and choose _Fold into Pitch_ to move any whole semitones from _Detune_ into _Pitch_, leaving the overall tuning unchanged. For a multi-sampled Instrument, _Transpose_ on the [CONFIG tab](/docs/usage/config-tab) may sound more natural.

See [Controls](/docs/usage/controls) for the ways to adjust knobs, sliders and number fields.

## The tabs

Below the header, each layer's controls are grouped into six tabs. Each has its own chapter:

-   [**PLAYBACK**](/docs/usage/playback-tab) — how the layer plays its samples: play mode, sample start, reverse, [granular synthesis](/docs/usage/playback-tab#granular-synthesis) and [looping](/docs/usage/playback-tab#looping).
-   [**MAIN**](/docs/usage/main-tab) — the [volume envelope](/docs/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope) and [filter](/docs/usage/main-tab#filter).
-   [**LFO**](/docs/usage/lfo-tab) — add movement to various aspects.
-   [**EQ**](/docs/usage/eq-tab) — a three-band equaliser to shape the layer's tone.
-   [**ARP**](/docs/usage/arp-tab) — the arpeggiator, which turns held notes into rhythmic patterns.
-   [**CONFIG**](/docs/usage/config-tab) — how the layer responds to your playing: transpose, pitch bend, keytracking, monophonic, MPE, [key ranges](/docs/usage/config-tab#key-ranges) and the velocity curve.

Right-click a tab to copy, paste or reset all of its settings at once. Copy a tab on one layer and paste it into another to give both layers the same settings, or reset a tab to start it afresh.

![The menu that opens when you right-click a layer's MAIN tab](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-tab-menu.43085b4dca75ff1e.png)

---

# LFO Tab

> Add movement to a layer by modulating its volume, filter, pan, pitch or grain position

Use the LFO (low frequency oscillator) to add movement to the sound, modulating one of the layer's controls such as its volume or filter cutoff.

![A layer's LFO tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-lfo.dee1730f34b4599a.png)1234

1.  **On/off** — switch the LFO on or off. A dot on the _LFO_ tab shows that it's on.
2.  **LFO display** — a live preview of the LFO's shape and speed. Drag it left and right to change _Time_, and up and down to change _Amount_.
3.  **Target, Shape and Mode**:
    -   **Target** — what the LFO moves: _Volume_, _Filter_, _Pan_, _Pitch_ or _Grain Position_. The movement happens around the target's current setting. Some targets need their feature switched on first: for example, the filter must be on for the _Filter_ target, and the play mode must be _Granular Fixed_ for _Grain Position_.
    -   **Shape** — the LFO's waveform. Alongside the classic shapes there are random and plucky ones.
    -   **Variation** — appears when a random shape (_Random Steps_ or _Random Glide_) is selected. It allows you to remove the element of chance from random movement. _Different on every note_ gives each note a fresh random pattern. _Identical on all notes_ plays exactly the same pattern every time, chosen by the **Seed** number: try a few until you find a movement you like. It's saved with the preset, so everyone hears the same movement. _Identical on each key_ gives each key its own repeatable pattern. In _Free_ mode, a note that joins already-sounding notes follows their pattern. The Seed works because the random steps follow a sequence of numbers that only looks random: the Seed is where that sequence starts. Learn more about seeds and reproducibility on the [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility) page.
    -   **Mode** — with _Retrigger_, every note starts the LFO from the beginning of its cycle. With _Free_, a new note joins in wherever the layer's sounding notes have reached, so all the notes move together.
4.  **Amount and Time**:
    -   **Amount** — how far the LFO moves its target. Negative values flip the shape upside down. If MPE press or slide is routed to the LFO amount (see the [CONFIG tab](/docs/usage/config-tab)), red marks show each voice's current amount.
    -   **Time** — how long each cycle lasts. With _Sync_ on, it's a note length at your DAW's tempo, such as 1/4; a D means dotted and a T means triplet. With _Sync_ off, it's a speed in Hz.
    -   **Sync** — tie the LFO to your DAW's tempo. Both the synced and free _Time_ settings are remembered, so you can switch between them without losing either.

---

# Macros

> Shape a sound with knobs that move several controls at once, and make your own

A macro is a knob that moves other controls for you. Floe has four of them, and each can be linked to up to six controls anywhere in Floe, each by its own amount.

![The four macro knobs in the bottom panel, each named for what it does in the preset](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/macros-play.33614f920333aa4e.png)

Preset authors use macros in two main ways. Sometimes a macro simply brings forward one control that matters a lot for this particular sound, tuned to a useful range, so you don't have to go looking for it. Other times it moves several controls together to create something that feels like a brand-new control made for the preset. A macro called _Surge_ might push up a distortion's drive, open a low-pass filter and thicken a granular texture, all with one turn.

Each macro has a name, chosen by whoever made the preset, that hints at what it does. Not every preset uses all four.

## Playing with macros

The macro knobs appear on the [_Perform_](/docs/usage/perform) page, and on the _PLAY_ tab of the bottom panel when you're on the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers) or [_Effects_](/docs/usage/effects) page. They're the same four knobs in both places. A greyed-out macro isn't linked to anything, so it does nothing.

Your MIDI keyboard's mod wheel is linked to the first macro, so you can shape the sound as you play. You can change this, and link the other macros to knobs or faders on your controller, in the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) panel. Macros are also handy for automation in your DAW: one lane can move several controls at once.

When a macro moves a knob, the knob's coloured arc separates from its dial. The dial shows the knob's own setting; the arc shows the value you actually hear. See [Controls](/docs/usage/controls).

## Making your own macros

Macros aren't only for preset authors. Once you're comfortable designing your own sounds, a macro or two can give your own presets a few expressive controls that shape the sound exactly the way you want, ready for your MIDI controller or DAW automation. The first macro is a good one to start with, since your mod wheel already moves it.

To set up macros, go to the _Layers_ or _Effects_ page and click the _MACROS_ tab on the left of the bottom panel. Each macro's knob is shown alongside its settings.

![The MACROS tab of the bottom panel, showing the first macro with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/macros.dda7e4e0ecfb2b8a.png)123

1.  **Destination knobs** — one blue knob for each control the macro is linked to, setting how far the macro moves it.
2.  **Add destination** — link another control to the macro.
3.  **Name** — click to rename the macro.

_Linking controls, setting their amounts, and renaming a macro_

### Linking a control

1.  **Click** next to the macro (2). Every control you can link to gets a blue plus icon of its own, across the whole window.
2.  **Hover** over one of them. A line joins it to the macro, with a note of what's about to be connected.
3.  **Click** to make the link. A new blue destination knob (1) appears next to the macro. To cancel instead, press `escape` or click somewhere empty.

You can link knobs, sliders and number fields. You can also link the handles you drag around, such as the points on the envelopes and the EQ graph, or the loop points on the waveform.

### Setting the amount

There are two kinds of knob here, and they do different jobs. The macro knob is the one you play: turning it moves every control linked to it at once. Each blue destination knob (1) is one you set and then leave alone: it decides how far the macro moves its one control, anywhere from a subtle nudge to a sweep across the control's whole range. A new link starts at zero, so the macro does nothing to that control until you change it.

The easiest way to set it is to turn the macro all the way up, then drag the destination knob while you play. Watch the linked control's coloured arc move, and listen until it sounds right.

-   **Right of centre** — the control goes up as the macro goes up.
-   **Left of centre** — the control goes down as the macro goes up.

The destination knob isn't linear: more of its travel is given to small amounts, so they're easier to set precisely.

Hover over a destination knob to see what it's linked to. It also shows the control's value right now, and what it will be with the macro at 0% and at 100%. Rest the cursor there for a moment and Floe draws a line to the linked control, scrolling it into view if needed.

Double-click a destination knob to type an amount, or right-click it for more options: copy and paste the amount between destinations, type a value, reset it to zero, invert it, or edit its range.

### Editing the range

Instead of setting an amount, you can set the two values the control moves between, in the control's own units: a filter sweeping from 200 Hz to 2 kHz, say. Right-click a destination knob and choose _Edit Range…_. The popup has two knobs:

-   **Macro at 0%** — the control's value when the macro is fully down.
-   **Macro at 100%** — the control's value when the macro is fully up.

Each knob changes only its own end, so you can raise the bottom of a filter sweep without changing where it ends up. While you hold either knob, you hear the sound as it would be with the macro at that end, though the macro itself doesn't move. Play some notes as you drag to find exactly the right values.

Changing an end also changes what you hear with the macro where it is now. To keep the current sound, tick _Move (macro name) to keep this value_: Floe moves the macro to whichever position gives the control the value it has now. Everything else the macro controls moves with it.

### How a macro moves a control

A macro moves a control relative to the control's own setting. With the macro at 0%, the control is exactly where you set it, and turning the macro up adds the amount on top. So adjusting the control itself shifts the whole sweep up or down.

If more than one macro is linked to the same control, their movements add together. A control can never go beyond its normal range, however far the macros push it.

### Removing a link

Hover over a destination knob and a red appears beneath it. Click it to remove the link. The control keeps its own setting; it just stops following the macro.

### Naming macros

Click the name (3) and type a new one. Choose a name that says what the macro does to the sound, such as _Brightness_ or _Swell_. The name is saved with the preset and labels the macro knob everywhere it appears.

### Copying, swapping and resetting

Right-click a macro knob for these options, alongside the usual ones for any knob:

-   **Copy Macro** and **Paste Macro** — copy a macro's value, name and links onto another macro.
-   **Swap with Left** and **Swap with Right** — exchange the macro with its neighbour, along with its value, name and links. This doesn't move MIDI CC assignments or DAW automation, though.
-   **Reset Macro to Default** — start the macro afresh, with no links and its original name. The next option resets it to how it was in the loaded preset instead.

### Legacy destinations

A yellow on a destination knob means it's linked to a [legacy parameter](/docs/reference/legacy-parameters). These are kept so older DAW projects still work, and you'll only hear the macro move it while the legacy override is active. Legacy destinations can't use _Edit Range…_.

---

# Main Tab

> Shape each note's volume and tone over time with a layer's volume envelope and filter

The _MAIN_ tab shapes how each note's volume and tone change over time, using the volume envelope and the filter.

![A layer's MAIN tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-main.86776d3fc54ab4a0.png)1234

1.  **Volume envelope** — its switch and graph.
2.  **Filter** — its switch and graph.
3.  **Filter controls** — _Type_, _Cut_, _Res_ and _Env_.
4.  **Filter envelope** — shapes how the cutoff moves over time.

## Volume envelope

-   **On/off** — the volume envelope is typically best left on. If you turn it off every note plays its sample straight through to the end, however briefly you press the key: handy for one-shot sounds that should always be heard in full. Looping is disabled while the envelope is off. And since notes can't be cut short, voices can pile up and use a lot of CPU if you play quickly.
-   **Envelope graph** — drag its three points to shape each note's volume over time: the first sets the _Attack_, the second the _Decay_ and _Sustain_ together, and the third the _Release_.

## Filter

Each note gets its own filter, so the filter envelope and the LFO can sweep every note independently. It's a clean, digital-sounding state-variable filter (12 dB per octave). For broader tone shaping, see the [EQ tab](/docs/usage/eq-tab).

-   **On/off** — switch the filter on or off.
-   **Filter graph** — shows the filter's response. Drag the point left and right to set the cutoff, and up and down for the resonance.
-   **Type** — choose the kind of filter, such as low-pass, high-pass or band-pass. Hover over the options in the menu for a description of each.
-   **Cut** — the cutoff frequency, where the filter takes effect. The filter envelope and LFO move the cutoff around this setting. If MPE press or slide is routed to the filter (see the [CONFIG tab](/docs/usage/config-tab)), red marks show each voice's current cutoff.
-   **Res** — resonance, which emphasises the frequencies around the cutoff. It never self-oscillates. For the band-pass, notch and band-shelving types it also narrows the band, and for the peak type it sets the size of the boost.
-   **Env** — how strongly the filter envelope moves the cutoff on each note. At the centre it does nothing. Turn it up and the cutoff rises and falls with the envelope; turn it down and the cutoff moves the opposite way. With a low-pass filter, for example, a long attack opens the sound up gradually as each note begins.
-   **Filter envelope** — works like the volume envelope, shaping how the cutoff moves over time, scaled by _Env_.

---

# MIDI

> Information about MIDI control in Floe

Floe responds to MIDI the way you'd expect from a software instrument: notes and velocity, the sustain pedal and pitch wheel, CC controllers mapped to its parameters, and MPE for expressive controllers.

-   **Velocity** — how hard you play sets each note's volume, shaped by each layer's [velocity to volume curve](/docs/usage/config-tab#velocity-to-volume-curve) on its _CONFIG_ tab. On multi-sampled Instruments with velocity layers, it also picks which samples play.
-   **Sustain pedal** — CC-64 holds notes after you release the keys, until you lift the pedal, just like a piano's sustain pedal.
-   **Pitch wheel** — how far it bends is set per layer with _Pitch Bend Range_ on the layer's [_CONFIG_ tab](/docs/usage/config-tab), so one layer can bend a whole tone while another underneath it stays put. A range of 0 disables pitch bend for that layer.
-   **All Notes Off and All Sound Off** — the channel messages that DAWs and controllers send to stop stuck notes. All Notes Off (CC-123) releases every note on that channel, including sustained ones, so they fade out naturally; All Sound Off (CC-120) silences them immediately.

## MIDI CC

All automatable parameters can be assigned to a MIDI CC, so you can move them with the knobs and faders on your MIDI controller.

### Creating a mapping

Right-click a parameter (a knob or slider anywhere on the UI) and select _MIDI CC Learn_, then move the dial on your MIDI controller that you want to assign. To remove a mapping, right-click the parameter and select _Remove MIDI CC_ (followed by the CC number). A mapped CC works on any MIDI channel.

You can also add and remove mappings from the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) panel, which lists every mapping on the current instance in one place.

![MIDI CC tab of the Performance Controls panel](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/midi-cc.2063ddce6cec1071.png)

### Default mappings

Unless you have changed your default Performance Controls, these mappings will be assigned:

-   **CC 1 (Modwheel)** — Macro 1
-   **CC 7** — Master Volume
-   **CC 11** — Master Timbre

### How mappings are saved

MIDI CC mappings are part of the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) system. They apply only to the current instance of Floe, but you can set up a default configuration that all new instances start with. Presets never touch them, so you can browse presets without your settings changing each time.

## MPE

MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE) lets compatible controllers, such as the Seaboard, LinnStrument, Osmose and Haken Continuum, shape each note independently.

To switch it on, open the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) panel with in the top panel, click the _MPE_ tab, and tick _MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression)_.

![The MPE tab of the Performance Controls panel](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/mpe.2d6bff66cf1a9aa7.png)

Once it's on, each note responds to the standard MPE per-note messages:

-   **Glide**: pitch bend on a note's channel bends just that note, following the MPE ±48-semitone convention (or whatever range your controller negotiates). The master channel's pitch wheel still bends everything, using each layer's pitch bend range parameter.
-   **Press**: each note's channel pressure (aftertouch).
-   **Slide**: each note's CC74.

Choose what press and slide control for each layer with the _MPE_ button on its [_CONFIG_ tab](/docs/usage/config-tab). Each has a target (_Volume_, _Filter_, _Timbre_ or _LFO Amount_) and an amount. The amount can be negative to invert the response, or beyond 100% to reach the full effect with a smaller gesture.

With the _Volume_ target, press brings each note up to the level of the layer's _Volume_ slider, and slide works like a fader for each note, topping out at the slider's level. So until you apply expression, notes play quieter than the slider. The _Filter_, _Timbre_ and _LFO Amount_ targets nudge a setting for each note individually: _Filter_ moves the layer's filter cutoff, _Timbre_ the master _Timbre_ control, and _LFO Amount_ the layer's LFO _Amount_. Press adds to the setting, while slide can move it either way, with its centre position leaving it unchanged.

The _MPE smoothing_ setting in the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) panel sets how gradually press and slide respond: lower is more responsive, higher is smoother.

While notes are sounding, each active voice gets a red line on whichever control press or slide is routed to — the filter cutoff knob, the LFO Amount knob, or the master Timbre knob in the top panel — so you can see the expression from each voice.

The MPE Configuration Message for zone setup is supported too, and a sustain pedal on a zone's master channel sustains the whole zone.

CLAP note expressions (per-note pitch, pressure, and brightness) work the same way in supporting hosts regardless of the MPE setting.

---

# Perform Page

> The distraction-free page for exploring presets and variations

![Floe's window with the PERFORM page tab highlighted](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/page-perform.2da3c92ed66c142e.png)

The _Perform_ page is a good place to start when you're getting to know a sample library and its presets. It shows the artwork in full, and gathers the controls you'll reach for most often into one uncluttered panel.

Most of the controls here also appear elsewhere in the interface. They're the same controls, so a change on one page shows up on the other.

When you're ready to go deeper, everything else can be found on the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers) and [_Effects_](/docs/usage/effects) pages.

![Floe's Perform page and top panel with their controls numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/perform.a40ff59a2509fcb3.png)12345678910

1.  **Preset box** — in the top panel. Click it to open the preset browser.
2.  **Preset** — the name of the current preset's sample library, with the preset's name beneath it. The arrows either side, and , step to the previous or next preset, just like the arrows in the top panel.
3.  **Folder** — the folder the preset lives in, which usually tells you what kind of sound it is.
4.  **Macros** — four knobs set up to shape this particular sound.
5.  **Layers** — the Instrument on each of the three layers, with its mute, solo and volume controls.
6.  **Random variation** — click the strip for a fresh take on the preset.
7.  **Compare** — switch between the preset as it was loaded and your changes.
8.  **Description** — more about the preset, from its author or written automatically by Floe.
9.  **Hide panel** — hides the panel so you can see the artwork in full. The arrow only appears when you hover just above the panel.
10.  **Keyboard** — lights up with the notes you play, and you can click it to play notes too. See [Keyboard](/docs/usage/keyboard).

## Choosing presets

The arrows (2) are the quickest way to audition presets: play a few notes, click an arrow, and play again. To look through them by folder or tag, click the preset name in the top panel (1) to open the preset browser. See [Loading Presets](/docs/presets/loading-presets) for more ways to find presets.

Once you change anything, the preset's name is marked _(modified)_.

## Macros

Use the macros (4) to shape the preset to your liking. Each one is tuned to move one or more settings in a musical way, and the knob's name hints at what it does. A greyed-out macro isn't used by the preset. By default, your mod wheel is linked to the first macro, so you can shape the sound as you play. See also [Macros](/docs/usage/macros) and [MIDI](/docs/usage/midi).

## Layers

Each preset is built from up to three layers (5). Not every preset uses all three. For each active layer you'll see:

-   **Instrument** — the name of the layer's Instrument, with the folder it comes from in italics. Click it to open the [Instrument browser](/docs/usage/browsers) and choose a different one.
-   **Waveform** — a picture of the Instrument's sound.
-   **Mute and Solo** — _M_ silences the layer, and _S_ lets you hear it on its own. Try each layer in turn to hear what it adds to the whole.
-   **Volume** — the slider sets the layer's level, with its level meter alongside.

For everything else a layer can do, switch to the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers) page.

## Random variation

Click anywhere on the _Random Variation_ strip (6) for a fresh take on the preset. Where you click sets how far it strays. Towards the left gives gentle, related tweaks; towards the right gets wilder, with Instruments swapped, layers added and effects changed. Hover over the strip to see how big a change you'll get. The button at its left edge rolls another variation at the same amount as last time.

Every variation starts from the preset as you loaded it, so you can keep clicking without drifting ever further away. _Undo_ in the top panel steps back through them. When you find one you like, save it as a preset to keep it. See [Randomisation](/docs/usage/randomisation).

## Compare

Once you've changed something, the _Original/Modified_ switch (7) lets you flick between the preset as it was last loaded or saved and your changed version. It's an easy way to check that your changes really are an improvement. If you edit anything while you're listening to the original, that edit replaces your modified version, but you can always get it back with _Undo_.

## Description

The description tells you about the preset, such as any unusual tuning or tips for playing it. The top panel shows its opening, usually a summary of the sound, and the rest continues here (8).

If the whole description fits in the top panel, Floe fills this space with a generated summary of the preset instead.

## Seeing the artwork in full

Hover just above the panel, in the middle, and a small arrow appears (9). Click it to hide the panel and see the artwork uncovered. Click the arrow again to bring the panel back.

---

# Performance Controls

> The Performance Controls panel — MIDI CC mappings, MPE, Reproducibility, and Profiles

The _Performance Controls_ panel is where you set up how Floe responds to your playing and your controllers. Open it with in the top panel, or from the main menu.

![The Performance Controls panel with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/performance-controls.2063ddce6cec1071.png)123

1.  **Profiles menu** — load and save profiles. It reads _Profiles_ until you load one, and then shows that profile's name.
2.  **Settings for new instances** — make this panel's settings the ones new instances start with.
3.  **Tabs**:
    -   **MIDI CC** — every [MIDI CC mapping](/docs/usage/midi#midi-cc) on this instance. Remove one with its button, or click _Add_ to create one by choosing a CC number and a parameter, as an alternative to right-clicking a knob and using _MIDI CC Learn_.
    -   **Reproducibility** — the _Seed_ and reset settings that make Floe's random elements play back the same every time. See [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility).
    -   **MPE** — switch on [MPE](/docs/usage/midi#mpe) for expressive controllers, and set how smoothly per-note expression responds.

## Scope

Everything in this panel belongs to the current instance rather than being a global preference. When you save your DAW project, these settings are saved with it, so the next time you open the project you can perform it the same way. Different instances in the same project can each have their own settings. However, loading a _preset_ leaves it untouched, meaning you can audition presets without disturbing your performance setup.

## Settings for new instances

Each Floe instance has its own performance controls, but you can choose what new instances start with: their MIDI CC mappings, MPE, and Reproducibility settings. Set the panel up the way you like, then click _Make default_ (2), just below the panel's title. The reset button beside it does the reverse, returning this instance to your defaults. Both only appear when the current settings differ from your defaults; otherwise a _Default for new instances_ label shows in their place.

For example, say your keyboard has a fader that you always want on the second macro. Assign it once with _MIDI CC Learn_, click _Make default_, and every new instance you add from then on starts with that fader ready to go. Instances already in your projects keep their own settings.

Floe's own defaults include some common MIDI CC mappings, such as the mod wheel (CC1) to the first macro. See [MIDI](/docs/usage/midi#default-mappings) for the full list.

## Profiles

A profile is a named, saved bundle of the panel's settings, like a save file for this Performance Controls. Profiles are useful when you switch between MIDI controllers regularly: save one profile per controller, then switch between them as you swap hardware.

Open the _Profiles_ menu (1) at the top-right of the panel to:

-   Load a profile, applying it to the current instance immediately. This is a one-shot copy, not a persistent link: further changes to the instance don't affect the saved profile unless you save over it.
-   Save the current settings as a new profile.
-   Overwrite, rename, or delete an existing profile.

Once a profile is loaded, the menu shows its name, with an asterisk when you've changed the settings since.

---

# Playback Tab

> How a layer plays its samples, including granular synthesis and looping

The _PLAYBACK_ tab controls how the layer plays its Instrument's samples: straight through, rebuilt into textures by the [granular engine](#granular-synthesis), or [looping](#looping) for as long as you hold a note.

![A layer's PLAYBACK tab with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-playback.306deb78b66d7fc2.png)12345

1.  **Play mode** — there are three modes:
    -   _Standard Playback_ plays each sample straight through (or [loops](#looping) part of it).
    -   _Granular Playback_ uses [granular synthesis](#granular-synthesis), with the point the grains come from moving through the sample at a speed you choose (and looping, if a loop is set).
    -   _Granular Fixed_ also uses granular synthesis, with the point the grains come from set directly by a _Position_ control rather than moving on its own.
2.  **Waveform display** — for a single-sample Instrument, this is the sample itself. A multi-sampled Instrument contains many samples, so this shows the one from the most recent note (or a representative one until you play). If notes change too quickly to follow, it pauses on a recent sample, shown with a checkered overlay. When you play, red markers track each voice through the sample. The waveform often has [looping](#looping) controls as well.
    -   **Sample start** — the arrow on the bottom edge of the waveform sets where playback begins. Drag it to skip the beginning of the sound; the skipped part is shaded. If you move it into the audio, a few milliseconds of _Attack_ on the [volume envelope](/docs/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope) avoids clicks. It isn't available for sliced Instruments.
3.  **Sample info** — shows whether the Instrument is a single sample or a multisample, with details such as the number of samples, or a single sample's length and root key.
4.  **Reverse** — play the samples backwards. It works in every play mode, with or without looping. The waveform flips to match, so playback always runs from left to right.
5.  **Loop mode** — choose how the sound loops, if at all. For example, you can use the Instrument's built-in loops, or set your own loop points on the waveform. Hover over the selector to see what the current setting does for this Instrument, and why some options may be unavailable.

Floe comes with a few simple built-in waveforms (oscillators). Many of the controls above don't apply to them, and so are hidden. Since they're algorithmic waveforms, the red voice markers are placed left to right by pitch instead of moving through a sample.

## Granular synthesis

As well as playing samples the usual way, from start to finish, each layer can switch to the granular engine. Granular synthesis plays lots of small snippets of the sample, called grains. Each grain can come from a different part of the sample, and play in a different direction, at a different pitch, or from a different place in the stereo field. It can completely transform a sample.

It's particularly good at smooth, lush textures. You can isolate a tiny fraction of a sample, such as one particular tonal moment, and hold it for as long as you like by running lots of grains over it. It's just as good at crackly, gritty textures, or at sparse ones where the grains are spread out so you can hear each one coming from a different point in the sample.

The granular engine works with any sampled Instrument. For each note, the grains come from the sample that note would normally play.

Granular synthesis uses randomness to keep the grains spontaneous and natural-sounding, rather than a mechanical, machine-gun-like repetition. Because of that, the sound can vary from note to note. When you want the same result every time, you have full control over that too: see [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility).

### The two granular modes

Choose a granular mode from the play mode menu at the top of the tab, where _Standard Playback_ is the usual way of playing samples.

-   **Granular Playback** — the point the grains come from travels through the sample at a steady speed, set by _Speed_. Use it to slow a sample down or speed it up without changing its pitch. It's not as precise as a dedicated time-stretching algorithm, but it gives a grainy or lush kind of time-stretch that's useful in its own right. Turn _Speed_ right down and the playhead barely moves, so a sample only a couple of seconds long can give you a whole minute of slowly changing texture. _Speed_ at 100%, the centre of the knob, is the sample's original speed, and the playhead still follows the sample start, looping and _Reverse_ settings.
-   **Granular Fixed** — instead of _Speed_ there's a _Position_ knob, which picks a precise point in the sample for all the grains to come from. _Spread_ sets how wide that region is.

Apart from _Speed_ and _Position_, the two modes have exactly the same controls.

### Getting started

Granular Fixed is perhaps the best place to start, because you can see and hear exactly what each control does.

![A layer's PLAYBACK tab in Granular Fixed mode with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/layer-playback-granular-fixed.2140192424972f7d.png)123456

1.  **Share grains** — how grains build up when you play several notes at once.
2.  **Variation** — take the element of chance out of the grains.
3.  **Waveform display** — shows where the grains come from.
4.  **Playhead** — where in the sample the grains come from.
5.  **Grains** — the shape of each grain, and how much they overlap.
6.  **Random** — how much each grain differs from the next.

Choose _Granular Fixed_ from the play mode menu, then use _Position_ to pick the point in the sample you want to isolate. The highlighted region on the waveform shows where grains will come from. Play some keys: all the sound you hear is coming from that exact point, and lilac lines on the waveform show each grain as it plays.

From there, try these controls:

![The PLAYHEAD and GRAINS controls](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/granular-controls.9551a5fa66a30bfb.png)

-   **Density** — perhaps the next most useful control. It works a bit like an overlap percentage: at 0%, each grain starts as the previous one ends. Turn it up and new grains start sooner, so they overlap more and more, up to 100% where there may be hundreds of grains playing. Low values give an open texture where you can pick out individual grains; high values build a thick, continuous wash. High _Density_ uses more CPU.
-   **Length** — how long each grain lasts. Short grains chop the sound into a fine, buzzy texture; long grains keep much more of the sample's natural character. _Density_ and _Smooth_ are both measured relative to _Length_, so changing it changes how they feel too.
-   **Smooth** — how gently each grain fades in and out. High values give a softer texture, with neighbouring grains blending into each other. Low values make grains start and stop abruptly, for a grittier, glitchier texture.
-   **Spread** — widens the region that grains can come from, which you can see straight away on the waveform: each grain starts somewhere between _Position_ and a point this far past it. A narrow spread gives an isolated, pinpoint tone. Spread it out completely and grains come from all over the sample, for a texture that's much more varied, unexpected and full of different tones.

### Random

The controls under the _RANDOM_ heading (6) make the texture even more varied. Each grain picks its own settings at random as it starts, within the range you set. At 0% every grain is the same.

![The RANDOM controls and the Intervals menu](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/granular-random.2567c6ef69428431.png)

-   **Pan** — the higher it goes, the more likely grains are to be panned left and right. Especially with a high _Density_, it gives a rich stereo image, with grains spread right across it.
-   **Detune** — sets each grain's pitch at random, up to a semitone up or down. Low values give a chorus or unison-like thickness; high values sound obviously out of tune.
-   **Direction** — the chance of each grain playing in the opposite direction, backwards if the playhead is going forwards. At 100%, each grain is equally likely to play either way.
-   **Harmony** — the chance of a grain playing at a musical interval from the note you played. It works with the _Intervals_ menu beside it, and does nothing until you've chosen at least one interval there. For example, click _12_ in the menu's grid and some grains will play 12 semitones (an octave) above your note; turn up _Harmony_ and more of them will. Click a selected interval again to turn it off. You can pick lots of intervals at once, or choose a preset such as _Wide Octaves_, _Major Triad_ or _Pentatonic_. The note you played is always included. It's a great way to make lush, interesting tones.

![The open Intervals menu, with presets on the left and the grid of intervals on the right](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/granular-harmony.7692588f84b54478.png)

### Share grains

The button just to the right of the mode's name, showing a cloud of dots (1), chooses how grains build up when you play several notes at once. Hover over it to see which way it's set. It's there for both granular modes.

-   **Shared grains** — the number of grains stays the same however many notes you play. If you're after a sparse texture, it stays sparse even when you play a whole chord. Each grain plays from one of the held notes, so at a low _Density_ you can hear the grains hop between the notes of the chord. This is the default setting.
-   **Per-voice grains** — every note you play adds its own full set of grains. If your _Density_ setting gives 20 overlapping grains, a second note adds another 20, so the sound gets denser, and possibly louder, with each note.

### Variation

![The Variation and Seed settings, open beneath the Variation button](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/granular-variation.865ff2e8cbd88c95.png)

Each grain picks its starting point, pan, detune and so on at random, so every note you play scatters its grains differently. That keeps a granular sound alive, but it also means a pattern of grains you love might not come back. _Variation_ lets you make the grains the same every time instead.

Click the button (2), to the right of the share grains button, and choose one of these:

-   **Different on every note** (default) — every note scatters its grains differently. The best choice for most sounds, especially dense, textural ones. Even in this mode, you can get reproducible renders of your DAW track, see [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility).
-   **Identical on all notes** — every note plays exactly the same grains. Hold a chord and each note plays them at its own pitch. With shared grains, the notes take turns, so you hear the same grains come back at different pitches.
-   **Identical on each key** — each key gets its own pattern of grains. C3 always sounds the same, D3 always sounds the same (but is different to C3), etc..

With either _Identical_ option, the _Seed_ number picks which pattern repeats. Try a few numbers until you find one you like. It's saved with the preset, so the grains you chose are the grains everyone hears. The button lights up while one of the _Identical_ options is chosen.

See [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility) for more on seeds, and on making a whole performance come out the same every time in your DAW.

### Granular tips

-   In _Granular Fixed_ mode, the point the grains come from only moves when _Position_ does. To make it wander through the sample on its own, set the [LFO's](/docs/usage/lfo-tab) target to _Grain Position_: the LFO sweeps _Position_ back and forth, so the texture keeps changing as you hold a note. Or link _Position_ to a [macro](/docs/usage/macros) to move it by hand as you play.
-   The volume envelope, filter, EQ and effects all shape the granular sound just as they would in _Standard Playback_.
-   When designing a sound, try _Identical on all notes_ with a low _Density_ and step through a few _Seed_ values. Once you hear a grain scatter you like, save the preset and it's kept exactly.

## Looping

You can loop part of a sample for as long as you hold a note. Even a short sample can then sustain indefinitely, or you can pick out a section that has some movement in it, so the sound cycles through it over and over. You have full control over where the loop sits and how smoothly it joins up.

Looping works in _Standard Playback_ and in the _Granular Playback_ [granular mode](#granular-synthesis).

![A layer's waveform and loop controls with their parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/looping.4f51878d98be7c61.png)123456

1.  **Loop start** — where the loop begins.
2.  **Loop end** — where the loop finishes, and playback goes back round.
3.  **Crossfade** — how smoothly the loop joins up.
4.  **Sample start** — where playback begins when you press a key. It isn't part of the loop, but it lives alongside it.
5.  **Reverse** — play the samples, and the loop, backwards. The loop end then appears on the left and the loop start on the right, though the loop points themselves don't change.
6.  **Loop mode** — how the sound loops, if at all.

### Loop modes

There are two modes of looping:

-   **Standard** — when playback reaches the loop end, it jumps back to the loop start, optionally smoothing the jump with a crossfade.
-   **Ping-pong** — uses the same start and end points, but at each end of the loop the playback direction reverses, so it goes back over what it just played, the other way.

Choose the loop mode from the selector (6). Which options are available depends on the Instrument. Some let you set your own loop points, some come with loops already built in, and some keep that control to themselves, such as sounds that are perfectly sustained or already loop.

![The loop mode menu](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/loop-mode-menu.96adc5ab47405221.png)

-   **Default** — let the Instrument decide: each sound loops, or doesn't, just as it was designed to. The menu shows what that means for the current Instrument.
-   **Built-in Loop - Standard** and **Built-in Loop - Ping-pong** — use the loop points that come built into the Instrument, looping in the direction you choose.
-   **No Loop** — each sound plays straight through.
-   **Custom Loop - Standard** and **Custom Loop - Ping-pong** — set your own loop points on the waveform.

Options that aren't available for the current Instrument are dimmed: hover over one to see why. Some Instruments have no built-in loops, for example, or don't allow custom loop points, or have sounds that must always loop. The selector itself shows what's actually happening, and hovering over it explains the current setting. The arrows beside it, and , step through only the options that are available.

### Setting your own loop

Choose one of the _Custom Loop_ modes, and the loop's handles appear on the waveform. Drag the loop start (1) and loop end (2) to set where the loop sits. The highlighted region between them is the part that loops. Drag inside the region to move the whole loop without changing its length.

The handles work like Floe's other [controls](/docs/usage/controls): double-click one to type an exact value, `shift`\-drag for finer control, and `ctrl`/`cmd`\-click to reset it. Double-clicking the highlighted region types a value for the loop start.

For a multi-sampled Instrument, the loop points are positions through the sample, as a percentage of its length. Whichever sample a note triggers, it loops between those same percentages.

With a built-in loop on an Instrument that has just one sample, the handles show where the loop sits, but they're greyed out and can't be moved. To set your own, choose one of the _Custom Loop_ modes.

### Crossfade

A loop can click as playback jumps from one point in the sample to another. The crossfade (3) blends the audio across the join to smooth it out. A small crossfade usually helps, especially for sustained or tonal sounds. Drag its handle to change it.

-   In _Standard_ mode, the crossfade happens as playback nears the loop end, blending into the audio just before the loop start. Its handle sits inside the loop.
-   In _Ping-pong_ mode, the crossfade smooths each turnaround, blending in the audio just beyond the loop point. Its handle sits outside the loop.

The crossfade needs audio before the loop start to blend in from, so it can't be used while the loop starts at the very beginning of the sample: its handle is greyed out until you move the loop start later. The crossfade also has to fit within the loop and the sample, so it shrinks automatically if you make the loop too small for it. In _Ping-pong_ mode, it also needs room after the loop end.

### Looping tips

-   Looping needs the [volume envelope](/docs/usage/main-tab#volume-envelope) to be on. With it off, nothing would ever bring a looping note to an end.
-   Pitch is changed by speeding up or slowing down playback. So the higher you play, the faster the loop cycles, and the lower you play, the slower. In _Granular Playback_ mode, the loop cycles at the rate set by _Speed_ instead.
-   In _Granular Fixed_ mode the grains always come from the _Position_ you choose, so there's no looping and the loop controls are hidden.
-   A loop can be moved by a [macro](/docs/usage/macros). The highlighted region then shows where the loop actually is, while the handles stay at their own settings.

-   Release samples, which some Instruments play when you let go of a key, never loop.

---

# Randomisation

> Use an element of chance to find sounds you might not have found yourself

Floe has a few features that bring in an element of chance. It's a way to find spontaneous inspiration, and sounds you might not have reached for yourself. They're also good fun.

As with anything left to chance, sometimes the results are great and sometimes they're a bit too wacky. The _Undo_ button in the top panel is always available.

All of these randomisation buttons use the same shuffle icon, so you can identify them at a glance.

## Random variation

The main random feature is the _Random Variation_ strip on the [_Perform_](/docs/usage/perform) page. It takes the preset you've loaded and changes some of its properties, giving you a fresh take on the sound.

![The Random Variation strip on the Perform page](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/perform-variation-strip.68e36d0f47412a76.png)

Click anywhere on the strip. Where you click sets how far the variation strays from the preset. Towards the left, the changes are mostly subtle and the sound keeps its character. Move towards the right to venture into wilder changes. As you hover, the strip shows the amount and a word for it, from _small variation_ to _extreme variation_.

The button at the left of the strip rolls another variation at the same amount as last time, so you can try several takes at an intensity you like.

Every variation starts from the preset as you loaded it, not from the previous variation, so you can keep clicking without drifting ever further away. When you find one you like, save it as a preset. That keeps it, and makes it the new starting point for further variations.

If nothing is loaded, the strip builds a random sound instead, around an Instrument picked at random.

### What a variation changes

A variation reworks the preset rather than starting from scratch, so it usually keeps something of the original's feel. Depending on how far right you click, it may:

-   **Swap Instruments** — each layer can get a different Instrument. Further left, the new one is usually a close relative, from the same library or folder or with similar tags. Further right, it can come from anywhere. With more than one layer in use, one is sometimes left as it is. Layers using a built-in waveform are never changed.
-   **Fill or empty layers** — an empty layer may get an Instrument, and occasionally a layer is cleared. Filling is much more likely than emptying, so wilder variations tend to add to the sound rather than thin it out. At least one layer always keeps an Instrument.
-   **Move the macros** — some of the preset's [macros](/docs/usage/macros) are turned by a noticeable amount, taking everything they control with them.
-   **Change the effects** — some effects' mix levels move, and a few effects are switched on or off. An effect that's switched on gets fresh settings, kept within sensible limits so it won't suddenly jump in level.
-   **Shift octaves** — now and then, a layer's _Transpose_ moves up or down an octave or two.

## Jumping to a random item in a browser

Wherever you can choose a preset, an Instrument or an impulse response, there's a button that jumps to a random one:

-   **Presets** — in the top panel, next to the preset name.
-   **Instruments** — in each layer's header on the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers#layer-header) page. It loads a random Instrument into that layer only.
-   **Impulse responses** — on the [Convolution Reverb](/docs/usage/effects#convolution-reverb) effect.

Each button is linked to its [browser](/docs/usage/browsers): it only picks from what that browser's filters allow, so you can set the bounds of what "random" means. Filter the preset browser to one library and a tag such as _ambient_, say, then keep clicking to jump around within that selection. The same goes for the browser's own button while it's open.

## Layers and effects

The button at the top right of the [_Layers_](/docs/usage/layers) page loads a random Instrument into all three layers at once, as if you'd clicked each layer's button in turn. Each layer has its own Instrument browser filters, so narrow the first layer to bass sounds and the second to textures, for example, then click it to roll through combinations that stay within those bounds.

The button at the top right of the [_Effects_](/docs/usage/effects) page randomly puts each effect in or takes it out of the rack, and shuffles their order. It leaves each effect's settings alone, so anything you've dialled in is still there when the effect comes back.

## Randomness in the sound itself

Parts of the audio engine, such as the [granular engine](/docs/usage/playback-tab#granular-synthesis), also use randomness while you play, to create varied, natural-sounding performances. See [Reproducibility](/docs/usage/reproducibility).

---

# Reproducibility

> How to make Floe's playback exactly reproducible in a DAW

Some features, most noticeably granular synthesis and the random LFO shapes, are designed around randomness to make the sound more natural and lively. Normally you don't need to worry about reproducibility: Floe's default setting, _Reset on transport_, covers most uses by making every render of your track in your DAW come out exactly the same. But sometimes those choices aren't quite what you want, such as grains landing in the wrong places or a random LFO moving the wrong way at a key moment. For that, Floe has _seed_ settings that let you take more control.

To understand what a seed does, it helps to know that Floe's randomness isn't truly random. It comes from a sequence of numbers that looks random. The sequence is so long that it never comes round again in practice, but it's fixed: from the same starting point, it always unfolds the same way. The seed is that starting point. So you keep all the spontaneity of random choices, but the same seed always gives the same choices.

Floe goes back to the start of the seed's sequence only at certain moments, called resets. You choose when they happen, and which seed to use, on the _Reproducibility_ tab of the [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls) panel:

![Reproducibility tab of the Performance Controls panel, with its settings numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/reproducibility.acda98d8ce410fef.png)123

1.  **Reset on transport** — reset whenever you press play or start a render in your DAW. Play your track from the top twice and you hear exactly the same thing both times. It's on by default.
2.  **Reset keyswitch** — reset whenever Floe receives the MIDI note you choose here. Put that note in your MIDI just before a section, and that section plays back identically every time, wherever you start playback from. The keyswitch note makes no sound, and it's shown as a blue marker on the on-screen keyboard.
3.  **Seed** — which sequence Floe starts from. Change it to hear a different take, just as lively as the last and just as repeatable.

You can use either kind of reset, or both.

The _Seed_ also covers these smaller sources of variation:

-   The arpeggiator's _Humanise_ and random note orders

-   Which round robin sample plays first after a reset

-   The _White Noise_ Instruments

## Workflow

The _Seed_ settings are a finishing step. You choose a seed once your MIDI is recorded and you're getting ready to render, rather than while you're improvising.

There's one _Seed_ for the whole instance of Floe, and every random choice Floe makes moves its sequence along. So each choice affects all the choices that come after it. That's why it's important to ensure that you play the exact same notes with the exact same timing. A saved MIDI item in your DAW ensures this.

### With _Reset on transport_

This is the default. Floe starts from the _Seed_ whenever you press play or render, so everything from that point on comes out the same every time.

To judge a seed properly, render the whole track again, or play it from the very start. It won't sound the same if you start playback in the middle of a MIDI item, or between MIDI items played by the same instance of Floe, because Floe needs to make all the same choices from start to finish, not starting in the middle.

So the workflow is:

1.  Render your track, or play it from the very start.
2.  If something isn't quite right, change the _Seed_.
3.  Render again and listen, repeating until you have a take you like.

If Floe only plays in one part of your track, you don't need to go right back to the start. Anywhere before Floe's first note works just as well, since Floe hasn't made any choices before then.

### With _Reset keyswitch_

A _Reset keyswitch_ lets you lock in a performance with more granularity. Floe starts again from the _Seed_ every time the keyswitch note plays, so everything after it comes out the same no matter where you started playback or what Floe played before. You can add several of these lock-in points through your track, allowing you to audition the section after each one by starting playback just before its keyswitch.

This also suits looping a section: put the keyswitch at the start of the loop. A DAW loop jumping back to its start doesn't count as pressing play, so without the keyswitch each pass carries on from where the last one left off.

The catch is that every keyswitch uses the same _Seed_. If you change the seed to get a better take of one section, every other section that follows a keyswitch changes too. If a seed suits one section of your track but not another, load a second instance of Floe for that section and give it its own seed.

### Per-layer seeds instead

The [granular engine](/docs/usage/playback-tab#variation) and the LFO's [random shapes](/docs/usage/lfo-tab) offer an alternative to all of this: a per-layer seed , saved with the preset. Rather than waiting for a reset, it applies every time a note starts, so each note gets its own sequence. Choose one of the _Identical_ modes and try a few _Seed_ values until you like the result. It then sounds exactly the same on any computer, in any instance of Floe, without needing any of the settings above. Unlike the instance's _Seed_, it's a sound-design setting you can choose at any time.

## Tips

-   Floe can't recapture a variation after the fact. If an improvised take sounds great, the random choices behind it are gone. Record the MIDI first, then try seeds against it.
-   Performance Controls settings belong to the instance, so loading a preset leaves them untouched: you can try out presets without losing your seed and reset setup.
-   When designing a granular sound, try _Identical on all notes_ with a low _Density_ and step through a few _Seed_ values.

---

# Top Panel and Main Menu

> The top panel's preset box, buttons, master controls and meters, and everything in the main menu

The top panel runs along the top of Floe's window and stays there on every page. It holds the things that apply to the whole sound rather than to one page: the current preset, undo and redo, the master controls and the output meters, along with the buttons that open Floe's other windows.

![Floe's top panel with its parts numbered](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/top-panel-overview.6c17c53c76feceb5.png)12345

1.  **Logo and version** — the version of Floe you're running. If you turn on _Show instance name_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences, this instance's [name](/docs/support/autosave#instance-names) appears after it.
2.  **Preset box** — the current preset's name and description, with buttons to step through presets, save, and load a preset from a file. Click the name to open the preset browser. See [The preset box](/docs/presets/loading-presets#the-preset-box).
3.  **Buttons** — Preferences, Performance Controls, undo and redo, and the main menu.
4.  **Timbre and Volume** — the master controls, which act on everything you hear.
5.  **Meters** — the level of the final output.

## Buttons

-   **Preferences** — settings for Floe itself rather than for your sound, such as how the interface looks and where your sounds and presets are installed. They're saved on your computer and apply to every instance of Floe.
-   **Performance Controls** — how you play Floe: mostly MIDI settings, plus options for making performances exactly reproducible. They're saved with this instance in your DAW project, and loading a preset never changes them. See [Performance Controls](/docs/usage/performance-controls).
-   **Undo** — step back through your changes to the sound, including tweaks to controls and loading Instruments or effects, so you can experiment freely. Hover over the button to see which change it will undo.
-   **Redo** — bring back a change you've just undone. If you make a new change instead, there's nothing left to redo.

-   **Attribution** — appears in red when a sound you've loaded comes from a library that asks to be credited. Click it for the exact text to use. See [Attribution](/docs/reference/attribution).

-   **Main menu** — more options, and Floe's other windows. A red dot on the button means a new version of Floe is available: see [Updating](/docs/installation/download-and-install-floe#updating).

## Master controls

-   **Volume** — the final stage of the sound. It comes after the [effects rack](/docs/usage/effects), so it sets the overall level of everything just before the audio leaves Floe.

-   **Timbre** — some Instruments are built with crossfade layers: variations of the same sound, such as soft to hard or dark to bright. _Timbre_ sweeps between them, so you can shape the tone. While you drag it, the Instruments that respond are highlighted. When none of the loaded Instruments have crossfade layers, the knob is greyed out. An MPE controller can move it for each note separately: see [MIDI](/docs/usage/midi#mpe).

## Meters

The peak meter (5) shows the level of the final output, measured after the master _Volume_. It flashes red if the signal clips above 0 dB.

There's also an optional loudness (LUFS) meter, mostly useful if you're making presets and want them to sit at a consistent level. Turn on _Show Loudness (LUFS) meter_ on the _General_ tab of Preferences, and hover over it for details.

## The main menu

Click , the last of the buttons (3), to open the main menu.

![Floe's main menu, open beneath its button in the top panel](https://assets.floe.audio/website/screenshots/main-menu.f549d251ee1a692d.png)

-   **Load Blank Preset** — return every setting to its default and clear all the Instruments and IRs, ready to build a sound from scratch. Remember, if you need it, _Undo_ brings back what you had.
-   **Panic (Stop All Sound)** — stop all audio and clear every playing note. Handy if a note gets stuck.
-   **Rescan Libraries & Presets** — Floe notices new and changed files in its folders by itself, but if something you've added doesn't show up, this makes it look through every folder again.
-   **Preferences** and **Performance Controls** — the same as the buttons in the top panel.
-   **Info** — the _Libraries_ tab shows what's installed and is where you can [uninstall](/docs/installation/uninstalling) it. The other tabs show your version of Floe and whether an update is available, the legal notices, and some metrics, such as how many voices are playing and how much memory the samples use.
-   **Share Feedback** — send a message to the developers, such as a bug report or an idea. See [Share feedback](/docs/support/error-reporting#share-feedback).
-   **Legacy Parameters** — controls kept from older versions of Floe so that projects made with them still sound the same. You only need this window if a control shows a yellow badge. See [Legacy Parameters](/docs/reference/legacy-parameters).
-   **Library Developer Tools** — tools for people making their own sample libraries for Floe. See [Library Development](/docs/develop/develop-libraries).

-   **Add Mirage Folders** — add the library and preset folders of Mirage, Floe's predecessor, if you had it installed. Not shown on Linux.

-   **Help** — open Floe's documentation website.
